title: CareGraph: An Auditable Hybrid AI Framework for Evidence-Grounded Personalized Longitudinal Health Intelligence
summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming personalized healthcare, yet fragmented clinical, self reported, and wearable evidence remains difficult to interpret and trace. We present CareGraph, an auditable hybrid AI framework that converts heterogeneous records into prioritized trends, missing context indicators, bounded next steps, discussion questions, and provenance linked explanations. CareGraph organizes evidence without diagnosing, predicting outcomes, selecting treatment, or making autonomous clinical decisions. Its pipeline covers deterministic analysis, context detection, graph construction, constrained language model synthesis, evidence validation, safety controls, and release gating. Tests used synthetic cohorts of 400 patients each for development, validation, and holdout. On holdout data, a frozen ordinary least squares trend rule with a sufficiency gate achieved 0.827 accuracy, 0.837 macro F1 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.819 to 0.854, and 0.974 insufficient data F1. Missing context detection achieved 0.815 strict micro F1 versus 0.318 for the legacy detector. On an authored holdout benchmark, safety ruleset version 1.2 achieved 1.000 precision, 0.950 recall, and 0.974 F1. An audit requiring graph retrieval across 80 patients yielded 79 syntheses and 78 presentations without fallback; one output was blocked and one failed closed because of an invalid evidence key. Against monolithic GPT 5.6 on 56 matched patients, CareGraph was faster at 40.15 versus 49.62 seconds, shorter at 661 versus 1,163 words, and showed better exploratory lexical alignment with longitudinal targets; the baseline used fewer tokens and cited more raw evidence. Graph auditing verified provenance and deterministic retrieval; incremental graph effects on generation require paired evaluation. CareGraph offers a safety bounded foundation for intelligent personalized health systems.

AI.tldr: CareGraph is an auditable hybrid AI framework that organizes heterogeneous health data into trends, missing context indicators, and bounded next steps with provenance-linked explanations, achieving high accuracy and safety in tests.
AI.motivation: Artificial intelligence is transforming personalized healthcare, but fragmented clinical, self-reported, and wearable evidence remains difficult to interpret and trace. There is a need for an auditable system that can convert heterogeneous health records into actionable insights while maintaining safety and transparency.
AI.method: CareGraph is an auditable hybrid AI framework that processes heterogeneous health records through a pipeline of deterministic analysis, context detection, graph construction, constrained language model synthesis, evidence validation, safety controls, and release gating. It organizes evidence without diagnosing, predicting outcomes, selecting treatment, or making autonomous clinical decisions. The framework was tested using synthetic cohorts of 400 patients each for development, validation, and holdout.
AI.result: On holdout data, CareGraph achieved 0.827 accuracy, 0.837 macro F1 (95% CI: 0.819–0.854), and 0.974 insufficient data F1. Missing context detection achieved 0.815 strict micro F1 versus 0.318 for legacy detector. Safety ruleset version 1.2 achieved 1.000 precision, 0.950 recall, and 0.974 F1. An audit across 80 patients yielded 79 syntheses and 78 presentations without fallback. Compared to monolithic GPT-5.6 on 56 matched patients, CareGraph was faster (40.15 vs 49.62 seconds), shorter (661 vs 1,163 words), and showed better exploratory lexical alignment with longitudinal targets.
AI.conclusion: CareGraph offers a safety-bounded foundation for intelligent personalized health systems, demonstrating that a hybrid AI framework can effectively organize and synthesize heterogeneous health data while maintaining auditability and safety controls.

title: FedEHR-Agents: Federated Agentic Optimization for Automated EHR Modeling
summary: Recent advances in large language models are enabling autonomous clinical agents to perform increasingly complex electronic health record (EHR) modeling workflows. However, agents deployed at individual hospitals remain constrained by institution-specific data and modeling environments, while direct cross-hospital collaboration is restricted by the sensitivity of patient-level EHR data. Although federated learning (FL) provides a natural foundation for privacy-preserving collaboration, existing approaches remain predominantly model-centric, limiting federation to prediction models or their updates while overlooking the richer modeling experience accumulated by autonomous agents. To address this limitation, we propose FedEHR-Agents, an experience-centric federated agentic optimization framework for automated EHR modeling. Each hospital deploys an autonomous clinical EHR agent that performs data preprocessing and model development while refining local clinical modeling experience through historical memory, task-specific evaluation, and TextGrad-based prompt refinement. The federated server performs evidence-guided experience aggregation to integrate reliable and complementary modeling experience across heterogeneous hospitals and distills the aggregated experience into global meta-prompts for subsequent local refinement. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-hospital EHR benchmarks demonstrate that FedEHR-Agents consistently outperforms local and federated baselines across diverse clinical prediction tasks and remains robust across different federation scales and LLM backbones. These results establish clinical modeling experience as a promising collaborative object beyond conventional parameter-centric FL and point toward federated autonomous clinical intelligence.

AI.tldr: FedEHR-Agents is an experience-centric federated agentic optimization framework for automated EHR modeling that enables autonomous clinical agents to share modeling experience across hospitals while preserving privacy, outperforming existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of existing federated learning approaches that are predominantly model-centric, limiting federation to prediction models or their updates while overlooking the richer modeling experience accumulated by autonomous agents in clinical EHR workflows.
AI.method: Each hospital deploys an autonomous clinical EHR agent that performs data preprocessing and model development while refining local clinical modeling experience through historical memory, task-specific evaluation, and TextGrad-based prompt refinement. The federated server performs evidence-guided experience aggregation to integrate reliable and complementary modeling experience across heterogeneous hospitals and distills the aggregated experience into global meta-prompts for subsequent local refinement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world multi-hospital EHR benchmarks demonstrate that FedEHR-Agents consistently outperforms local and federated baselines across diverse clinical prediction tasks and remains robust across different federation scales and LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: FedEHR-Agents establishes clinical modeling experience as a promising collaborative object beyond conventional parameter-centric federated learning, pointing toward federated autonomous clinical intelligence.

title: GOD: Govern, Observe, and Direct - A Real-Time Control Room for Agent Societies
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 System Demonstrations Track
summary: Generative-agent systems are easier to start than to inspect. A run can contain many agents, locations, messages, commands, and model calls, yet the operator often gets either a finished replay or raw logs. That makes it hard to ask why an agent moved, test a small intervention, or package a run for another researcher. GOD is a local-first control room for agent societies. From the same browser workflow, an operator can issue targeted questions or interventions and inspect the resulting replay state. The system combines a setup wizard, Agent Studio, Map Studio, a spatial replay interface, Ask and Intervene commands, and portable experiment, map, and agent packs. Its technical contribution is the command and artifact loop: live controls and replay evidence share the same operator command model, while package contracts separate scenario, map, and profile data from local runtime state. The public release includes hosted Smallville-style and PKU replays, the open-source repository, and downloadable packs. We evaluate this path on 15 completed run slots. Across the 14 intervention runs, 78 of 84 target-agent checks recorded the commanded destination, and 169 of 182 state answers matched a saved location or action string.

AI.tldr: GOD is a local-first control room for inspecting and intervening in generative agent societies, addressing the difficulty of analyzing complex agent runs by providing targeted questioning, interventions, and portable packaging.
AI.motivation: Generative-agent systems are easier to start than to inspect. A run can contain many agents, locations, messages, commands, and model calls, yet the operator often gets either a finished replay or raw logs. That makes it hard to ask why an agent moved, test a small intervention, or package a run for another researcher.
AI.method: The system combines a setup wizard, Agent Studio, Map Studio, a spatial replay interface, Ask and Intervene commands, and portable experiment, map, and agent packs. Its technical contribution is the command and artifact loop: live controls and replay evidence share the same operator command model, while package contracts separate scenario, map, and profile data from local runtime state.
AI.result: Across the 14 intervention runs, 78 of 84 target-agent checks recorded the commanded destination, and 169 of 182 state answers matched a saved location or action string.
AI.conclusion: GOD provides a practical and effective local-first control room for inspecting and intervening in generative agent societies, with strong evaluation results demonstrating its reliability in targeted interventions.

title: Prove2Me: An Open Collaborative Platform for Scaling Math Formalization
summary:
Proof assistants such as Lean 4 promise the paradigm of formally verified mathematics, but large-scale formalization projects have faced major barriers to entry, including the need for expertise in formal verification (as well as the underlying mathematics) and the significant time required for writing formal proofs. AI coding agents have dramatically reduced these barriers; human users can now use natural language to prompt agents to write complex proofs in Lean. This opens up the intriguing possibility of internet-scale mathematical collaboration involving both humans and AI agents, where correctness is machine-checked.
  To realize this possibility, we introduce Prove2Me (https://prove2.me), an open collaborative platform for formalizing mathematics. Users launch formalization "missions", to which AI agents contribute formal proofs toward completion. We designed mechanisms and a specialized harness in Prove2Me that enable large-scale collaboration so that agents can build on one another's work and freely reuse existing results. In doing so, Prove2Me aims to turn math formalization into a scalable, crowd-sourced effort open to anyone with an agent.

AI.tldr: Prove2Me is an open collaborative platform that uses AI agents to help formalize mathematics in Lean 4, making large-scale formal verification accessible through crowd-sourcing and AI assistance.
AI.motivation: Traditional formal verification in mathematics has high barriers: requires specialized expertise in both mathematics and formal verification tools like Lean 4, and takes significant time. AI coding agents can now write complex proofs using natural language, opening opportunities for scalable collaboration.
AI.method: Created Prove2Me platform where users launch formalization "missions". AI agents contribute formal proofs using a specialized harness and mechanisms that enable large-scale collaboration, allowing agents to build on each other's work and reuse existing results.
AI.result: Prove2Me platform was developed as an open collaborative platform (prove2.me) that transforms math formalization into a scalable, crowd-sourced effort accessible to anyone with an AI agent.
AI.conclusion: The platform enables internet-scale mathematical collaboration between humans and AI agents with machine-checked correctness, potentially revolutionizing how mathematics is formalized and verified.

title: Time Capsule of Testable Human Knowledge: 41 Years of Jeopardy! in a Single Free Local Model
summary: In 2011, IBM's Watson was something like a sealed capsule of its era's queryable knowledge. Its DeepQA system defeated the strongest human Jeopardy! champions, but the knowledge that let it do so lived in a curated billion-document corpus running on a cluster of POWER7 servers, frozen at build time and impossible to move or copy. We show that the same kind of artifact, a snapshot of what a culture can answer, is now portable and essentially free. We evaluate a single 9 GB open-weight model (Qwen2.5-14B, 4-bit) against the complete open Jeopardy! clue dataset, 529,939 clues across all 41 broadcast seasons from 1984 to 2025. To our knowledge this is the first time a model has been run over the full corpus. The 41 years mark only how long the questions were collected. What they test is far older and broader: the accumulated body of human general knowledge a culture considers worth knowing, from ancient history and dead languages to science, literature, and geography, with a verified answer for every item. The model answers 67.0% of all clues under a strict forced-response protocol with exact and fuzzy matching, and exceeds 85% on factoid categories. We treat training-data exposure as something both systems share rather than a flaw unique to language models. Watson's case is in fact the more extreme one. Its corpus was assembled to contain Jeopardy answers and it was tuned on past clues, and it could not answer anything outside that curated distribution. The decisive test is whether a model can answer clues that did not exist when it was built. On clues aired after its training cutoff, the local model holds 65% and Claude Opus 4.8 holds 95%, while Watson by construction scores zero. The capability survives the move from a server room to a file you could seal in a time capsule, and unlike Watson it is not frozen to its own moment.

AI.tldr: A single 9GB open-weight LLM (Qwen2.5-14B) achieves 67% accuracy on the full Jeopardy! dataset spanning 1984-2025, showing portable, inexpensive knowledge that can answer new questions unlike IBM's Watson which was frozen at build time.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate how modern language models have made portable, accessible knowledge systems that overcome the limitations of IBM's Watson, which required curated corpora on server clusters and couldn't answer questions about events after its build time.
AI.method: Evaluated a 4-bit quantized Qwen2.5-14B model against the complete open Jeopardy! clue dataset (529,939 clues across 41 seasons, 1984-2025). Used strict forced-response protocol with exact and fuzzy matching, comparing to IBM's Watson and testing on post-training-cutoff clues.
AI.result: Model achieved 67.0% accuracy overall and over 85% on factoid categories. On clues aired after training cutoff: local model 65%, Claude Opus 4.8 95%, Watson 0%. Shows capability survives compression to a single portable file unlike Watson's server-room system.
AI.conclusion: Modern language models represent a fundamental shift: portable, inexpensive knowledge systems that can answer questions about future events, unlike the frozen-in-time systems like IBM's Watson that were bound to their build-time knowledge.

title: Marginal Coverage Credit Reduces Redundant Exploration in Parallel State-Entropy Optimization
summary: Policy Gradient for Parallel State Entropy maximization (PGPSE) expands state-space coverage by training independently parameterized policies in replicated copies of the same environment. However, its pooled team-entropy score measures only collective exploration and cannot identify policies that contribute non-redundant coverage. We introduce Marginal Coverage Credit for PGPSE (MCC-PGPSE), which combines leave-one-policy-out coverage with state-owner specialization to estimate policy-specific credit. MCC-PGPSE preserves PGPSE's pooled objective and redistributes non-negative auxiliary intrinsic rewards according to these credits without changing their total mass. This redistribution is designed to discourage redundant visitation and promote complementary coverage. We evaluated MCC-PGPSE in controlled environments, seven public discrete-state benchmarks, and representative Room and Maze settings from the original PGPSE protocol. Across all tested settings, MCC-PGPSE produced positive final window gains in normalized team state entropy and state support over the Entropy baseline. Controlled-task comparisons and the fixed-suite public aggregate were significant, whereas five-seed original-protocol comparisons were directionally consistent. Ablations and credit alignment controls indicate that most gains arise from leave-one-policy-out coverage rather than non-uniform weighting, mismatched credit, or neural novelty alone. These results support contribution-conditioned auxiliary reward allocation as an interpretable approach to improving complementary coverage among parallel policies in discrete state spaces.

AI.tldr: MCC-PGPSE improves on PGPSE by using marginal coverage credit and state-owner specialization to redistribute intrinsic rewards, reducing redundant visitation and promoting complementary exploration among parallel policies.
AI.motivation: PGPSE's pooled team-entropy score cannot identify which policies contribute non-redundant coverage, leading to inefficient exploration where multiple policies may cover the same states without complementary exploration.
AI.method: Introduces Marginal Coverage Credit for PGPSE (MCC-PGPSE), which combines leave-one-policy-out coverage estimation with state-owner specialization. It preserves PGPSE's pooled objective while redistributing non-negative auxiliary intrinsic rewards based on policy-specific credits that measure marginal contributions to exploration.
AI.result: MCC-PGPSE achieved positive gains in normalized team state entropy and state support across all tested settings (controlled environments, seven public discrete-state benchmarks, Room and Maze settings). Results showed significant improvements in controlled tasks and fixed-suite aggregates, with directional consistency in original-protocol comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Contribution-conditioned auxiliary reward allocation via MCC-PGPSE is an effective, interpretable approach for improving complementary coverage among parallel policies in discrete state spaces, with most benefits coming from the leave-one-policy-out coverage mechanism rather than other factors like neural novelty.

title: Logos: An Agent Harness on a Cross-Process Bus
summary: Modern agent systems assemble capabilities at runtime, and this dynamic composition has recently received a complete formal treat ment in the spatiotemporal-composability calculus, in which a capability is a component carrying a tracked inverse, and agents are assembled as plugins. This plugin form is carried by a single process sharing one context, a carrier that places all components in one physical failure domain, a fault suspends every component at once, and process death interrupts every session the process hosts. This paper shows that neither the modeling nor the calculus binds an agent to one process, the statelessness of the language model keeps all cross-step state outside the model, and the soundness invariant is defined on the state space alone. These observations condense into four lemmas whose premises are the hypotheses of the calculus and the statelessness of language-model inference. On these lemmas this paper constructs Logos, a ROS-like cross process agent harness in which a plugin is a process and the only shared state is an append-only transcript. Eighty sessions resume with no repeated effect after kills placed at the four boundaries of the tool-call cycle, and a same-fault comparison with a single process reference configuration shows one fault interrupting every co-resident session while under the peer-process construction one fault ends at one node.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Logos, a ROS-like cross-process agent harness where plugins are processes and the only shared state is an append-only transcript, enabling fault isolation across processes rather than having all components fail together in a single process.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from limitations in current agent systems where dynamic composition binds all components to a single process, creating a single physical failure domain where one fault suspends every component at once. This paper shows that neither the modeling nor the calculus of spatiotemporal-composability requires agents to be bound to one process.
AI.method: The method involves constructing Logos based on four lemmas derived from the hypotheses of the spatiotemporal-composability calculus and the statelessness of language-model inference. Logos is a ROS-like cross-process agent harness where each plugin is a separate process, and the only shared state is an append-only transcript.
AI.result: Eighty sessions successfully resumed with no repeated effects after kills placed at the four boundaries of the tool-call cycle. A same-fault comparison with a single process reference configuration showed that one fault interrupts every co-resident session in the single-process setup, while under the peer-process construction, one fault ends at only one node.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that agent systems can be architected across multiple processes rather than being confined to single processes, enabling better fault isolation. The Logos system successfully isolates faults to individual processes while maintaining session resumability, proving the feasibility and advantages of cross-process agent architectures.

title: Rating the Raters: Rasch Measurement Theory for LLM Evaluation
summary: LLMs now sit on every side of evaluation: as examinees scored on benchmarks, judges of other models' outputs, and raters of human-generated content. Each paradigm can be viewed as a measurement problem, where a latent property of an object is probed with items from an instrument (e.g., benchmark) by raters. Standard evaluation practices often neglect the contributions of each core component to the end result, limiting our understanding of what is being measured. Rasch measurement theory (RMT) is well-suited to this kind of problem. RMT decomposes ordinal ratings into separable facets on a common scale. It further provides a battery of diagnostics that can identify miscalibrated measurements and rater biases. We present a case study of RMT applied to the LLM-as-rater paradigm using the Measuring Hate Speech corpus, whose construct was itself built under RMT. We fit a series of many-facet Rasch models to annotations from nine LLMs spanning families and capability levels. Our analyses show that LLMs systematically differ from human raters in severity, item-level calibration, question-order robustness, target-identity sensitivity, and rating scale use, which all would be obscured by standard evaluation practice. Overall, we argue that RMT belongs in the toolkit for evaluating LLM-as-examinee, -judge, and -rater paradigms.

AI.tldr: The paper argues for using Rasch measurement theory (RMT) to better understand LLM evaluation by decomposing ratings into separate facets, revealing systematic biases that standard methods miss.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM evaluation practices neglect the contributions of different components (benchmarks, raters, examinees) in measurement, limiting understanding of what's actually being measured. LLMs are involved in all aspects: as examinees, judges, and raters.
AI.method: Applied Rasch measurement theory (RMT) to decompose ordinal ratings into separable facets on a common scale. Conducted a case study on the LLM-as-rater paradigm using the Measuring Hate Speech corpus. Fit many-facet Rasch models to annotations from nine LLMs across different families and capability levels.
AI.result: Found systematic differences between LLM and human raters in: severity, item-level calibration, question-order robustness, target-identity sensitivity, and rating scale use. These differences would be obscured by standard evaluation practices.
AI.conclusion: Rasch measurement theory should be included in the evaluation toolkit for all LLM paradigms (as-examinee, -judge, -rater) to provide better diagnostics and understanding of measurement quality.

title: Quantization-Triggered Backdoors in Language Models: Cross-Quantizer Transferability and the Validation--Deployment Gap
comment: Accepted at the 21st International Conference on Availability, Reliability and Security (ARES 2026)
summary: Post-training quantization is often treated as a semantically neutral optimization for edge deployment of Large Language Models. When a full-precision source checkpoint is evaluated and quantization is applied downstream without equivalent re-evaluation, this workflow creates a structural validation--deployment gap: because quantization is a many-to-one mapping over parameter space, source-precision certification does not guarantee behavioral equivalence in the deployed configuration. We formalize this gap through Quantization Behavioral Equivalence Classes (QBECs) and prove that QBEC membership does not imply behavioral equivalence, providing a theoretical basis for quantization-triggered backdoor attacks. Building on a three-stage adversarial fine-tuning framework, we embed latent malicious payloads into models that satisfy the source-precision checks used in our evaluation, yet activate targeted adversarial behavior upon INT8 or 4-bit compression. We evaluate this threat in two operationally motivated scenarios, tactical machine translation and political content analysis, extending prior work from decoder-only causal LMs to multilingual encoder-decoder sequence-to-sequence models. Results show that backdoored translation models move from zero measured friend--foe corruption at repaired FP16 to up to 85.02% inversion after quantization, and that a paired stance classifier measures an ideological shift of up to $Δ\mathrm{Bias}=0.33$ upon compression. A cross-quantizer transferability analysis further shows that attack persistence varies across quantization schemes and model architectures, rather than being determined by nominal bit-width alone. These findings demonstrate that source-precision auditing alone does not rule out quantization-triggered behavior and that the final deployed configuration must be included in behavioral certification for trustworthy edge AI.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that post-training quantization can trigger hidden backdoor attacks in LLMs, as source-precision evaluation doesn't guarantee behavioral equivalence after compression, demonstrating attacks that activate only when models are quantized.
AI.motivation: The authors identify a structural validation-deployment gap where quantization (a many-to-one mapping) can change model behavior even when source checkpoints pass certification, creating a vulnerability for quantization-triggered attacks.
AI.method: They formalize Quantization Behavioral Equivalence Classes (QBECs), prove QBEC membership doesn't guarantee behavioral equivalence, and develop a three-stage adversarial fine-tuning framework to embed latent malicious payloads that activate only upon INT8 or 4-bit compression.
AI.result: Backdoored translation models show 0% corruption at FP16 but up to 85.02% inversion after quantization. Political content classifiers exhibit ideological shifts up to ΔBias=0.33. Attack persistence varies across quantization schemes and architectures, not just bit-width.
AI.conclusion: Source-precision auditing alone is insufficient; final deployed configurations must be included in behavioral certification for trustworthy edge AI, as quantization can trigger hidden adversarial behaviors.

title: Not All Explanations Are Sought: Information-Seeking Psychology for Human-Centered XAI
comment: Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Human-Centered Explainable AI (HCXAI), CHI 2026
summary: This position paper argues that human-centered explainable AI (HCXAI) should incorporate insights from the psychology of information seeking. Drawing on Sharot and Sunstein's framework of information-seeking motives, we propose that people evaluate whether to engage with explanations based on three types of expected utility: instrumental (will it help me act better?), hedonic (will it make me feel better?), and cognitive (will it improve my understanding?). Each utility is estimated through a lens shaped by well-documented cognitive biases, including illusion of control, automation bias, unrealistic optimism, impact bias, overconfidence, and confirmation bias. These biases can lead to two failure modes: excessive information-seeking that fragments attention without improving decisions, and insufficient information-seeking that leaves critical risks and misunderstandings unexamined. This challenge is particularly acute for agentic AI systems, where explanations must support not just understanding a single output but anticipating cascading actions, assessing risks, and deciding when to intervene. By integrating information-seeking psychology into HCXAI, we advocate for a shift from making explanations available to making them sought: designing systems that account for when and why users actually want to know.

AI.tldr: HCXAI should integrate psychology of information seeking, analyzing how users decide to engage with explanations based on instrumental, hedonic, and cognitive utilities, filtered through cognitive biases that can cause both excessive or insufficient information seeking.
AI.motivation: Current human-centered explainable AI lacks insights from information-seeking psychology. Users' decisions to engage with explanations are influenced by cognitive biases, leading to inappropriate information-seeking behaviors that can undermine AI system effectiveness, especially for agentic AI systems with cascading actions and risks.
AI.method: Proposes using Sharot and Sunstein's framework of information-seeking motives to analyze explanation engagement through three types of expected utility: instrumental (action improvement), hedonic (emotional benefit), and cognitive (understanding). Identifies how cognitive biases (illusion of control, automation bias, unrealistic optimism, impact bias, overconfidence, confirmation bias) affect these utility assessments.
AI.result: Identifies two failure modes: excessive information-seeking that fragments attention without improving decisions, and insufficient information-seeking that leaves critical risks and misunderstandings unexamined. These challenges are especially critical for agentic AI systems requiring anticipation of cascading actions and risk assessment.
AI.conclusion: HCXAI should shift from simply making explanations available to making them sought by designing systems that account for when and why users actually want explanations, integrating insights from information-seeking psychology to address cognitive biases and optimize explanation engagement.

title: DAMP: Decay-Aware Mixed-Precision Recurrent-State Quantization
summary: Softmax attention stores key and value vectors for every preceding token, causing inference memory to grow with sequence length. Recent language models incorporating Gated DeltaNet (GDN) or Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) reduce this cost by replacing the KV cache in most layers with fixed-size recurrent states. However, these recurrent states are commonly stored in FP32 and consume substantial GPU memory; their updates are memory-bandwidth bound and contribute significantly to decoding latency. To our knowledge, we are the first to study post-training quantization of recurrent states in GDN and KDA based language models. We find that uniform quantization provides a poor accuracy--storage trade-off: INT8 and FP8 already degrade accuracy on complex reasoning tasks, while INT4 and NVFP4 reduce it to near zero. We further find that most quantization-error energy is concentrated in a small subset of channels and that the relative decay strength of state channels remains stable across prompts and tasks. Motivated by these findings, DAMP uses both quantization-error energy and decay-based persistence to identify high-risk channels during offline calibration. It stores these channels at higher precision and the remainder in INT8. We evaluate DAMP on Qwen3.6-35B and Kimi-Linear-48B across six benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, general reasoning, and code generation. At 9.9 bits per state value, DAMP maintains average accuracy close to the FP32 baseline. DAMP reduces recurrent-state storage by 69.1%, accelerates the recurrent-state update kernel by up to 2.01x, and lowers full-model TPOT by up to 10.9%.

AI.tldr: DAMP introduces a quantization technique for recurrent states in Gated DeltaNet/Kimi Delta Attention models that identifies high-risk channels and stores them at higher precision while quantizing the rest to INT8, achieving 69.1% storage reduction with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Recurrent states in GDN/KDA models are stored in FP32 and consume substantial GPU memory, causing memory bandwidth bottlenecks and significant decoding latency. Current quantization methods provide poor accuracy-storage trade-offs, degrading performance on complex reasoning tasks.
AI.method: DAMP analyzes quantization-error energy and decay-based persistence to identify high-risk channels during offline calibration. It stores these critical channels at higher precision while quantizing remaining channels to INT8, using both energy concentration and stable decay patterns across tasks.
AI.result: At 9.9 bits per state value, DAMP maintains average accuracy close to FP32 baselines across six benchmarks (mathematical reasoning, general reasoning, code generation). Achieves 69.1% recurrent-state storage reduction, up to 2.01x kernel acceleration, and up to 10.9% TPOT improvement.
AI.conclusion: DAMP provides an effective solution for quantizing recurrent states in GDN/KDA models by intelligently allocating precision to high-risk channels, achieving significant memory and latency improvements while preserving accuracy on complex reasoning tasks.

title: Retrieving Relations, Detecting Fallacies: A RAG Approach to Political Debate Analysis
summary: Fallacies are arguments that employ invalid reasoning, making their automatic detection critical in sensitive contexts such as high-stakes political debates, where public opinion is shaped. Spotting a fallacious argument requires contextual knowledge beyond its pure surface text. This entails world knowledge pertaining to the subject matter under discussion, as well as knowledge of the relationships that exist between arguments within the argumentative discourse. Prior work on fallacy analysis has shown that argumentative discourse structure can beneficially improve classification performance. However, such structure is typically encoded only as static classifier features, limiting its flexibility. Building on this intuition while addressing this limitation, we introduce a guided retrieval-augmented methodology for fallacy detection and classification that leverages argumentative relations of support and attack to dynamically steer the extraction of relevant documents. We evaluate our approach on the ElecDeb60to20 benchmark across 42 retrieval configurations and 14 models, performing retrieval over a 15GB knowledge base of collected political-related documents. Our approach improves macro-F1 up to 0.864 for fallacy detection and up to 0.725 for classification over non-retrieval baselines. These results show that incorporating external knowledge significantly enhances fallacy detection and classification when retrieval is argumentatively guided.

AI.tldr: A novel retrieval-augmented methodology for fallacy detection that uses argumentative relations (support/attack) to dynamically guide document retrieval from a large knowledge base, significantly improving performance over non-retrieval baselines.
AI.motivation: Automatic fallacy detection is critical in sensitive contexts like political debates where public opinion is shaped. Current approaches have limitations: they require contextual knowledge beyond surface text (world knowledge and argumentative relationships), and prior work encodes argumentative structure only as static classifier features, limiting flexibility.
AI.method: Introduced a guided retrieval-augmented methodology for fallacy detection/classification that leverages argumentative relations (support and attack) to dynamically steer extraction of relevant documents. Used 42 retrieval configurations and 14 models, performing retrieval over a 15GB knowledge base of political documents on the ElecDeb60to20 benchmark.
AI.result: Improved macro-F1 up to 0.864 for fallacy detection and up to 0.725 for classification over non-retrieval baselines. The approach demonstrates that incorporating external knowledge significantly enhances fallacy detection and classification when retrieval is argumentatively guided.
AI.conclusion: Argumentatively-guided retrieval of external knowledge substantially improves fallacy detection and classification performance compared to static feature approaches, showing the importance of dynamic, context-aware knowledge extraction in complex argumentation analysis.

title: A Deeper Analysis of Block-Sparse Featurizers
summary: The recently introduced block-sparse featurizer (BSF; Fel et al., 2026) is similar to a sparse autoencoder (SAE), but its atomic unit is a small subspace (a block of directions) rather than a single direction. It is designed for features that live on low-dimensional manifolds, which are especially frequent in vision. This work studies the BSF's strengths and weaknesses, finding how it still somewhat suffers from classic SAE failure modes, like feature splitting and composition. We propose several architectural changes to the BSF, including a Tournament Top-K selection rule that significantly reduces feature splitting, and we also extend the block paradigm to the crosscoder.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes block-sparse featurizers (BSF), identifies problems with feature splitting and composition similar to sparse autoencoders, and proposes architectural improvements including a Tournament Top-K selection rule.
AI.motivation: The recently introduced BSF operates on small subspaces rather than single directions, which is designed for features that live on low-dimensional manifolds common in vision. The authors want to study its strengths and weaknesses, particularly addressing classic SAE failure modes that still persist in BSFs.
AI.method: The paper studies BSF's performance and identifies issues with feature splitting and composition. The authors propose several architectural changes to the BSF, including a novel Tournament Top-K selection rule, and extend the block paradigm to the crosscoder component.
AI.result: The proposed Tournament Top-K selection rule significantly reduces feature splitting in BSFs. The architectural improvements enhance BSF performance by addressing classic SAE failure modes while maintaining the benefits of the block-based approach.
AI.conclusion: While BSFs offer advantages for vision tasks with low-dimensional manifold features, they still suffer from traditional SAE problems. The proposed architectural modifications, particularly the Tournament Top-K rule, effectively mitigate feature splitting and improve overall featurizer performance.

title: LLM-Augmented Causal Discovery: Probabilistic Fusion of Edge Existence and Orientation
comment: Accepted as a poster at Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGM) 2026 Conference
summary: Bayesian network structure learning (BNSL) from observational data struggles with orientation identifiability, while large language models (LLMs) offer broad but often unreliable causal knowledge. We propose combining these complementary sources through a novel representation, termed Probabilistic Dependency Graphs (PDGs). In a PDG, each edge is associated with a distribution over directed, undirected, and absent states, enabling fusion via weighted averaging. We evaluate this approach on 26 benchmark networks, combining ensembles of three BNSL algorithms (FGES, Tabu, PC) with three LLMs (Gemini, Claude, GPT) across multiple prompts and random seeds. A simple 50/50 fusion improves F1 over the better of either source alone in 22 of 26 networks, with a statistically significant mean improvement of $0.056$ $(p<0.001)$. Analysis reveals that the two sources play complementary roles: BNSL contributes a high-recall edge skeleton (80\% vs 60\% for LLM), while LLM contributes accurate edge orientation (96\% vs 77\% for BNSL). Our results show that representing both sources as probabilistic uncertainty over edge existence and orientation is a practical and effective way to improve causal graph accuracy.

AI.tldr: Combining Bayesian network structure learning with LLM causal knowledge through Probabilistic Dependency Graphs improves causal graph accuracy by leveraging their complementary strengths.
AI.motivation: Bayesian network structure learning struggles with orientation identifiability from observational data alone, while LLMs offer broad causal knowledge but are unreliable. The paper aims to combine these complementary sources to overcome their individual limitations.
AI.method: Proposes Probabilistic Dependency Graphs where each edge has a distribution over directed, undirected, and absent states. Uses weighted averaging to fuse ensembles of three BNSL algorithms (FGES, Tabu, PC) with three LLMs (Gemini, Claude, GPT) across multiple prompts and seeds.
AI.result: Simple 50/50 fusion improves F1 score over the better source alone in 22 of 26 benchmark networks, with statistically significant mean improvement of 0.056 (p<0.001). Analysis shows BNSL contributes high-recall edge skeleton (80% vs 60% for LLM) while LLM contributes accurate edge orientation (96% vs 77% for BNSL).
AI.conclusion: Representing both Bayesian network structure learning and LLM knowledge as probabilistic uncertainty over edge existence and orientation is a practical and effective approach to improve causal graph accuracy by leveraging their complementary strengths.

title: When Muon Meets Task Interference: A Spectral Perspective on Continual Learning and Model Merging
summary: Continual learning (CL) and model merging (MM) both aim to obtain a single model that performs well across multiple tasks, challenged respectively by catastrophic forgetting and weight-disentanglement error. In the literature, these difficulties are merely treated separately and mitigated through a variety of solutions, while the geometry induced by the base optimizer is treated as an implementation detail. In this work, we show that the two difficulties are in fact two instances of the same phenomenon: a parameter update useful for one task shifts the model's outputs on another. We formalize this shared phenomenon as \textit{task interference} and reduce it to a common layer-wise Frobenius inner product $\langle ΔW_\ell, J_\ell(x)\rangle_F$. This quantity, in turn, is utilized to expose the role of the optimizer. We theoretically derive an upper bound that isolates the spectral norm $\|ΔW_\ell\|_2$ as an optimizer-controllable factor of task interference, and a per-mode analysis shows that this bound tracks the dominant part of the empirical interference. Specifically, we then identify the recent Muon optimizer as a mechanism that regulates this factor by construction. Our work reveals that its elegant control on spectral norm tightens the interference bound for both CL and MM, positioning Muon as a principled optimizer-centric approach complementary to existing solutions. Our theoretcal analysis is well validated by experimental results. Replacing the AdamW optimizer with Muon improves accuracy by up to +5.02 points on the eight-task model-merging benchmark across three CLIP backbones. For continual learning, Muon also delivers uniformly positive gains across ten class-incremental protocols, three task-incremental protocols, and the 11-task MTIL benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that catastrophic forgetting in continual learning and weight-disentanglement error in model merging are both instances of "task interference," formalized as layer-wise Frobenius inner products. The work identifies optimizer spectral norm as a controllable factor and demonstrates that the Muon optimizer reduces interference, improving performance in both settings.
AI.motivation: Continual learning (CL) and model merging (MM) both aim to create single models that perform well across multiple tasks, but face different challenges: catastrophic forgetting for CL and weight-disentanglement error for MM. The paper argues these are actually two instances of the same phenomenon called "task interference," where parameter updates for one task shift the model's outputs on another task. Existing literature treats these difficulties separately while overlooking the role of optimizer geometry.
AI.method: The paper formalizes task interference as a layer-wise Frobenius inner product ⟨ΔW_ℓ, J_ℓ(x)⟩_F. Through theoretical analysis, it derives an upper bound that isolates the spectral norm ‖ΔW_ℓ‖_2 as an optimizer-controllable factor of task interference. A per-mode analysis shows this bound tracks the dominant part of empirical interference. The work then identifies the Muon optimizer as a mechanism that naturally regulates this spectral norm factor by construction.
AI.result: Experimental validation shows Muon significantly improves performance: Replacing AdamW with Muon improves accuracy by up to +5.02 points on the eight-task model-merging benchmark across three CLIP backbones. For continual learning, Muon delivers uniformly positive gains across ten class-incremental protocols, three task-incremental protocols, and the 11-task MTIL benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The paper reveals that catastrophic forgetting and weight-disentanglement error are both manifestations of task interference, and that the optimizer's spectral norm control is key to mitigating this interference. Muon serves as a principled optimizer-centric approach that complements existing solutions by tightening interference bounds for both continual learning and model merging.

title: Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine: A Scientific Agent for PDE Discovery with Unknown Spatial Coefficient Fields
summary: Discovering PDEs in heterogeneous media requires jointly identifying the governing operator and the unknown spatial fields that parameterize it. These tasks are coupled: changing field placement changes the differential law, while a sufficiently flexible field can conceal structural error on a single trajectory. We present Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine for PDE Discovery (HER-PDE), a scientific-agent framework that discovers compositional PDE structure together with nonparametric, time-invariant coefficient fields. The Agent analyzes two noisy trajectories generated by different excitations, proposes complete expression-tree hypotheses, and combines creative structural exploration with local candidate refinement. Its Hypothesis Evaluation Interface (HEI) estimates only the fields explicitly declared in each hypothesis, never adds missing terms, and scores structures by bidirectional cross-excitation transfer. The selected law is subsequently audited on a sealed temporal interval. Across five controlled two-dimensional systems observed with 5 percent relative Gaussian state noise, the Agent recovers the generating operator in all five cases, including equivalent signed-field and product-rule parameterizations. Across nine unknown coefficient fields, the recovered fields attain a median Pearson correlation of approximately 0.85 and a median relative L2 error of approximately 0.28. These results show that agent-guided hypothesis refinement can recover heterogeneous governing laws without prescribing a parametric form for their spatial coefficients.

AI.tldr: HER-PDE is an AI agent framework that discovers compositional PDEs with unknown spatial coefficient fields from noisy trajectory data, achieving accurate recovery of both governing operators and nonparametric fields.
AI.motivation: Discovering PDEs in heterogeneous media requires simultaneously identifying both the governing differential operator and the unknown spatial fields that parameterize it, which is challenging because these tasks are coupled and flexible fields can conceal structural errors.
AI.method: The HER-PDE framework uses a scientific-agent approach with Hypothesis Evaluation Interface (HEI) that analyzes noisy trajectories from different excitations, proposes expression-tree hypotheses, combines creative structural exploration with local refinement, estimates only declared fields, and scores structures by bidirectional cross-excitation transfer.
AI.result: Across five 2D systems with 5% Gaussian noise, the agent recovered generating operators in all cases, including equivalent parameterizations. For nine unknown coefficient fields, median Pearson correlation was ~0.85 and relative L2 error ~0.28.
AI.conclusion: Agent-guided hypothesis refinement can successfully recover heterogeneous governing laws without requiring parametric forms for spatial coefficients, demonstrating the effectiveness of the HER-PDE framework for PDE discovery in complex media.

title: Dandelion: A Spherical Flower for Neural Simulation of Planetary Dynamics
summary: Many dynamical processes unfold on the sphere but the default scientific machine learning architectures are Euclidean. Applying these architectures on a regular lat-lon grid causes problems: Cartesian convolutions become distorted at high latitude; 2D FFTs in Fourier neural operators incorrectly assume double periodicity; Cartesian positional encodings in ViTs distort spherical geodesic distances. Recent work moves towards natively spherical primitives, including spherical convolutions (e.g., DeepSphere or DISCO), Spherical Fourier Neural Operators (SFNOs), and geodesic attention. Here we propose Dandelion, a spherical version of Flower, a warp-based neural PDE solver. Layers of Dandelion predict a tangent-plane displacement and transport features along great circles. We obtain a U-Net-like structure by implementing hierarchical pooling entirely in the spherical-harmonic domain. There are thus no convolutions: spatial mixing is achieved only through spherical coordinate changes, or warps. To compare Dandelion with existing spherical architectures, we release an evolving benchmark suite of challenging, natively-spherical PDE datasets including a modified Galewsky jet, anomalous chained turbulence, Cahn-Hilliard decomposition, spherical Riemann shocks, Held-Suarez dry atmospheric transport and global ocean dynamics. This new benchmark fills the gap in existing spherical datasets which are either too small and stylized, or much too large (ERA5) for model iteration. Dandelion is best or second-best on every dataset, and the gap to non-warp baselines widens with resolution: at $256\times 512$, Dandelion and Flower2D occupy the top two slots in both single-step prediction and rollout.

AI.tldr: Dandelion is a spherical neural PDE solver that uses warp-based coordinate changes instead of convolutions, outperforming existing spherical architectures on new benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Many dynamical processes occur on spheres, but standard machine learning architectures are Euclidean. Applying them on spherical grids causes problems: distorted convolutions at high latitudes, incorrect periodicity assumptions in Fourier neural operators, and distorted geodesic distances in positional encodings.
AI.method: Dandelion is a spherical version of Flower, using warp-based neural PDE solving. Layers predict tangent-plane displacements and transport features along great circles. It implements hierarchical pooling entirely in the spherical-harmonic domain, eliminating convolutions - spatial mixing occurs only through spherical coordinate changes (warps).
AI.result: Dandelion is best or second-best on every dataset in the new benchmark suite. The performance gap to non-warp baselines widens with resolution - at 256×512, Dandelion and Flower2D occupy the top two slots for both single-step prediction and rollout.
AI.conclusion: Dandelion provides an effective warp-based approach for spherical PDE solving that outperforms existing spherical architectures, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at higher resolutions.

title: Class-Based Heuristic Selection for Solving the Flying Block Puzzle
summary: Heuristic search underlies planning in autonomous systems ranging from warehouse logistics to robotic navigation, yet generic heuristics fail to exploit the structural constraints that govern constrained spatial domains, causing search performance to degrade catastrophically on harder instances. We study this problem through the two-column Flying Block Puzzle, a rigorously NP-complete spatial planning microworld whose bottleneck geometry mirrors clearance-to-size constraints encountered in multi-agent path finding, autonomous vehicle navigation, and block relocation systems. We introduce the Class-Based Heuristic A* (CBHA*) algorithm, which integrates a General Move Constraint to capture minimum displacement costs when vacant units are scarce, a formal kinematic taxonomy partitioning the state space into seven mutually exclusive classes with provably admissible heuristics based on vacancy ratio and goal-piece geometry, and a class-conditional tie-breaking mechanism that dynamically switches between depth-priority and vertical-distance ordering to overcome f-value plateaus. Over 146 benchmark instances, CBHA* achieves a 93.4% success rate against 64% for Depth-Prioritized A*, 39% for Standard A*, and 17% for BFS, while reducing node expansions by 87.98% relative to Standard A* and sustaining an average effective branching factor of approximately 3, demonstrating that class-triggered adaptive heuristics constitute a principled mechanism for efficient spatial planning that generalizes structurally to physical constraint systems.

AI.tldr: CBHA* algorithm uses class-based heuristics with kinematic taxonomy and adaptive tie-breaking to solve NP-complete spatial planning problems, achieving 93.4% success rate and 87.98% fewer node expansions than standard A*.
AI.motivation: Generic heuristics fail to exploit structural constraints in spatial domains, causing catastrophic performance degradation on harder instances. This problem is studied through the Flying Block Puzzle, which mirrors clearance-to-size constraints in real-world applications like multi-agent path finding and autonomous navigation.
AI.method: CBHA* integrates: 1) General Move Constraint for minimum displacement costs with scarce vacancies, 2) Formal kinematic taxonomy partitioning state space into seven mutually exclusive classes with provably admissible heuristics based on vacancy ratio and goal-piece geometry, and 3) Class-conditional tie-breaking that dynamically switches between depth-priority and vertical-distance ordering to overcome f-value plateaus.
AI.result: Over 146 benchmark instances, CBHA* achieves 93.4% success rate (vs 64% for Depth-Prioritized A*, 39% for Standard A*, 17% for BFS), reduces node expansions by 87.98% relative to Standard A*, and sustains average effective branching factor of approximately 3.
AI.conclusion: Class-triggered adaptive heuristics constitute a principled mechanism for efficient spatial planning that generalizes structurally to physical constraint systems, demonstrating that domain-specific structural exploitation is essential for solving complex spatial planning problems.

title: Self-Explainable Multi-Label Graph Neural Network for Correlated Evidence Attribution
summary: Multi-label graph learning intends to capture the intrinsic complexity of real-world applications, where one sample is often related to multiple groups or consists of multiple objects. To date, a handful of multi-label graph learning methods exist, but none of them integrate training-time interpretation capability. While post-hoc graph explainers have been developed, they do not explicitly model label-dependent evidence sharing in multi-label graph learners, especially when label pairs are weakly or negatively associated. As a result, post-hoc approaches may miss how evidence should be shared or separated across different labels. This paper advances a new end-to-end self-explainable multi-label graph neural network (SEMGNN), which aims to simultaneously classify multi-labeled nodes and identify edges significantly contributing to each target node w.r.t. predicted labels. Different from post-hoc methods, SEMGNN jointly learns a predictor and a sparse edge-mask explainer within a unified framework and training objective. Label-label correlations are used to improve multi-label node classification and enhance individual label explanations, so that different labels of a node can be supported by distinct yet coherent structural and/or correlated evidence. Experiments and comparisons on synthetic and real-world multi-label networks, in social networking, entertainment, and life sciences, show that SEMGNN achieves competitive or improved predictive performance while providing more faithful and compact label-conditioned explanations.

AI.tldr: SEMGNN is a new end-to-end self-explainable multi-label graph neural network that simultaneously classifies multi-labeled nodes and identifies edges contributing to each label prediction, using label correlations to improve both classification and explanations.
AI.motivation: Current multi-label graph learning methods lack training-time interpretation capabilities, and post-hoc graph explainers don't properly handle label-dependent evidence sharing, especially when labels have weak or negative correlations. This makes them miss how evidence should be shared or separated across different labels.
AI.method: SEMGNN is an end-to-end self-explainable framework that jointly learns a predictor and sparse edge-mask explainer within a unified training objective. It uses label-label correlations to enhance multi-label node classification and provide label-specific explanations, allowing different labels of a node to be supported by distinct yet coherent structural evidence.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world multi-label networks (social networking, entertainment, life sciences) show SEMGNN achieves competitive or improved predictive performance while providing more faithful and compact label-conditioned explanations compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SEMGNN successfully addresses the limitations of existing multi-label graph learning methods by integrating self-explainability, enabling simultaneous multi-label classification and label-specific explanation generation with improved performance and interpretability.

title: Benchmarking General Mobile Assistants in Challenging Real-World Scenarios
summary: Graphical user interfaces have emerged as an important environment for evaluating autonomous AI agents on multimodal interactive tasks. Existing benchmarks such as AndroidWorld and MobileWorld provide strong foundations for mobile agent evaluation, but their application coverage and task design do not yet fully capture the diversity and complexity of realistic mobile use. We present GMA, a benchmark for evaluating general mobile assistants in challenging real-world scenarios. GMA introduces seven applications based on open-source projects, spanning domains such as lifestyle sharing and travel planning, and 300 tasks across four difficulty tiers, from atomic actions to complex multi-step workflows. We evaluate eight frontier models and find that performance declines substantially as task complexity increases, with current agents remaining far from reliably handling realistic user requirements. We further conduct controlled ablation studies of agent harness choices, including context retention and explicit state tracking, under a shared environment, model setting, and task taxonomy. Results show that appropriate harness design can meaningfully improve performance, particularly on demanding workflows, while the effectiveness of specific designs can vary across foundation models. Overall, GMA complements existing benchmarks by expanding application coverage and task complexity, providing a challenging testbed for evaluating mobile agents and studying how harness design supports reliable execution in complex mobile workflows.

AI.tldr: GMA is a new benchmark for evaluating general mobile assistants with more realistic, complex tasks across seven diverse applications, showing current models struggle with workflow complexity but appropriate agent harness design can improve performance.
AI.motivation: Existing mobile agent benchmarks (like AndroidWorld and MobileWorld) have limited application coverage and task design that doesn't fully capture the diversity and complexity of real-world mobile use scenarios.
AI.method: Created GMA benchmark with: 1) Seven applications based on open-source projects across domains like lifestyle sharing and travel planning, 2) 300 tasks across four difficulty tiers from atomic actions to complex multi-step workflows, 3) Evaluated eight frontier models with controlled ablation studies on agent harness choices (context retention, explicit state tracking) under shared environment, model, and task taxonomy.
AI.result: Performance declines substantially as task complexity increases, with current agents far from reliably handling realistic user requirements. Appropriate harness design meaningfully improves performance on demanding workflows, but effectiveness varies across foundation models.
AI.conclusion: GMA complements existing benchmarks by expanding application coverage and task complexity, providing a challenging testbed for evaluating mobile agents and studying how harness design supports reliable execution in complex mobile workflows.

title: Curvature-Aware Radius Shrinkage for Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Classification
summary: Nearest neighbor classification relies fundamentally on how locality is defined, yet conventional $k$-NN imposes the same neighborhood cardinality throughout the feature space. This assumption can be inadequate for data whose local geometry varies substantially across the underlying manifold. We introduce Curvature-Aware Radius Shrinkage for Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Classification (CARSANN), a geometry-driven framework that adapts the spatial support of each neighborhood according to local geometric complexity. CARSANN first estimates intrinsic dimensionality using TwoNN and constructs an intrinsic representation through principal component analysis. Local mean curvature is then estimated using a shape-operator-based formulation and controls neighborhood scale: highly curved regions receive stronger radius shrinkage, whereas approximately flat regions retain broader spatial support. Unlike methods that modify only the number of neighbors or the local metric, CARSANN explicitly adapts the spatial extent of local evidence. Experiments on more than 70 real-world OpenML datasets show that CARSANN consistently improves upon standard $k$-NN and is competitive with adaptive nearest-neighbor methods. In a controlled comparison using the same base neighborhood size, CARSANN achieves higher balanced accuracy on 40 of 45 datasets, increasing mean balanced accuracy from 0.6506 to 0.7528. The advantage also persists against $k$-NN with fixed $k=5$. Friedman and Nemenyi tests confirm that the improvements are statistically significant. These results indicate that local manifold curvature can serve as an effective geometric control variable for adapting neighborhood support, providing a complementary paradigm to cardinality-based nearest-neighbor adaptation.

AI.tldr: CARSANN adapts nearest neighbor classification by shrinking neighborhoods based on local curvature, achieving better accuracy than standard k-NN.
AI.motivation: Standard k-NN uses the same neighborhood size everywhere, which fails when data geometry varies across the manifold. Local geometric complexity differs, requiring adaptive spatial support.
AI.method: Uses TwoNN to estimate intrinsic dimensionality, PCA for intrinsic representation, then estimates local mean curvature via shape-operator formulation to control neighborhood scale (strong shrinkage in curved regions, broad support in flat areas).
AI.result: Outperforms standard k-NN on 70+ real-world datasets; beats same-base-size methods on 40/45 datasets (accuracy improves from 0.6506 to 0.7528). Statistically significant improvements confirmed via Friedman and Nemenyi tests.
AI.conclusion: Local manifold curvature effectively adapts neighborhood support, providing a geometric alternative to cardinality-based nearest-neighbor adaptation.

title: Effectiveness of IoT and Deep Learning for Detection and Severity Assessment of Postelectrotermes militaris in Tea Plantations
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in The Journal of Agricultural Sciences, Sri Lanka
summary:
Tea plantations are vulnerable to Postelectrotermes militaris, commonly known as the Upcountry Live Wood Termite (ULWT), which can cause substantial damage when infestations remain undetected. This study proposes an IoT-enabled acoustic monitoring framework integrated with deep learning for early detection and severity assessment of ULWT infestations in tea plantations.
  Research Method: Audio signals were captured non-invasively from tea trunks using a high-sensitivity microphone connected to a Raspberry Pi-based IoT device, with geographic coordinates recorded for spatial tracking. After trimming, resampling, and segmentation, 2,000 ten-second samples were obtained, comprising 1,000 healthy and 1,000 infested samples, and divided into 1,600 training, 200 validation, and 200 test samples. The dataset used in this study is publicly available on Kaggle (Senevirathna et al. 2026). Fourier-derived spectrograms trained a CNN for infestation classification and probability estimation. A weighted severity model combined CNN probability, mean acoustic amplitude, and nearby infested plants within 5 m, with geospatial mapping used to visualize infestation distribution.
  Findings and Values: Field trials in a ULWT-affected tea plantation in Pundaluoya demonstrated feasibility under realistic environmental noise. On the held-out test set, the CNN achieved 81.5% accuracy, 80.6% precision, 83.0% recall, 81.8% F1-score, and 0.819 ROC-AUC. Beyond binary infestation detection, the framework introduced quantitative severity assessment using infestation probability, acoustic amplitude, and nearby infested plants. The resulting severity and geospatial outputs can support plantation managers in identifying high-risk areas, prioritizing field inspections, and implementing more timely and targeted control measures.

AI.tldr: An IoT-deep learning framework for detecting and assessing termite infestations in tea plantations using acoustic monitoring and CNN classification with severity scoring and geospatial mapping.
AI.motivation: Tea plantations are vulnerable to Upcountry Live Wood Termite (ULWT) infestations which cause substantial damage when undetected, creating a need for early detection and severity assessment methods.
AI.method: IoT-based acoustic monitoring with Raspberry Pi devices, collecting audio from tea trunks, processing into spectrograms, training CNN on 2,000 samples, and using weighted severity model combining CNN probability, acoustic amplitude, and nearby infestation density with geospatial mapping.
AI.result: The CNN achieved 81.5% accuracy, 80.6% precision, 83.0% recall, 81.8% F1-score, and 0.819 ROC-AUC. Framework successfully detected infestations and provided quantitative severity assessment with geospatial visualization for targeted intervention.
AI.conclusion: The IoT-enabled deep learning framework provides effective early detection and severity assessment of termite infestations in tea plantations, enabling targeted control measures and supporting plantation management through actionable geospatial insights.

title: More Data Cannot Break a Symmetry: Identifiability by Design
summary: Unsupervised representational alignment recovers a stimulus-by-stimulus correspondence from geometry alone, but the automorphism group of the stimulus geometry bounds what any such alignment can identify, before data exist. The obvious diagnostic for this degeneracy, the cheapest non-identity relabelling, ranks two published designs in the wrong order, because dense sampling creates near-duplicates whose transposition is nearly free. We turn this known invariance (Demetci et al., 2024) into a design-time diagnostic and intervention. In colour, where candidate geometries have closed form, we show that the failure is structural: sixty-four times the restart budget leaves a symmetric design unmoved while an asymmetric set at the same N recovers every time. Discriminating representational models and recovering a correspondence are essentially uncorrelated objectives (r = -0.02 over 3,000 subsets). Choosing nine colours by this diagnostic alone, without consulting any learned representation, moves all 93 model representations away from the degenerate point and cuts catastrophic alignment failures from 75% to 2% with the models, the layers, N and the solver all held fixed. The same risk arises wherever a regular design meets its candidate geometry's isometry group, including evenly spaced orientations, tones, or motion directions, and the check costs one function call before data collection.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a fundamental limitation in unsupervised representational alignment where stimulus geometry imposes bounds on what can be identified, shows that dense sampling creates near-duplicates that make alignment nearly free, and provides a pre-data diagnostic to detect and fix this structural failure.
AI.motivation: Current unsupervised representational alignment methods can fail catastrophically due to geometric symmetries in stimulus design, particularly when dense sampling creates near-duplicates that allow essentially free relabeling. This structural failure isn't detected by conventional diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors develop a design-time diagnostic based on geometric automorphism groups to detect when stimulus geometry bounds alignment identifiability. They demonstrate this with color stimuli (where geometries have closed form), showing that symmetric designs are unmoved by extensive restart budgets while asymmetric sets recover correspondences consistently.
AI.result: The diagnostic reveals that discriminating representational models and recovering correspondences are essentially uncorrelated objectives (r = -0.02). By selecting just nine colors using this diagnostic (without consulting learned representations), catastrophic alignment failures drop from 75% to 2% while holding all other factors constant. The risk extends to any regular design meeting its geometry's isometry group.
AI.conclusion: Geometric symmetries in stimulus design impose fundamental limits on unsupervised alignment, but these can be detected and addressed before data collection with a simple diagnostic. This approach significantly improves alignment reliability across various stimulus domains where regular designs meet geometric isometries.

title: Context Localization for Generalized Level-Based Evaluation in Knowledge-Based Systems
comment: Author preprint of the article published in Knowledge-Based Systems (2026)
summary: We study context localization for generalized level-based evaluation in knowledge-based systems. The framework models situations where a structured nonnegative score, defined on facts, rules, cases, criteria or evidence units, is evaluated through conditional aggregation tests on admissible knowledge contexts. The generalized level measure maximizes a monotone set function over all contexts whose aggregated support reaches a prescribed level. We characterize when filtering the score by a context $B$ is equivalent to localizing the admissible contexts by intersection with $B$. The main theorem shows that this consistency holds for all monotone set functions if and only if two structural conditions are satisfied: monotonicity with respect to contexts and a reduction property excluding positive localized support outside $B$. We analyze pointwise and block-generated mechanisms producing the reduction property, extend the result to parameterized systems, and interpret it as a stability criterion for context-dependent evidence selection, non-additive support evaluation and level-based knowledge aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when context filtering equals context localization in level-based knowledge systems, showing equivalence requires monotonicity and a reduction property.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand context localization in generalized level-based evaluation for knowledge-based systems, particularly when filtering by a context is equivalent to localizing admissible contexts through intersection. This addresses consistency issues in context-dependent knowledge aggregation.
AI.method: The framework models structured nonnegative scores on knowledge elements evaluated through conditional aggregation tests on admissible contexts. The method uses monotone set functions to characterize conditions where context filtering equals context localization, analyzing pointwise and block-generated mechanisms, and extending to parameterized systems.
AI.result: The main theorem shows consistency (filtering by context B equals localizing contexts by intersection with B) holds for all monotone set functions if and only if two structural conditions are satisfied: monotonicity with respect to contexts and a reduction property excluding positive localized support outside B.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes fundamental conditions for consistency in context-dependent knowledge systems, interpreting the result as a stability criterion for evidence selection, non-additive support evaluation, and level-based knowledge aggregation.

title: Unsupervised Continual Learning with Growing Self-Organizing Maps and Synthetic Replay
summary: This work presents a generative continual learning framework based on growing self-organizing maps (GSOMs) that are augmented with learned distributional statistics as well as encoder-decoder models for class-incremental learning. The proposed approach enables exemplar-free replay using distributional statistical memory, which eliminates the need to store raw data. Each GSOM unit maintains its own mean, variance, and covariance estimates, which are subsequently used to generate synthetic samples for replay; in encoder-decoder configurations, these samples are then decoded back into the input space (via ancestral sampling) for subsequent training. Our method is fully unsupervised, as it does not rely on explicit task boundaries or class labels during training. Results across multiple benchmarks show that the proposed approach achieves performance competitive even with supervised state-of-the-art memory-based methods while consistently outperforming memory-free approaches. In several settings, our framework matches or exceeds existing baselines, particularly in challenging single-class incremental scenarios. We also provide baseline results for single-class incremental TinyImageNet and MiniImageNet, offering a useful reference for future work. This work highlights the effectiveness of an unsupervised, adaptive, topology-driven neural form of statistical replay as a scalable, flexible approach to continual learning.

AI.tldr: An unsupervised continual learning framework using growing self-organizing maps with statistical memory for class-incremental learning without storing raw data.
AI.motivation: The need for exemplar-free continual learning that doesn't require storing raw data and can operate without explicit task boundaries or class labels during training.
AI.method: Uses growing self-organizing maps (GSOMs) augmented with distributional statistics (mean, variance, covariance). Each GSOM unit maintains statistical estimates to generate synthetic samples via ancestral sampling. In encoder-decoder configurations, samples are decoded back to input space for replay.
AI.result: Achieves performance competitive with supervised state-of-the-art memory-based methods while outperforming memory-free approaches. Particularly effective in challenging single-class incremental scenarios. Provides baseline results for TinyImageNet and MiniImageNet.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the effectiveness of unsupervised, adaptive, topology-driven neural statistical replay as a scalable, flexible approach to continual learning.

title: SegBench-GC: Testing Segmentation Invariance in Multi-Step Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
comment: 10 pages, 2 tables. Code and reproducibility artifacts: https://github.com/MusaShams/SegBench-GC
summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) often uses trajectory structure for future-goal sampling and multi-step targets, yet logged trajectories may be partitioned for administrative reasons that do not correspond to termination. We introduce SegBench-GC, a controlled stress test of segmentation invariance that holds transitions, source trajectories, goal sampling, optimization settings, and evaluation fixed while varying only artificial backup boundaries and whether those boundaries retain continuation value. Continuation-valid targets (CVT) provide the segmentation-consistent control: reward accumulation stops at an artificial cut, but the target bootstraps from its stored successor. In a matched-count PointMaze study with 35,000 artificial cuts, three segmentation realizations, and three optimization seeds, final 50-episode-per-task success is 50.5% uncut, 39.1% with CVT, and 19.1% when the same cuts are treated as absorbing; across segmentation realizations, naive mean success ranges from 4.8% to 31.9%. An independent published n-step baseline (n=25) from the Decoupled Q-Chunking codebase shows the same failure on Puzzle-4x5: 47.2% uncut, 58.5% CVT, and 0.27% naive across three optimization seeds. A target-level diagnostic verifies the analytic target difference to numerical precision, and learned-critic diagnostics show a large optimistic shift under naive handling while CVT remains approximately aligned with the uncut critic. CVT applies standard continuation bootstrapping rather than a new Bellman rule; the contribution is the controlled benchmark, failure isolation, and cross-learner evidence that administrative segmentation can materially change multi-step offline GCRL.
