AI.tldr: Controlled benchmark shows administrative trajectory segmentation in offline goal-conditioned RL can cause performance drops from 50% to 20% if not handled properly; continuation-valid targets (CVT) mitigate this by preserving value across artificial cuts.
AI.motivation: Offline goal-conditioned RL often uses trajectory structure for sampling and multi-step targets, but logged trajectories may be artificially partitioned for administrative reasons unrelated to termination, potentially harming learning performance.
AI.method: Introduces SegBench-GC, a controlled benchmark that holds everything constant (transitions, trajectories, goal sampling, optimization, evaluation) while varying only artificial backup boundaries. Uses continuation-valid targets (CVT) that stop reward accumulation at cuts but bootstrap from stored successors, maintaining segmentation consistency.
AI.result: In PointMaze with 35,000 artificial cuts: 50.5% success uncut, 39.1% with CVT, and 19.1% when cuts treated as absorbing. Naive segmentation reduced success to 4.8-31.9%. Independent baseline on Puzzle-4x5 shows similar pattern: 47.2% uncut, 58.5% CVT, 0.27% naive. Diagnostic confirms analytic target differences and shows naive handling causes optimistic value shift while CVT aligns with uncut critic.
AI.conclusion: Administrative segmentation can materially impact offline GCRL performance. CVT (standard continuation bootstrapping) effectively mitigates this issue without requiring new Bellman rules. The contribution is the controlled benchmark, failure isolation, and cross-learner evidence of segmentation effects.

title: Thinking Costs Tokens: When More Structure is Worth the Price
summary: Adding inference structure to a language model lets it search, verify, and revise, but these actions consume the very budget they are supposed to use well. In this paper, we investigate whether there exists a token-budget threshold, below which the overhead of planning and verification hurts performance and above which it helps. We evaluate two systems on FinQA and TAT-QA financial reasoning tasks, using GPT-5.4 mini across 14 budget tiers ranging from 250 to 42,000 output-equivalent tokens. The first system is a monolith, which is a single LLM call. The second is a verified search architecture that adds planning, label-blind checking, and repair capabilities. We run 1,000 cases for a total of 28,000 completed cells. Both systems score 0% at the two lowest tiers, where neither can fit a complete prompt. At 1,000 tokens, the monolith reaches 18% accuracy while verified search scores near 0%, since the planning overhead leaves no room for an answer. From 1,500 tokens onward, verified search surpasses the monolith and maintains a consistent advantage, reaching approximately 44% at the highest tiers while the monolith reaches approximately 40%. The crossover occurs between 1,000 and 1,500 output-equivalent tokens, confirmed by a strict intersection-union test ($p \le 0.001$ at both endpoints).

AI.tldr: Adding planning and verification to language models requires a minimum token budget threshold - below 1,000 tokens it hurts performance, but above 1,500 tokens it consistently outperforms monolithic approaches on financial reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: To determine whether there exists a token-budget threshold where the overhead of planning and verification (search, verify, revise) becomes beneficial rather than detrimental to language model performance on complex reasoning tasks.
AI.method: Evaluated two systems on FinQA and TAT-QA financial reasoning tasks using GPT-5.4 mini: (1) monolith - single LLM call, and (2) verified search architecture with planning, label-blind checking, and repair capabilities. Tested across 14 budget tiers from 250 to 42,000 output-equivalent tokens, running 1,000 cases total across 28,000 completed cells.
AI.result: Both systems scored 0% at the two lowest tiers (can't fit complete prompt). At 1,000 tokens: monolith reached 18% accuracy while verified search scored near 0% (planning overhead left no room for answer). From 1,500 tokens onward: verified search surpassed monolith and maintained consistent advantage, reaching ~44% at highest tiers vs monolith's ~40%. Crossover occurred between 1,000-1,500 tokens (p ≤ 0.001 at both endpoints).
AI.conclusion: There is a clear token-budget threshold (~1,000-1,500 tokens) where inference structure becomes beneficial - below it hurts performance due to overhead, but above it provides consistent advantages for complex reasoning tasks through better planning and verification capabilities.

title: SafeStep: An Interactive Demonstration of Semantic Communication for Pedestrian Safety Monitoring
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the Quality, Value, and Age of Information for Tactical Networks workshop at the IEEE Military Communications Conference (MILCOM). Christian McDowell, Andrea Panebianco, and Jeremiah Yang are co-primary authors
summary: In this paper, we develop SafeStep, an interactive browser-based semantic communication platform for live pedestrian safety monitoring. SafeStep extracts pedestrian information from four live traffic-camera feeds, transmits it through a semantic communication transceiver over an Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel, and renders user-specific positions, trajectories, and risk labels. The platform allows to independently select the transceiver, Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), codelength, and Age of Information (AoI), and demonstrates the transceiver performance of the selected configuration through live pedestrian safety monitoring to each browser. SafeStep compares a recently proposed semantic communication design called Meta-VIB with five baseline transceivers. Meta-VIB uses a compact neural model with only $4.16$ million parameters to generalize across varying SNR, codelength, and AoI values without online retraining. Experimental results show that Meta-VIB achieves mean task-loss reductions of up to $92.1\%$. On one high-end GPU server, the integrated concurrent-access workload maintains the target $5$ frames/s through $20$ users. At $100$ users, each requesting a distinct configuration, SafeStep records no request failures and a mean application response time below $1$ s, but its mean per-browser frame rate falls to approximately $1$ frame/s. To our knowledge, SafeStep is the first real-time semantic communication platform to make AoI-induced downstream degradation directly observable in live monitoring applications.

AI.tldr: SafeStep is a real-time browser-based semantic communication platform for pedestrian safety monitoring that compares Meta-VIB (a compact neural model) with baseline transceivers, achieving up to 92.1% task-loss reduction while supporting concurrent user access.
AI.motivation: There's a need for real-time semantic communication platforms for pedestrian safety monitoring that can handle varying communication conditions (SNR, codelength, AoI) without requiring online retraining, while providing interactive browser-based visualization of safety information.
AI.method: Developed SafeStep platform that extracts pedestrian data from four traffic cameras, transmits via semantic communication over AWGN channel. Compared Meta-VIB (a 4.16M parameter neural model) with five baseline transceivers. The system allows interactive selection of transceiver, SNR, codelength, and AoI configurations.
AI.result: Meta-VIB achieves mean task-loss reductions up to 92.1% and generalizes across varying conditions without retraining. Platform supports 20 users at 5 frames/s on one GPU server, handles 100 users with distinct configurations without request failures and <1s response time (though frame rate drops to ~1 frame/s at 100 users).
AI.conclusion: SafeStep is the first real-time semantic communication platform enabling direct observation of AoI-induced degradation in live monitoring applications, demonstrating practical deployment potential for semantic communication in safety-critical scenarios with multiple concurrent users.

title: WM-R1: Training GUI Agents to Reason and leverage World Models with Reinforcement Learning
summary: GUI agents trained with reinforcement learning (RL) have showcased strong environment learning capabilities on mobile platforms. However, RL typically demands extensive real-environment interactions, leading to high resource costs and instability, especially in GUI scenarios. To address these, we propose WM-R1, the first reinforcement learning framework that trains mobile GUI agents with world models instead of real environments. Specifically, world models serve as the source of state transitions during all rollouts, replacing the real Android environment within the training loop. WM-R1 also embeds world models directly into the thinking process, enabling agents to reason about the consequences of candidate actions before committing to the final action. Crucially, WM-R1 eliminates the need for real-environment interaction, supports massively parallelized and step-level granularized trajectory generation grounded in world models, and introduces a multi-dimensional rule-based reward that jointly optimizes task success, trajectory efficiency, and world model utilization. For efficient training, we curate a high-quality dataset of 2000 challenging tasks. Experiments on Android mobile benchmarks demonstrate that WM-R1-trained agents significantly outperform GRPO-only baselines and inference-time simulation methods. Code is available at https://github.com/genalyu/WM-R1 .

AI.tldr: WM-R1 is a reinforcement learning framework that trains mobile GUI agents using world models instead of real environments, eliminating real-environment interactions while improving efficiency and performance.
AI.motivation: RL-based GUI agents require extensive real-environment interactions which are costly in resources and unstable, especially in mobile GUI scenarios where real interactions are expensive and problematic.
AI.method: Proposes WM-R1 framework where world models replace real Android environments during training rollouts. World models are embedded in the thinking process for action consequence reasoning. Features include massively parallelized trajectory generation, step-level granularity, and multi-dimensional rule-based rewards optimizing task success, efficiency, and world model utilization.
AI.result: Experiments on Android mobile benchmarks show WM-R1-trained agents significantly outperform GRPO-only baselines and inference-time simulation methods. Achieved using a curated dataset of 2000 challenging tasks.
AI.conclusion: WM-R1 successfully addresses RL's resource and stability issues for GUI agents by using world models, enabling efficient training without real-environment interaction while maintaining strong performance on mobile platforms.

title: RiskBlend: A Multi-Signal Framework for Test Input Prioritization in Machine Learning Regression Testing
summary: When machine learning classifiers are retrained, inputs correctly classified by the previous model version may be misclassified by the updated version, creating regression faults that are costly to detect because verifying predictions against ground truth may require human annotation, expert review, or expensive simulation rather than inexpensive model inference. Test input prioritization addresses this problem by ranking inputs so that a limited verification budget reveals as many regression faults as possible. Existing approaches rely predominantly on single-model confidence scores and do not exploit how predictions, decision boundaries, and local neighborhoods change between model versions. We propose RiskBlend, a classifier-agnostic prioritization framework that combines four complementary risk signals: historical failure patterns, prediction shift, decision-boundary shift, and neighborhood change. These signals are combined using validation-learned APFD-squared weighting. Across four datasets, five classifiers, four regression-update scenarios, and 15 random seeds, totaling 1,200 experimental configurations, RiskBlend achieves the highest average APFD in all 80 dataset-classifier-scenario combinations, with improvements of up to 0.32 APFD over the strongest baseline. Confidence-based methods remain competitive primarily for linear classifiers on sparse categorical features, which we attribute to feature-space geometry. The results show that cross-version behavioral signals provide important complementary information for prioritizing regression faults in machine learning systems.

AI.tldr: RiskBlend is a regression test prioritization framework that combines multiple cross-version behavioral signals to efficiently detect misclassifications when ML models are updated, outperforming single-model confidence-based methods.
AI.motivation: When ML classifiers are retrained, regression faults occur where inputs previously classified correctly become misclassified. Verifying predictions is costly (requires human annotation, expert review, or expensive simulation), making efficient detection challenging with limited verification budgets.
AI.method: RiskBlend combines four complementary risk signals: 1) historical failure patterns, 2) prediction shift, 3) decision-boundary shift, and 4) neighborhood change. These signals are combined using validation-learned APFD-squared weighting, making it classifier-agnostic.
AI.result: Across 1,200 experimental configurations (4 datasets, 5 classifiers, 4 regression-update scenarios, 15 random seeds), RiskBlend achieved the highest average APFD in all 80 dataset-classifier-scenario combinations, with improvements up to 0.32 APFD over the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Cross-version behavioral signals provide important complementary information for prioritizing regression faults in ML systems. While confidence-based methods remain competitive for linear classifiers on sparse categorical features, RiskBlend's multi-signal approach significantly outperforms them in most scenarios.

title: SETU: An Agentic Ecosystem for Multilingual, Persona-Aware Communication Coaching
summary: Corporate training teams need scalable and explainable tools to improve workforce communication in multilingual settings. Existing systems often score text, audio, or video in isolation, or produce black-box outputs that are difficult to audit for coaching use. This paper presents SETU, an agentic ecosystem for corporate communication coaching aimed at recruiters, frontline sales professionals and training units who prepare for audience specific conversations. SETU is designed for two scoped scenarios: (i) recruiter-candidate eligibility-and-interest calls with persona context and (ii) sales pitches with target-audience adaptation; owing to limited evaluation resources, this paper reports results on scenario (ii) only. The ecosystem decomposes analysis into specialized video, audio-speech, text-relevance, scoring, notification and reporting agents coordinated through trust-aware orchestration. It generates modality-attributed coaching reports for formative training, with human reviewers retaining final judgment. The name SETU (bridge in several Indic languages) reflects the goal of bridging communication gaps across regional languages and audience expectations.

AI.tldr: SETU is an agentic ecosystem for corporate communication coaching that provides explainable, multimodal analysis for sales pitches and recruiter-candidate calls, with human-in-the-loop validation.
AI.motivation: Corporate training needs scalable, explainable tools for multilingual workforce communication improvement. Existing systems either analyze modalities in isolation or produce uninterpretable black-box outputs that lack auditability for coaching purposes.
AI.method: SETU decomposes communication analysis into specialized agents (video, audio-speech, text-relevance, scoring, notification, reporting) coordinated through trust-aware orchestration. It generates modality-attributed coaching reports with human reviewers retaining final judgment. Evaluated on sales pitch scenario (ii) due to limited resources.
AI.result: The paper reports results on scenario (ii) only - sales pitches with target-audience adaptation. The ecosystem produces explainable, modality-attributed coaching reports for formative training that can bridge communication gaps across regional languages and audience expectations.
AI.conclusion: SETU provides a scalable, explainable agentic ecosystem for corporate communication coaching that addresses the limitations of existing systems by offering multimodal, auditable analysis with human oversight, particularly valuable for multilingual business settings.

title: DART-FL: Burst-Aware Multitask Federated Learning under Dynamic Inference Demand at the Edge
summary:
Edge intelligence systems increasingly require model training and online inference to coexist on resource-constrained devices, while inference demand can vary substantially across tasks over time. This creates two coupled challenges: sufficient computation must be reserved for inference to maintain service-level objectives (SLOs), while the remaining training capacity should adapt to task-specific demand so that frequently requested tasks can improve earlier during training.
  We propose an SLO-aware, demand-driven multitask federated learning framework (DART-FL) that jointly adapts the inference-training resource split and task-level training emphasis. At each scheduling interval, DART-FL uses the inference backlog and profiled service capacity to determine the minimum resource allocation required for inference. The remaining training capacity is then distributed across tasks using a queue-aware DPP-inspired scheduler, and the resulting task allocations are mapped to dynamic loss weights. This allows tasks experiencing higher inference demand to receive greater training emphasis in earlier communication rounds. Clients train a shared backbone with task-specific heads, and the complete multitask model is aggregated through FedAvg.
  We evaluate DART-FL using Stanford Cars and Oxford Flowers 102 under both synthetic and real Alibaba trace-derived workloads. Results show that DART-FL dynamically adapts the inference-training resource split to time-varying inference demand and shifts the learning progress of high-demand tasks toward their burst periods, improving model accuracy when those tasks are frequently requested while maintaining comparable long-term multitask performance.

AI.tldr: DART-FL is a federated learning framework that dynamically balances inference and training resources on edge devices based on time-varying inference demand, allowing high-demand tasks to receive more training emphasis during their peak usage periods.
AI.motivation: Edge intelligence systems need to handle both model training and online inference on resource-constrained devices, with inference demand varying substantially across tasks over time. This creates challenges in maintaining service-level objectives for inference while adapting training capacity to task-specific demand patterns.
AI.method: DART-FL adapts the inference-training resource split and task-level training emphasis dynamically. It uses inference backlog and service capacity profiling to allocate minimum resources for inference, then distributes remaining training capacity across tasks using a queue-aware DPP-inspired scheduler. This maps to dynamic loss weights, allowing high-demand tasks to receive more training emphasis early. The framework employs a shared backbone with task-specific heads aggregated via FedAvg.
AI.result: Evaluation on Stanford Cars and Oxford Flowers 102 datasets with synthetic and real Alibaba trace workloads shows DART-FL successfully adapts resource allocation to time-varying inference demand and shifts learning progress of high-demand tasks toward their burst periods, improving model accuracy during frequent requests while maintaining comparable long-term multitask performance.
AI.conclusion: DART-FL effectively addresses the coupled challenges of inference SLO maintenance and demand-adaptive training in edge intelligence systems, enabling efficient resource utilization and timely model improvement for frequently requested tasks.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Moderator: A Compact Multimodal, Multilingual, and Reasoning Enabled Content Safety Moderator
summary: Safety moderation for deployed AI applications is moving beyond text-only prompts: systems increasingly need to judge images, documents, screenshots, and generated responses under policies that vary across domains. Existing guardrails usually cover only part of this setting, making it difficult to combine broad coverage, custom policy control, and low compute cost. We present Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Moderator, also referred to as Nemotron 3.5 CS in this paper for brevity, a compact 4B vision-language safety moderator that jointly classifies user prompts, images, and assistant responses across 12 languages. Nemotron 3.5 CS returns safety labels for latency-sensitive moderation and can additionally produce concise reasoning traces that apply supplied custom policies and identify violated categories when reasoning is requested. We also release a multimodal and multilingual safety dataset for guard training, spanning human-labeled real-image moderation, benign vision-language and document tasks, synthetic rare-risk and jailbreak cases, and custom-policy examples. Across evaluations spanning multimodal safety, text moderation, multilingual robustness, custom-policy following, benign false positives, and latency, Nemotron 3.5 CS demonstrates a practical coverage tradeoff: it adds image-conditioned and policy-conditioned moderation while remaining broadly competitive with specialized guard models. These results suggest that compact vision-language moderators can serve as deployable front-line safety components, with reasoning used selectively for audit and policy review.

AI.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 CS is a compact 4B vision-language safety moderator that classifies user prompts, images, and assistant responses across 12 languages, offering both latency-sensitive moderation and optional reasoning traces with custom policy support.
AI.motivation: Current AI safety moderation systems are inadequate for real-world deployment needs - they typically focus only on text, lack custom policy control, or are computationally expensive. There's a need for systems that can handle multimodal content (images, documents, screenshots, generated responses) with varying domain-specific policies while maintaining low compute costs.
AI.method: The authors present Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Moderator, a 4B parameter vision-language model trained on a released multimodal and multilingual safety dataset. This dataset includes human-labeled real-image moderation, benign vision-language tasks, synthetic rare-risk and jailbreak cases, and custom-policy examples. The system jointly classifies user prompts, images, and assistant responses across 12 languages.
AI.result: Nemotron 3.5 CS demonstrates practical coverage tradeoffs: it adds image-conditioned and policy-conditioned moderation while remaining competitive with specialized guard models. It performs well across evaluations including multimodal safety, text moderation, multilingual robustness, custom-policy following, benign false positives, and latency.
AI.conclusion: Compact vision-language moderators like Nemotron 3.5 CS can serve as effective deployable front-line safety components, with reasoning used selectively for audit and policy review purposes.

title: Beyond Non-IID: Learner--Client Distribution Mismatch in Federated Learning
summary:
Federated learning systems are increasingly deployed to facilitate collaborative model training across a heterogeneous client population. Existing practice mostly implicitly assumes that the aggregated client data distribution is representative of the learner's target distribution or that learning from all available clients is uniformly beneficial for the learner distribution. However, such an assumption often does not hold in reality. Traditional client selection strategies in FL literature largely overlook such misalignment, while most existing work on multi-source transfer learning either requires direct access to local data or uses one-shot model/feature aggregation.
  In this paper, we take the initiative to understand and mitigate the impacts of such learner-client population misalignment. In particular, we consider the practical setting where the learner keeps a small proxy dataset. We observe that client contributions vary significantly across training rounds, and traditional technology is insufficient to identify beneficial sources under multi-source transfer diversity. Then, we propose a dynamic, influence-aware client selection framework that estimates each client's potential utility to the learner's optimization objective using proxy influence signals on a learner-specific proxy set. Via using leave-one-out evaluations, we prioritize the most informative sources of knowledge while controlling the negative impacts of statistical noise and data heterogeneity. Experiments on CIFAR-10 under heterogeneous data partitions demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms static and dynamic baselines, achieving faster convergence and higher accuracy.

AI.tldr: Dynamic client selection framework for federated learning that uses proxy influence signals to prioritize informative clients when learner-client populations are misaligned.
AI.motivation: Existing FL systems assume aggregated client data represents target distribution, but this often doesn't hold in reality. Traditional client selection overlooks learner-client population misalignment, while multi-source transfer learning requires direct data access or simple aggregation.
AI.method: Proposes dynamic, influence-aware client selection framework that estimates each client's utility using proxy influence signals on a learner-specific proxy set. Uses leave-one-out evaluations to prioritize informative sources while controlling statistical noise and data heterogeneity.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 under heterogeneous data partitions show the approach consistently outperforms static and dynamic baselines, achieving faster convergence and higher accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed influence-aware client selection framework effectively addresses learner-client population misalignment in federated learning, enabling better knowledge transfer from heterogeneous clients.

title: LongGuard: Mechanistic Analysis and Training-Free Mitigation of Long-Context Failure in Safety Guardrails
summary: Safety guardrails serve as the last line of defense against harmful inputs and outputs of large language models (LLMs), yet they are trained and evaluated almost exclusively on short text. We present LongGuard, a framework that evaluates, mechanistically analyzes, and mitigates long-context guardrail failure. We formulate the task as Safety Needle-in-a-Haystack (SafetyNIAH) over a 0.25k-32k length grid; across 15 mainstream guardrails, unsafe recall drops monotonically by more than 50% on average, and a paired Benign-Fill vs. Needle-Repeat design attributes the failure to proportional dilution of the unsafe needle rather than to absolute length. A three-layer attention-logit-behavior analysis on six guardrails locates the mechanism: attention mass on the unsafe needle is diluted, the unsafe-over-safe logit margin is compressed in lockstep, and the detection decision collapses accordingly, with this attention->logit->behavior chain remaining consistent after partialling out length. We further isolate a sparse set of guard-specialized retrieval heads that exhibit partial specificity relative to their base models. Building on the analysis, we propose two training-free mitigations - Chunked Detection (CD) and Attention-Head Sharpening (AHS) - and a deployment protocol, Context-Aware Hyperparameter Routing (CAHR), that selects configurations by context length and audit side. Across five benchmarks spanning synthetic data, long-context attacks, and reasoning-model outputs, CAHR-CD and CAHR-AHS improve the six-guardrail average by 22% and 13%, respectively. Code and data are available online.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LongGuard, a framework for evaluating and improving safety guardrails for LLMs on long-context inputs, showing that current guardrails fail on long text and proposing mitigations.
AI.motivation: Current safety guardrails for LLMs are trained and evaluated almost exclusively on short text, creating a vulnerability where harmful content in long contexts can evade detection.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Safety Needle-in-a-Haystack (SafetyNIAH) task across 0.25k-32k length ranges, conduct mechanistic analysis using attention-logit-behavior analysis, and propose training-free mitigations including Chunked Detection and Attention-Head Sharpening.
AI.result: Unsafe recall drops by more than 50% on average across 15 mainstream guardrails as context length increases. The proposed Context-Aware Hyperparameter Routing with CD and AHS improves performance by 22% and 13% respectively across five benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: LongGuard successfully addresses the critical vulnerability of safety guardrails on long-context inputs through systematic evaluation, mechanistic understanding, and practical mitigation strategies.

title: Leveraging a Foundation Model for the EEG-Based Diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Accepted and presented at the 48th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC 2026)
summary: Biological heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) poses a critical diagnostic challenge, particularly for traditional linear methods that fail to capture non-linear neural dynamics. To address this, we propose a diagnostic framework utilizing the Large Brain Model (LaBraM), pretrained on over 2,500 hours of EEG data. By integrating these high-dimensional latent embeddings with a non-linear Random Forest classifier, our approach effectively isolates robust disease markers. Under a rigorous subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation protocol, the method achieves an ROC-AUC of 89.36% +/- 3.49%, PR AUC of 81.45% +/- 4.43%, and Balanced Accuracy of 82.44% +/- 4.34% in distinguishing dementia patients from healthy controls. Notably, this performance uses only 8-second EEG segments, surpassing traditional spectral baselines, including band-power and parameterized oscillatory features (FOOOF). Post-hoc occlusion analysis confirms the model captures clinically validated biomarkers, specifically occipital-frontal Alpha and Theta rhythm degradation. Additional neurophysiological alignment analysis demonstrated that higher LaBraM-predicted dementia probability significantly correlated with worse cognitive performance, greater clinical severity, increased theta and alpha relative power, and higher aperiodic exponent. These findings demonstrate that deep latent representations extract clinically relevant signatures from noisy signals, enabling precise, rapid, and data-efficient diagnosis.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework (LaBraM) using EEG data achieves high accuracy in Alzheimer's diagnosis by capturing non-linear neural dynamics with only 8-second segments.
AI.motivation: Biological heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease poses diagnostic challenges for traditional linear methods that fail to capture non-linear neural dynamics in EEG signals.
AI.method: Proposes a diagnostic framework using Large Brain Model (LaBraM) pretrained on 2,500+ hours of EEG data, integrating high-dimensional latent embeddings with a non-linear Random Forest classifier for disease marker isolation.
AI.result: Achieves ROC-AUC of 89.36% ± 3.49%, PR AUC of 81.45% ± 4.43%, and Balanced Accuracy of 82.44% ± 4.34% under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation. Post-hoc analysis confirms capture of clinically validated biomarkers (occipital-frontal Alpha/Theta degradation). Higher dementia probability correlates with worse cognitive performance and clinical severity.
AI.conclusion: Deep latent representations can extract clinically relevant signatures from noisy EEG signals, enabling precise, rapid, and data-efficient Alzheimer's diagnosis that surpasses traditional spectral methods.

title: Generative AI Expands the Intellectual Reach of Course Based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs)
summary: Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) broaden access to authentic scientific inquiry through responsive instructor support as research problems become increasingly complex. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may extend this support by providing individualized assistance that can adapt as student needs change. However, how embedding GenAI within a CURE to provide support across the research process impacts student inquiry, collaboration, and scientific reasoning remains unresolved. Here we use longitudinal qualitative data collected across three semesters of a bioinformatics and genomics CURE to show that GenAI expanded the intellectual reach of the research experience in three distinct ways. First, personalized, on-demand scaffolding allowed students to move beyond the boundaries of instructor expertise and transform their own interests into researchable inquiry, with all teams developing distinct self-directed projects rather than selecting instructor-provided topics. Second, GenAI became part of the distributed cognitive system of research teams, helping novice researchers communicate and coordinate across differentiated expertise without eliminating specialization. Third, expanded capability did not replace the need for disciplinary judgment. Students increasingly validated, revised, or rejected AI-generated contributions, such that research independence emerged through retained intellectual responsibility. Together, these findings suggest that GenAI can extend the reach of CUREs by expanding what novice researchers can investigate, how they can collaborate, and the level of responsibility they can assume while preserving human judgment central to authentic scientific inquiry.

AI.tldr: GenAI integration in CUREs expands research capacity, enabling personalized student-driven projects, enhancing team collaboration, and fostering research independence while preserving human scientific judgment.
AI.motivation: Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) broaden access to authentic scientific inquiry, but complex research problems require responsive instructor support. Generative AI may provide individualized, adaptive support throughout the research process, though its impacts on student inquiry, collaboration, and scientific reasoning in CUREs remain unknown.
AI.method: Used longitudinal qualitative data collected across three semesters of a bioinformatics and genomics CURE to examine how embedding GenAI within the research process impacts student learning and scientific practices.
AI.result: GenAI expanded the intellectual reach of the research experience in three ways: 1) Personalized scaffolding allowed students to move beyond instructor expertise boundaries, with all teams developing distinct self-directed projects; 2) GenAI became part of distributed cognitive systems, helping novice researchers coordinate across expertise without eliminating specialization; 3) Students increasingly validated, revised, or rejected AI-generated contributions, with research independence emerging through retained intellectual responsibility.
AI.conclusion: GenAI can extend the reach of CUREs by expanding what novice researchers can investigate, how they can collaborate, and the level of responsibility they can assume while preserving human judgment central to authentic scientific inquiry.

title: Diffusion Distillation for Efficient Weather Ensembles
summary: Diffusion models generate skillful weather ensembles but require costly iterative sampling. We introduce a supervised energy-distance distillation method that compresses a multi-step diffusion teacher into a single-step student by aligning student forecasts with teacher samples and ground-truth observations. Experiments on global forecasting and typhoon-track prediction show that our student outperforms existing distillation methods and preserves skill for extreme events. It matches or surpasses the teacher across key metrics using only one neural function evaluation per autoregressive step.

AI.tldr: A supervised distillation method compresses multi-step weather diffusion models into single-step students using energy-distance alignment, achieving comparable skill with dramatically reduced computational cost.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models produce accurate weather ensembles but suffer from high computational costs due to iterative sampling, limiting their practical deployment for real-time forecasting.
AI.method: Energy-distance distillation that compresses a multi-step diffusion teacher into a single-step student by aligning student forecasts with both teacher-generated samples and ground-truth observations.
AI.result: The distilled single-step student outperforms existing distillation methods, preserves skill for extreme events, matches or surpasses the teacher across key metrics, and requires only one neural function evaluation per autoregressive step.
AI.conclusion: The proposed distillation method enables efficient weather forecasting with diffusion model quality, making ensemble weather prediction practical for operational use through dramatically reduced computational requirements.

title: If Agents Were Angels, No Governance Would Be Necessary: Out-of-Band Policy Enforcement at a Trusted Tool Boundary
summary:
Give an agent a human's credential and it inherits the person's reach without the judgment that limits its use. It can sweep every reachable record into model context, where hidden instructions steer its next call, and every request stays credential-valid while the agent exceeds its job or absorbs a secret. Prompts are a brittle guardrail: one fallible reasoner interprets the task and enforces its limits.
  We present Out-of-Band Policy Enforcement (OBPE), a trusted boundary outside agent reasoning. It authorizes the typed operation and resource, narrows the query before the backend call, then filters records and fields or masks values in the response. Semantic gating can deny or hold an authorized call on argument values or external state. A data policy owner sets the maximum grant; agent policy can only narrow it. We prove, under stated conditions, that the policy plan is order-independent and agent policy cannot widen the ceiling. Field removal covers one execution; masking and history rules claim less.
  We release an HTTP proxy prototype simplified from our production system, with conformance tests tying its typed Cedar policy core to the model. Against Jira and ServiceNow mocks, our benchmark compares prompted agents with and without OBPE on four models, including 20 adaptive red-team tasks. A trace failure means protected data entered agent context, an exact value appeared in the answer, or a forbidden effect completed. In 3,621 trials it fell from 57.6% to 0.2%, a cluster-weighted reduction of 41.2 points [95% CI: 27.7, 54.9]; fulfillment fell from 79.1% to 60.9%, while paired safe-useful completion rose 21.8 points [9.5, 35.2]. Some answers reconstructed a value that never entered context or used filtered row counts as an oracle: shaping one execution is not noninterference. Write controls, durable approval, and temporal and aggregate policies lie outside this evaluation.

AI.tldr: Out-of-Band Policy Enforcement (OBPE) is a security framework that places a trusted boundary outside AI agent reasoning to prevent unauthorized data access and actions, reducing security failures from 57.6% to 0.2% while maintaining task completion rates.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents with human credentials can access all reachable records without proper judgment limits, making prompts brittle guardrails that fail to prevent unauthorized data access, secret absorption, or job scope exceedance.
AI.method: OBPE creates a trusted boundary that: 1) authorizes typed operations and resources, 2) narrows queries before backend calls, 3) filters records/fields or masks values in responses, and 4) uses semantic gating to deny/hold authorized calls based on arguments or external state. Policies have a ceiling (maximum grant set by data owner) and agent policies can only narrow permissions. The approach includes an HTTP proxy prototype with Cedar policy core tied to the model.
AI.result: In 3,621 trials across four models with 20 adaptive red-team tasks against Jira and ServiceNow mocks, security failures (protected data entering agent context, exact value appearing in answer, or forbidden effect completion) dropped from 57.6% to 0.2% - a cluster-weighted reduction of 41.2 points [95% CI: 27.7, 54.9]. Task fulfillment fell from 79.1% to 60.9%, but paired safe-useful completion rose 21.8 points [9.5, 35.2].
AI.conclusion: OBPE effectively secures AI agents from unauthorized data access while maintaining reasonable task completion rates, though some limitations remain (answers can reconstruct values that never entered context, filtered row counts can serve as oracles, and shaping single executions doesn't guarantee noninterference). Write controls, durable approval, temporal and aggregate policies were outside this evaluation scope.

title: The Calls are Coming from Inside the Model: Investigating Probe-based Detection of Tool-Calling Errors in LLMs
comment: 4 main pages, 8 pages of references and appendices
summary: The hidden states of large language models (LLMs) are known to capture rich information relating to model knowledge and behavior that can be hard to extract from examination of input and output alone. As LLM-based systems increasingly interface with the external world, one area of concern is detecting incorrect or improper use of tools. Motivated by this, we study the effectiveness of using linear probes to detect incorrect tool-calls, measuring probe efficacy across 18 tool-calling LLMs evaluated on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard. Overall, we find that probing is an effective means to catch a range of different tool-calling errors, including errors arising from using an argument that has the wrong value but the correct type, which might not be recorded by standard logging frameworks. Important factors in success include model size, probing layer, and model post-training type. We also show that probes are capable of generalizing to novel types of errors, which is critical in real world deployments.

AI.tldr: Using linear probes on LLM hidden states effectively detects various tool-calling errors across 18 models, with generalization capabilities to novel error types.
AI.motivation: LLM hidden states contain rich information about model knowledge and behavior that's hard to extract from just input/output. As LLMs increasingly interface with external tools, there's a need to detect incorrect or improper tool usage to ensure reliable system operation.
AI.method: Applied linear probes to LLM hidden states to detect incorrect tool-calls. Evaluated across 18 different tool-calling LLMs using the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard. Studied factors affecting probe efficacy including model size, probing layer, and model post-training type.
AI.result: Probing is effective for catching various tool-calling errors, including subtle errors like wrong argument values with correct types (which standard logging might miss). Success factors identified: model size, probing layer, and post-training type. Probes generalize to novel error types, crucial for real-world deployments.
AI.conclusion: Linear probing of LLM hidden states provides a promising approach for detecting tool-calling errors in real-world deployments, with demonstrated generalization capabilities to novel error types and effectiveness across diverse model architectures.

title: A Framework for Object-Centric Predictive Monitoring of Collaborative Processes
comment: Submitted to Information Systems, under review
summary: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) of collaborative, inter-organizational processes requires reasoning over multiple interdependent entities, including participants, messages, local executions, and the global collaboration case. Existing approaches extend traditional event logs with collaboration attributes but retain a single-case perspective, leaving much of this structure implicit. Object-centric process mining (OCPM) provides an alternative by representing these entities as first-class objects with explicit relations and multiple notions of case. This study connects collaborative PPM and OCPM through three contributions: (i) a formal semantic mapping from extended collaborative event logs to an OCED-conformant object-centric representation, serialized in OCEL 2.0; (ii) a reformulation of collaborative prediction tasks as object-centric prediction tasks; and (iii) a reproducible converter and prediction pipeline implementing the proposed mapping. We evaluate the framework on four public collaborative event logs and a fifth derived from the BPI Challenge 2013 incident-management log by executing the fourteen reformulated tasks using five predictive strategies across tabular, sequential, and graph-native encodings. We further discuss the benefits, limitations, and threats to the approach's validity. The representation makes collaboration structure explicit and makes it natural to state prediction targets based on object relations that fall outside the case-centric taxonomy, at the cost of increased relational complexity and dependence on object-centric tooling.

AI.tldr: This paper connects collaborative predictive process monitoring with object-centric process mining by mapping collaborative event logs to object-centric representations, reformulating prediction tasks, and providing an implementation pipeline.
AI.motivation: Existing collaborative process monitoring approaches retain a single-case perspective, leaving complex collaboration structures implicit and limiting the ability to reason about multiple interdependent entities like participants, messages, and executions.
AI.method: Three contributions: 1) formal semantic mapping from collaborative event logs to object-centric representation (OCEL 2.0), 2) reformulation of collaborative prediction tasks as object-centric tasks, 3) reproducible converter and prediction pipeline implementation.
AI.result: Evaluation on four public collaborative logs and one derived from BPI Challenge 2013 shows successful execution of 14 reformulated tasks using five predictive strategies across tabular, sequential, and graph-native encodings.
AI.conclusion: The object-centric representation makes collaboration structure explicit and enables natural specification of prediction targets based on object relations, though it introduces increased relational complexity and dependence on specialized object-centric tooling.

title: Beyond Search-Imitation: Prior-Directed Exploration for Searchless Chess
summary: Searchless chess networks reach human master strength from a single forward pass by imitating a stronger teacher: the strongest, Leela Chess Zero's (Lc0) released Chessformer, distills the visit counts of an AlphaZero-style Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Imitating a search is a poor proxy for playing without one, so we fine-tune for single-pass strength with self-play reinforcement learning (RL). Its exploration is usually supplied by an entropy bonus, the reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to uniform. We replace it with a forward, mass-covering KL toward the network's own MCTS prior (prior-directed exploration), so exploration covers the moves the prior judges promising, and pair it with an entropy-adaptive sampling temperature, set by the value head's outcome uncertainty, that sharpens once a position is decided. In about two thousand steps it raises puzzle accuracy from 93.9% to 94.9% on a 100,000-puzzle suite and mate-in-four accuracy from 77% to 81% while holding searchless strength at or slightly above the base. Measuring tactical accuracy and playing strength together across a matched-compute sweep, we find the two dissociate: accuracy gains fall in a one-point band while ratings straddle the base, and a control fine-tuned on puzzles alone posts the study's largest tactical gains while shedding roughly 260 Elo; a better puzzle-solver is not thereby a stronger player. Distribution-level measurements show what anchoring buys: without a regularizer self-play collapses onto a single line of play, and the puzzles newly solved are the near misses whose winning move the prior kept alive. The forward-KL prior tops the rating ladder, statistically tied with a reverse-KL anchor that concentrates twice as hard and drops the hardest solutions the mass-covering prior keeps in support.

AI.tldr: Searchless chess networks achieve master strength via teacher imitation and RL fine-tuning with prior-directed exploration and adaptive temperature, improving tactical accuracy while maintaining playing strength.
AI.motivation: Current searchless chess networks imitate stronger teachers with search, but this is a poor proxy for actual single-pass play. There's a need to improve the fine-tuning process to better balance tactical accuracy with overall playing strength.
AI.method: 1) Start with Lc0's Chessformer distilled from MCTS visit counts; 2) Replace standard entropy-based exploration with forward KL divergence toward network's own MCTS prior (prior-directed exploration); 3) Use entropy-adaptive sampling temperature based on value head's outcome uncertainty; 4) Fine-tune with self-play RL.
AI.result: Improved puzzle accuracy from 93.9% to 94.9% on 100,000-puzzle suite, mate-in-four accuracy from 77% to 81% while maintaining searchless strength. Forward-KL prior tops rating ladder, tied with reverse-KL anchor that concentrates more but drops hardest solutions.
AI.conclusion: Tactical accuracy and playing strength dissociate - better puzzle-solving doesn't automatically mean stronger play. Prior-directed exploration anchors exploration to promising moves, preventing self-play collapse while solving previously near-miss puzzles.

title: Agents for Everyone: A Workshop Framework for Building Agentic AI Capabilities in a Distributed Curation Community
summary: Agentic AI has the potential to accelerate curation of biological databases and knowledge bases. However, uptake has been hindered by a number of challenges and obstacles, including access to agents and appropriate training. Here we describe how we have attempted to address and mitigate these challenges and obstacles through the deployment of a cloud-based agentic environment, and the development of an interactive training workshop for the Gene Ontology Consortium. Our cloud environment for agentic-assisted curation was based on the JupyterHub platform, and utilized Claude Code as a universal harness. This allows curators to interact with an agent session through a terminal running in the browser, and has additional benefits such as centralization of access through a single API gateway, removing the need for participants to manage subscriptions or install software locally. We created four training modules, walking participants through basic agentic tool use first and then working up to agentic biological pathway curation using the existing GO-CAM (GO Causal Activity Model) curation tool. Thirty-seven participants took part in the four-hour workshop. Our key takeaway from this workshop is that building community capability with agentic AI is primarily a problem of access, workflow design, and training. Removing technical barriers, introducing capabilities gradually, grounding exercises in familiar curation tasks, and giving curators direct experience evaluating agent output can provide a practical route toward building shared agentic AI capability in distributed scientific communities.

AI.tldr: A practical approach to overcoming barriers to agentic AI adoption in biological curation through cloud-based deployment and interactive training workshops for the Gene Ontology Consortium.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI has potential to accelerate biological database curation but faces adoption challenges including limited access to agents, technical barriers, and lack of appropriate training within scientific communities.
AI.method: Deployed a cloud-based agentic environment using JupyterHub with Claude Code as a universal harness, allowing browser-based terminal interaction. Developed four training modules progressing from basic tool use to biological pathway curation using GO-CAM tool. Conducted a four-hour workshop with 37 participants.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrated that removing technical barriers and providing hands-on training enables curators to effectively use agentic AI. The workshop showed curators could gain practical experience evaluating agent output for familiar curation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Building community capability with agentic AI is primarily about access, workflow design, and training. Gradual introduction of capabilities, grounding exercises in familiar tasks, and direct experience evaluating agent output provide practical routes to shared AI capability in distributed scientific communities.

title: Fast Weight Attention for Continual Learning
summary: Recurrent fast-weight memories and selective state-space models compress an expanding context into a fixed-size recurrent state, making the state transition an online learning rule. We study this rule under read-after-write autoregressive semantics. For the prefix-prediction objective considered here, the local fast-memory example revealed at step $t$ is the prefix-aligned pair $(\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{y}_t)=(φ(\mathbf{k}_{t-1}),\mathbf{v}_t)$. The common same-step association $(φ(\mathbf{k}_t),\mathbf{v}_t)$ remains causal, but optimizes a different internal objective. We derive normalized first-order updates for squared-error regression and negative inner-product objectives. The regression family comprises Falcon-1 (a scalar NLMS update), Falcon-2 (its per-column extension), and Falcon-3 (a sliding-window mini-batch update); Falcon-1A/Falcon-2A/Falcon-3A are the corresponding inner-product variants. We provide recurrent, masked-parallel, and chunk-parallel forms, together with numerically stable positive-decay renormalization. Representative variants remain competitive in language modeling and improve length extrapolation on variable-digit addition. This framework separates temporal alignment, plasticity, forgetting, and bounded rehearsal in recurrent sequence models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Falcon family of fast-weight memory models that implement online learning rules for sequence modeling, with variants for different objectives and parallelization forms.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of compressing expanding context into fixed-size recurrent states in sequence models, and to separate temporal alignment, plasticity, forgetting, and bounded rehearsal in recurrent architectures.
AI.method: Derives normalized first-order updates for squared-error regression and negative inner-product objectives under read-after-write autoregressive semantics, creating the Falcon family (1-3 for regression, 1A-3A for inner-product variants) with recurrent, masked-parallel, and chunk-parallel forms using stable positive-decay renormalization.
AI.result: The Falcon framework produces competitive language modeling performance and improves length extrapolation on variable-digit addition tasks, demonstrating effective online learning in recurrent models.
AI.conclusion: The Falcon framework successfully separates key components of sequence modeling (temporal alignment, plasticity, forgetting, bounded rehearsal) in recurrent architectures and provides a unified approach to fast-weight memories with practical variants for different computational constraints.

title: PCFBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Product Carbon Footprint Estimation
summary: AI systems are being deployed on high-stakes, domain-specific workflows that demand correctness not just in the final output, but at every intermediate step. One such workflow is estimating a product carbon footprint (PCF), the greenhouse-gas emissions attributable to a physical product. AI agents are increasingly being used to generate PCFs, but existing evaluations score either total emissions (hiding error sources and cancelling mistakes) or sub-tasks in isolation (missing compositional interactions). We introduce PCFBench, the first benchmark to carve PCF modeling into independently-evaluable tasks that require decomposition, retrieval, ontology matching, and numerical extraction. It comprises 614 expert-labelled items across six tasks. Together they probe reasoning under under-specification, conflicting context, and numerical constraints. Across eight frontier LLMs from four providers, no single model dominates. Although the strongest models estimate total product emissions within 2 times of declared totals on 77% of products, this rate drops to 37-58% when the PCF is generated step by step, with only 45-75% obeying mass conservation. These failures undermine the transparency practitioners need to compare products and drive decarbonization. We release the dataset and evaluation harness to support targeted progress.

AI.tldr: AI systems struggle with compositional reasoning in product carbon footprint (PCF) estimation, where step-by-step accuracy is crucial despite overall emission estimates appearing reasonable.
AI.motivation: AI agents are increasingly used for high-stakes PCF estimation workflows that demand correctness at every intermediate step, not just final outputs, but existing evaluations either hide error sources or miss compositional interactions.
AI.method: Introduces PCFBench, the first benchmark that carves PCF modeling into six independently-evaluable tasks requiring decomposition, retrieval, ontology matching, and numerical extraction, comprising 614 expert-labelled items.
AI.result: Across eight frontier LLMs, no single model dominates. While strongest models estimate total emissions within 2x of declared totals on 77% of products, this drops to 37-58% when generated step-by-step, with only 45-75% obeying mass conservation.
AI.conclusion: Current AI failures in stepwise PCF estimation undermine transparency needed to compare products and drive decarbonization, highlighting the need for compositional reasoning in high-stakes domain workflows.

title: Initialization Is Critical: Advancing Federated Short-Term Load Forecasting under Load Heterogeneity via Model Initialization
summary: Short-term load forecasting (STLF) provides essential information for numerous applications in modern power systems. However, accurate STLF often relies on fine-grained smart-meter data from distributed users, raising increasing concerns about data privacy. Federated learning (FL) has therefore emerged as a promising privacy-preserving paradigm for STLF. Nevertheless, this paper reveals structured heterogeneity in clients' load data. Specifically, clients exhibit different responses to exogenous factors and distinct temporal load profiles, which can degrade forecasting performance in FL. To mitigate these issues, this paper studies the role of model initialization in federated STLF, and proposes two initialization strategies from global and local perspectives. For global model initialization, when auxiliary public load data are available, a pretrained initialization strategy is developed to initialize the global model before federated training, thereby reducing client drift during the training process. For local model initialization, we propose SLIAvg, a sequential local initialization strategy that promotes a more consistent training process by allowing participating clients to start from progressively adapted models within each communication round. Since the proposed strategies only modify the initialization process, they are compatible with most existing FL frameworks and privacy-enhancing techniques. Experiments on real smart-meter data with two representative forecasting architectures demonstrate that the proposed strategies effectively improve forecasting performance, as evidenced by reduced client drift, improved convergence behavior, and lower forecasting errors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two model initialization strategies for federated short-term load forecasting to address data heterogeneity issues: global pretraining on public data and sequential local initialization, both compatible with existing FL frameworks.
AI.motivation: Federated learning (FL) is promising for privacy-preserving STLF but suffers from performance degradation due to structured heterogeneity in clients' load data - different responses to exogenous factors and distinct temporal load profiles.
AI.method: Two initialization strategies: 1) Global perspective - pretrained initialization using auxiliary public load data to initialize global model before federated training. 2) Local perspective - SLIAvg (sequential local initialization strategy) where clients start from progressively adapted models within each communication round.
AI.result: Experiments on real smart-meter data show both strategies effectively improve forecasting performance, evidenced by reduced client drift, improved convergence behavior, and lower forecasting errors across two representative forecasting architectures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed initialization strategies provide effective solutions to mitigate structured heterogeneity in federated STLF while maintaining compatibility with existing FL frameworks and privacy techniques, offering practical improvements for privacy-preserving load forecasting.

title: Probing Perceptual Priors of MLLMs via Gibbs Sampling with Interpretable Generative Controls
summary: A model's behavior on a task is jointly determined by the input it receives and the prior it brings in, i.e. the distribution over stimuli it implicitly expects. Interpretability research has traditionally studied models by holding inputs fixed and examining model responses either mechanistically, probing how internal structure represents inputs, or behaviorally, measuring how variation in inputs leads to variation in outputs. Neither reconstructs the prior distribution itself, since internal structure shows what a model can represent, not what it expects, and any fixed stimulus set leaves most of the possible input space unseen. In particular, such an input space in real-world settings, such as images seen by VLMs, is extremely high-dimensional and diverse. These priors thus remain a poorly understood component of models that nonetheless influence real-world behavior. We propose a method to sample from models' perceptual prior distributions directly, by steering a generative model to produce stimuli along controllable axes and running Gibbs sampling over that space with the model under study as the judge. We apply this to a variety of categories and target variables (such as trustworthiness in faces and cheapness in art images) and recover both canonical biases and surprising novel priors invisible to direct prompting, warranting further investigation of their downstream effects.

AI.tldr: A method to directly sample from models' perceptual priors using generative models and Gibbs sampling, revealing hidden biases and expectations that influence model behavior but are normally invisible to traditional interpretability approaches.
AI.motivation: Current interpretability research fails to reconstruct models' perceptual priors - their implicit expectations about input distributions. Traditional methods either examine internal representations (what models can represent) or measure input-output variations, but both hold inputs fixed and thus leave most of the possible input space unseen, especially in high-dimensional real-world settings like images for VLMs. These priors remain poorly understood yet significantly influence real-world model behavior.
AI.method: Propose a method to directly sample from models' perceptual prior distributions by steering a generative model to produce stimuli along controllable axes and running Gibbs sampling over that space with the target model as the judge. This allows exploration of the full input space rather than being limited to fixed stimulus sets.
AI.result: Applied the method to various categories and target variables (such as trustworthiness in faces and cheapness in art images). Recovered both canonical biases and surprising novel priors that were invisible to direct prompting. The findings warrant further investigation of these priors' downstream effects on model behavior.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully reveals hidden perceptual priors in models, providing a new approach to understanding how models' implicit expectations shape their behavior. These discovered priors, including both expected biases and unexpected patterns, demonstrate the importance of studying models' prior distributions as a crucial component of their overall behavior in real-world applications.

title: Node-wise Feature Encoding for Neural Performance Prediction
summary: As neural networks are increasingly deployed on resource constrained edge devices, accurate prediction of latency and energy is critical for efficient neural architecture search. Existing GNN and transformer based predictors achieve strong results but largely ignore node-level computational cost, limiting their ability to model performance critical operations. To address this, we introduce FeatureFormer, a neural performance predictor that incorporates explicit node-wise encodings of FLOPs, parameter counts, and memory proxies within a gated graph attention architecture. We also present NNEQ, a new large-scale energy consumption dataset that enables unified evaluation of latency and energy prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FeatureFormer achieves state-of-the-art performance across both metrics, including challenging out-of-domain settings. Finally, we show that the proposed encoding is broadly applicable and consistently improves existing predictors with negligible overhead.

AI.tldr: FeatureFormer is a neural performance predictor that incorporates node-level computational cost encodings (FLOPs, parameters, memory) into a gated graph attention architecture, achieving state-of-the-art performance for latency and energy prediction in neural architecture search.
AI.motivation: As neural networks deploy on resource-constrained edge devices, accurate prediction of latency and energy is critical for efficient neural architecture search (NAS). Existing GNN and transformer predictors ignore node-level computational cost, limiting their ability to model performance-critical operations.
AI.method: Introduces FeatureFormer, a neural performance predictor that incorporates explicit node-wise encodings of FLOPs, parameter counts, and memory proxies within a gated graph attention architecture. Also presents NNEQ, a new large-scale energy consumption dataset for unified evaluation.
AI.result: FeatureFormer achieves state-of-the-art performance across both latency and energy prediction metrics, including challenging out-of-domain settings. The proposed encoding consistently improves existing predictors with negligible overhead.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating node-level computational cost encodings is crucial for accurate performance prediction in NAS, and FeatureFormer's approach provides a broadly applicable solution that significantly outperforms existing methods while introducing minimal overhead.

title: Why Didn't It Check? Unsupported Final Claims and Their Repair in Two Tool-Equipped Language Models
summary: A language model with access to tools can commit to a final claim unsupported by the evidence it has seen, even when a single available tool call would resolve the uncertainty and its instructions explicitly forbid assumptions and guesses. We separate this failure into two precisely defined quantities: occurrence, how often the model makes an unsupported claim on its own, measured from the visible evidence and final claim without using the hidden correct answer; and conditional repair, how often those same naturally occurring unsupported claims are repaired when the missing evidence is supplied. On one fixed Qwen3-32B setup, 33 of 512 first responses to 256 new prompt templates ended with an unsupported established claim. We replayed each case from an exact copy of the state in which the claim occurred; within each matched replay, the alternative tool responses had the same structure and length and differed only in a one-character response code. Resolving evidence repaired 33 of 33 claims; a matched response carrying no useful information repaired 0 of 33. When the evidence supported the original answer, the model preserved 33 of 33, with no observed harm. In a separate experiment, on 64 cases where evidence was needed, an automatic checking rule added 21 evidence calls, corrected all 10 wrong unsupported claims, preserved the 11 that were correct by accident, and never changed a correct answer into a wrong one. On a fixed Gemma 4 setup using the same sampling settings, the model called the tool in all 512 first responses and never made an unsupported final claim, so conditional repair could not be measured for that setup. These results describe two local fixed model setups on two synthetic task families. They do not show how common this failure is in real-world deployments, nor that it reflects a general mechanism shared across models.

AI.tldr: LLMs can make unsupported claims despite available evidence tools, but automatically providing missing evidence can effectively repair these errors without harming correct answers.
AI.motivation: To investigate how language models with tool access sometimes commit to unsupported final claims even when available tools could resolve uncertainty, contrary to explicit instructions against assumptions and guesses.
AI.method: Define two metrics: occurrence (frequency of unsupported claims based on visible evidence) and conditional repair (how often those claims are fixed when missing evidence is supplied). Conduct controlled experiments on Qwen3-32B and Gemma 4 models with synthetic tasks, replaying claim states and testing alternative tool responses.
AI.result: On Qwen3-32B: 33/512 first responses had unsupported claims; all 33 were repaired when missing evidence provided; 0/33 repaired with non-informative responses; 33/33 correct claims preserved when evidence supported them. Automatic checking added 21 evidence calls and corrected all 10 wrong unsupported claims without harming correct answers. Gemma 4 always called tools and never made unsupported claims.
AI.conclusion: Models can make evidence-lacking claims even with available tools, but systematic evidence provision effectively repairs these errors. However, findings are limited to specific setups and synthetic tasks - real-world prevalence and cross-model generalizability remain unknown.

title: Actionable CBFI: Integrating Structural Decomposition and Causal Counterfactual Recourse for Tabular Machine Learning
summary: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) increasingly calls for actionable counterfactual recourse, yet current methodologies face challenges related to causal invalidity, excessive cognitive burden, and predictive failure. Exhaustive causal search algorithms often require modifications to multiple attributes, whereas additive attribution-guided methods, such as SHAP, ignore higher-order feature synergies, leading to suboptimal predictive momentum and diffuse intervention effort in complex nonlinear models, such as XGBoost. To bridge this gap, we introduce actionable case-based feature importance (A-CBFI), a diagnosis-prescription integrated framework for tabular machine learning. Grounded in structural causal models (SCMs), A-CBFI isolates synergistic interaction bottlenecks and releases suppressive structural locks, translating them into targeted interventions. By mathematically separating the active user intervention space (L_{\mathrm{active}}) from downstream effects and concentrating over 98.3% of the intervention effort on diagnosed root causes, A-CBFI enables highly targeted interventions. Empirical evaluations across the financial and healthcare domains demonstrate that A-CBFI reduces the active human intervention burden by 76.9% while maintaining comparable global recourse cost to exhaustive causal baselines. By prioritizing the diagnosed causal bottlenecks, A-CBFI provides targeted and actionable recourse while maintaining causal validity and achieving full relative convergence across all causally feasible instances.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces A-CBFI, an actionable case-based feature importance framework that provides targeted counterfactual recourse by isolating synergistic interaction bottlenecks and concentrating intervention effort on root causes, reducing human intervention burden by 76.9% while maintaining causal validity.
AI.motivation: Current XAI methods for counterfactual recourse face challenges: causal invalidity, excessive cognitive burden, and predictive failure. Exhaustive causal search requires modifying many attributes, while additive attribution methods like SHAP ignore higher-order feature synergies, leading to suboptimal results in complex nonlinear models like XGBoost.
AI.method: Proposes A-CBFI (actionable case-based feature importance), a diagnosis-prescription framework grounded in structural causal models (SCMs). It isolates synergistic interaction bottlenecks, releases suppressive structural locks, and mathematically separates active user intervention space from downstream effects, concentrating over 98.3% of intervention effort on diagnosed root causes.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations in financial and healthcare domains show A-CBFI reduces active human intervention burden by 76.9% while maintaining comparable global recourse cost to exhaustive causal baselines. It achieves full relative convergence across all causally feasible instances.
AI.conclusion: A-CBFI provides targeted, actionable recourse that maintains causal validity while significantly reducing human intervention burden, bridging the gap between exhaustive causal search and additive attribution methods for complex nonlinear models.

title: Credo: Reusable Declarative Primitives for Agentic Workflows
summary: An LLM application depends on both a model and a harness: the program that determines what each call sees, how many calls to make, and which answers to trust. Coding agents can now discover strong harnesses by searching over candidate programs, but the resulting artifact is an opaque block of imperative code whose logical steps, runtime signals, physical execution decisions, and prompt strategies remain implicit and task-specific, forcing subsequent tasks to start the harness search process from scratch. The potential for reuse, however, is substantial. A searched harness encodes significant knowledge, such as the logical steps that work, the signals that matter, the physical operator decisions that adapt execution, and the prompt strategies that are effective, yet this knowledge is buried in imperative code with no inspectable or reusable structure, nor does it carry any provenance or metadata. Credo addresses this problem by recovering a structured declarative description of a searched harness, tagging each extracted primitive with relevant metadata, and cataloguing all of it with provenance. A compiler can then bind stored primitives to generate harnesses for new tasks without having to start the search over from scratch. This paper provides preliminary results demonstrating the potential of our approach and lays out a related research agenda that the database community is well-positioned to tackle, including cost-based compilation over declarative catalogs and catalog maintenance under model and workload drift.

AI.tldr: Credo extracts structured declarative knowledge from opaque imperative harness code discovered by LLM agents, enabling reuse across tasks without restarting search from scratch.
AI.motivation: LLM applications combine models with harnesses (programs that control calls, execution, and trust), and while coding agents can discover effective harnesses through search, the resulting imperative code is opaque and task-specific, forcing new tasks to restart the search process despite the valuable knowledge embedded in existing harnesses.
AI.method: Credo recovers structured declarative descriptions from searched harnesses by extracting primitives (logical steps, runtime signals, physical execution decisions, prompt strategies) with relevant metadata, cataloging them with provenance, and enabling compilers to bind stored primitives for new tasks.
AI.result: Preliminary results demonstrate the potential of this approach to enable harness reuse across tasks, eliminating the need to restart search from scratch for each new task.
AI.conclusion: This work introduces a research agenda for the database community, including cost-based compilation over declarative catalogs and catalog maintenance under model and workload drift, addressing the challenge of harnessing knowledge reuse in LLM applications.

title: ReToolSQL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Robust Text-to-SQL
summary: Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning from execution feedback can substantially improve text-to-SQL performance, often enabling smaller models to match or exceed much larger systems. However, most existing approaches treat SQL generation as a single-turn task, limiting the model's ability to recover from errors through iterative refinement. We present ReToolSQL, a two-stage training framework for text-to-SQL that combines (i) a supervised warm-start on rejection-sampled reasoning traces with (ii) agentic reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) over multi-turn tool-use trajectories. The key insight is that the two stages act on complementary axes, the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on verified privileged-teacher traces expands the set of solvable questions (raising pass@k coverage on the hardest cases), while RFT converts that expanded capability into higher single-pass accuracy by teaching the model when to verify, what evidence to retrieve, and how to repair faulty SQL from execution feedback. Applied to Gemma 4 instruction-tuned (31B), RFT alone achieves 73.66% execution accuracy (EX) on the BIRD-SQL development benchmark (74.12% EX with self-consistency). Initializing RFT from the SFT checkpoint (SFT$\to$RFT) yields our strongest model at 74.32% EX single-pass and 74.77% EX with self-consistency. At the time of writing, this ranked first on the BIRD single-model development-set leaderboard. The approach uses composite rewards anchored on execution correctness, requires no human annotation beyond the benchmark itself, and operates within a single dense 31B model, showing that a properly designed SFT$\to$RFT pipeline over tool-use trajectories is a practical path toward robust enterprise-grade text-to-SQL.

AI.tldr: ReToolSQL: A two-stage training framework combining supervised warm-up with agentic reinforcement learning that achieves state-of-the-art text-to-SQL performance on BIRD benchmark using a 31B model.
