AI.motivation: Existing text-to-SQL approaches treat SQL generation as single-turn tasks, limiting error recovery through iterative refinement. Current reinforcement learning methods improve performance but don't fully leverage multi-turn tool-use capabilities.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: 1) Supervised fine-tuning on rejection-sampled reasoning traces (SFT stage), 2) Agentic reinforcement fine-tuning over multi-turn tool-use trajectories (RFT stage). Uses composite rewards based on execution correctness without human annotation.
AI.result: Achieved 74.32% execution accuracy single-pass and 74.77% with self-consistency on BIRD-SQL benchmark using Gemma 4 (31B). Ranked first on BIRD single-model development-set leaderboard at time of writing.
AI.conclusion: SFT→RFT pipeline over tool-use trajectories is a practical path to robust enterprise-grade text-to-SQL, showing complementary benefits: SFT expands solvable question coverage, while RFT converts capability to higher accuracy through iterative refinement.

title: SOMTab: Set-Order Mamba for Efficient Tabular In-Context Learning
summary: Tabular foundation models based on in-context learning have recently emerged as strong alternatives to task-specific model fitting. However, the current performance frontier remains dominated by attention-heavy architectures, where attention is used throughout the modeling pipeline. This raises a natural question: is attention necessary at every stage of tabular in-context learning? We introduce SOMTab, a Set-Order Mamba architecture for efficient tabular in-context learning. SOMTab separates representation construction from query-conditioned retrieval. For row and column representations, it maps unordered table tokens into stable latent slots and applies Mamba-based state-space mixing to construct compact representations. For final prediction, it retains attention-based in-context learning to preserve query-conditioned retrieval from labeled context examples. We further introduce DCH-TailMix, a synthetic prior that combines degree-corrected graph heterogeneity with mixed heavy-tailed regimes to diversify synthetic dependency structures. Across tabular benchmarks, SOMTab approaches the performance of strong Transformer-based tabular foundation models while achieving faster inference and lower GPU memory usage, yielding a favorable efficiency--accuracy trade-off.

AI.tldr: SOMTab is a Set-Order Mamba architecture for efficient tabular in-context learning that separates representation construction (using Mamba-based state-space mixing) from query-conditioned retrieval (using attention), achieving comparable performance to Transformers with better efficiency.
AI.motivation: Current tabular foundation models are dominated by attention-heavy architectures throughout the pipeline, raising the question of whether attention is necessary at every stage. There's a need for more efficient alternatives to Transformers for tabular in-context learning.
AI.method: SOMTab uses a two-stage approach: (1) Set-Order representation construction where unordered table tokens are mapped into stable latent slots using Mamba-based state-space mixing, and (2) attention-based in-context learning for query-conditioned retrieval. Also introduces DCH-TailMix synthetic prior combining degree-corrected graph heterogeneity with mixed heavy-tailed regimes.
AI.result: SOMTab approaches the performance of strong Transformer-based tabular foundation models while achieving faster inference and lower GPU memory usage, yielding a favorable efficiency-accuracy trade-off across tabular benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Attention is not necessary at every stage of tabular in-context learning; SOMTab demonstrates that Mamba-based architectures can effectively handle representation construction while attention-based retrieval is sufficient for final prediction, offering a more efficient alternative to pure attention models.

title: CEDAR: Automata as Verifiable Interfaces for Language-Guided Embodied Action
summary: Natural-language tasking of embodied agents is rarely just goal specification: users also impose constraints that must persist while the world changes. Code-generating LLM agents can produce plausible behaviors for such instructions, but their free-form programs provide no stable object to verify, compose with new constraints, or repair from a failing trace. We present CEDAR, a counterexample-guided framework that grounds instructions as regular languages over environment event traces. CEDAR uses a language model for semantic judgments and execution traces for correction, then represents both skills and specifications as deterministic finite automata. This turns constraints into executable finite-state objects: a learned skill can be intersected with a learned sleep at night or stay in this biome specification, yielding a controller that enforces the learned constraint by construction rather than by repeated prompting. In Minecraft, with the same simulator/API observations available to a program-generating baseline, CEDAR maintains temporal and spatial constraints that the baseline fails to preserve and amortizes reuse of learned skills, reducing cumulative LLM queries. These results suggest that regular languages offer a practical verification layer between natural-language instructions and embodied-agent policies.

AI.tldr: CEDAR is a counterexample-guided framework that grounds natural language instructions as regular languages over environment event traces, enabling constraint verification and composition via deterministic finite automata.
AI.motivation: Current code-generating LLM agents for embodied tasking produce free-form programs that lack stable verification objects, making it difficult to verify, compose with new constraints, or repair failing traces of natural language instructions with persistent constraints.
AI.method: CEDAR uses a counterexample-guided approach with LLMs for semantic judgments and execution traces for correction, representing both skills and specifications as deterministic finite automata (DFAs). This transforms constraints into executable finite-state objects that can be intersected to enforce learned constraints.
AI.result: In Minecraft experiments, CEDAR successfully maintains temporal and spatial constraints that program-generating baselines fail to preserve, while amortizing reuse of learned skills and reducing cumulative LLM queries compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Regular languages provide a practical verification layer between natural-language instructions and embodied-agent policies, enabling constraint enforcement by construction rather than through repeated prompting.

title: Beyond Pairwise Graphs in Science: Hypergraph Adaptive Wavelet Operators for Parametric PDEs
summary: Physical systems are often modeled by solution operators that map input fields, parameters, geometries, or past states to steady or future physical states. Learning these maps is difficult, especially for time-dependent systems that must assimilate history and remain stable under autoregressive rollout. Many neural operators work best on regular, structured grids, while realistic simulations often require unstructured meshes or point clouds to resolve complex geometries; in such settings, grid-centric representations can lose accuracy. Graph neural operators handle these domains through message passing or spectral graph filtering, but pairwise edges do not directly capture group-wise couplings among mesh cells, local neighborhoods, or conservation volumes. We introduce the Hypergraph Adaptive waveLet Operator (HALO), which lifts the domain to a hypergraph and learns in its spectral wavelet domain. HALO avoids explicit hypergraph-Laplacian eigendecomposition through Chebyshev polynomial wavelet filters, giving localized spectral kernels at linear sparse-matrix cost. Its trainable dyadic wavelet scales are regularized toward tight-frame coverage, allowing the frequency response to adapt to each PDE while encouraging stable multi-scale spectral coverage. Across 2D and 3D benchmarks on structured and unstructured discretizations, HALO achieves best or near-best accuracy among frequency-, transformer-, DeepONet-, state-space-, and graph-based baselines and sustains stable multi-step rollouts. The same model scales to industrial aerodynamic geometries: on meshes of a few hundred thousand points it is on par with, or better than, the strongest fixed-discretization transformers, while remaining resolution-equivariant.

AI.tldr: HALO is a hypergraph-based neural operator that learns PDE solution operators in spectral wavelet domains, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on diverse 2D/3D benchmarks while handling unstructured meshes and enabling stable multi-step rollouts.
AI.motivation: Learning solution operators for PDEs is challenging, especially for time-dependent systems requiring history assimilation and stable autoregressive rollout. Existing approaches have limitations: neural operators work best on regular grids, while realistic simulations need unstructured meshes; graph neural operators use pairwise edges that don't capture group-wise couplings among mesh cells, local neighborhoods, or conservation volumes effectively.
AI.method: HALO (Hypergraph Adaptive waveLet Operator) lifts the domain to a hypergraph and learns in its spectral wavelet domain. It avoids explicit hypergraph-Laplacian eigendecomposition through Chebyshev polynomial wavelet filters, providing localized spectral kernels at linear sparse-matrix cost. The method uses trainable dyadic wavelet scales regularized toward tight-frame coverage, allowing frequency response adaptation to each PDE while encouraging stable multi-scale spectral coverage.
AI.result: Across 2D and 3D benchmarks on structured and unstructured discretizations, HALO achieves best or near-best accuracy among frequency-, transformer-, DeepONet-, state-space-, and graph-based baselines and sustains stable multi-step rollouts. The same model scales to industrial aerodynamic geometries: on meshes of a few hundred thousand points it is on par with, or better than, the strongest fixed-discretization transformers, while remaining resolution-equivariant.
AI.conclusion: HALO successfully addresses limitations of existing neural operators by leveraging hypergraph representations and spectral wavelet learning, enabling effective handling of complex geometries on unstructured meshes while maintaining accuracy and stability in multi-step predictions.

title: CURA: Certified Runtime Alarms for Computer-Use Agents
summary: Self-report is the cheapest oversight channel a deployer has, and on capable computer-use agents (CUAs) it fails precisely where oversight matters. On 361 OSWorld tasks our pipeline, a read-only feasibility gate, a planner, and a GUI executor, reaches a mean task score of 82.9, above the 72.4 human reference, yet 64 of its 71 failures (90%) end with a success claim, 61 acknowledging no blocker, and the explicit failure affordance is never used in roughly 9,100 calls. We introduce CURA (Certified Runtime Alarms for Computer-Use Agents), an external monitor that reads only harness-visible telemetry, with no model internals, extra LLM calls, or prompt changes, and turns the running trajectory into a sequential test with certified false-alarm control. At alpha = 0.10 its CUSUM alarm detects 42.3% of failures a median of 31 steps before termination at a realized false-alarm rate of 0.066, and risk is partly resolvable before the first action (gate probe, 0.69 AUROC). Retrospectively the composite reaches 0.828 AUROC (fold-internal floor 0.802), but its margin over a total-token baseline is not significant (Delta = +0.026, p = 0.101); the separation is online, where CURA recalls more at matched certified budgets: 0.41 versus 0.34 at alpha = 0.10, 0.56 versus 0.38 at alpha = 0.20. Alarm-gated mid-execution oversight recovers 23 of 70 failures while spending a frontier overseer on 38, giving a deployable cascade at mean score 86.8 and 84.5% full-solve (305 of 361). The certificate bounds false alarms only. We also report where behavioral monitoring is uninformative.

AI.tldr: CURA monitors computer-use agents using runtime telemetry to detect failures with certified false-alarm control, enabling mid-execution oversight recovery that improves task performance.
AI.motivation: Self-report oversight fails precisely where it matters most for capable computer-use agents. The paper shows that agents often claim success when they've actually failed (90% of failures end with success claims), making external monitoring essential.
AI.method: CURA (Certified Runtime Alarms for Computer-Use Agents) uses an external monitor that reads only harness-visible telemetry without model internals or extra LLM calls. It converts running trajectories into sequential tests using CUSUM alarm with certified false-alarm control and includes a gate probe for early risk assessment.
AI.result: At alpha=0.10, CURA detects 42.3% of failures a median of 31 steps before termination with 0.066 false-alarm rate. Alarm-gated mid-execution oversight recovers 23 of 70 failures, achieving mean task score of 86.8 (84.5% full-solve on 361 OSWorld tasks), outperforming human reference (72.4) and baseline pipeline (82.9).
AI.conclusion: External runtime monitoring with certified false-alarm control enables effective oversight of computer-use agents where self-report fails, providing deployable cascades that recover failures mid-execution while maintaining performance improvements over human baselines.

title: There and Back Again: Bidirectional Diffusion Bridges for Multimodality Translation
summary: Multimodality translation (e.g., text-to-image) is a core generative AI task. However, existing approaches (1) follow generative paths that do not directly represent the source modality, limiting the flexibility of some sampling algorithms; and (2) are unidirectional, preventing inversion (e.g., image-to-text). We propose BIT: Bidirectional Image-Text Diffusion Bridges. In contrast to previous approaches, BIT starts directly from text and interpolates into images, providing (1) a source-aware generative path that enables diverse and flexible sampling algorithms; and (2) an endpoint-conditioned process that can be traversed from image to text, providing a unified, bidirectional generative framework. BIT is derived through stochastic calculus, yielding SDE forms amenable to simulation and tractable loss functions that scale to high dimensions. Our experiments show that BIT is competitive with denoising-diffusion and deterministic-flow baselines, and outperforms them on several vision--language and natural-science evaluations.

AI.tldr: BIT introduces a bidirectional diffusion bridge framework for multimodal translation that directly represents source modalities and enables both text-to-image and image-to-text generation.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal translation approaches have two key limitations: (1) they follow generative paths that don't directly represent source modalities, limiting sampling algorithm flexibility, and (2) they are unidirectional, preventing inversion tasks like image-to-text generation.
AI.method: BIT uses bidirectional image-text diffusion bridges that start directly from text and interpolate into images. This provides a source-aware generative path and an endpoint-conditioned process that can be traversed in both directions. The approach is derived through stochastic calculus, yielding SDE forms for simulation and tractable loss functions that scale to high dimensions.
AI.result: BIT is competitive with denoising-diffusion and deterministic-flow baselines, and outperforms them on several vision-language and natural-science evaluations.
AI.conclusion: BIT provides a unified, bidirectional generative framework for multimodal translation that addresses limitations of previous approaches through mathematically grounded diffusion bridges that enable flexible sampling and inversion capabilities.

title: AcCoRD: Evaluating User-Agent Collaboration Under Realistic User Preference Dynamics
summary: User preferences in user-agent collaboration are rarely static and fully-specified upfront: preferences are formed, revealed, adjusted, and relaxed during interaction. Existing benchmarks for evaluating user-agent collaboration focus almost exclusively on resolving underspecified preferences, thereby failing to capture the richer dynamics of real-world interaction. We introduce AcCoRD, a user-agent collaboration benchmark requiring agents to handle diverse user preference dynamics in two domains: online shopping and travel planning. We evaluate five frontier LLMs under two prompting strategies: vanilla ReAct, and an uncertainty-guided variant that prompts models to identify and resolve ambiguity about user preferences. Our results reveal that frontier models can handle underspecification but struggle to satisfy preferences that emerge or evolve mid-interaction and require more sophisticated uncertainty modeling. Further, prompting alone fails to elicit the required uncertainty recognition. We release AcCoRD as a resource for developing agents that can navigate the full complexity of real-world user preferences.

AI.tldr: AcCoRD is a new benchmark for evaluating user-agent collaboration that tests agents' ability to handle dynamic, evolving user preferences, beyond just resolving underspecified preferences.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for user-agent collaboration focus only on resolving underspecified preferences, missing the richer dynamics of real-world interactions where user preferences are formed, revealed, adjusted, and relaxed during interaction.
AI.method: Introduces AcCoRD benchmark with two domains (online shopping and travel planning) requiring agents to handle diverse user preference dynamics. Evaluates five frontier LLMs under two prompting strategies: vanilla ReAct and an uncertainty-guided variant that prompts models to identify and resolve ambiguity about user preferences.
AI.result: Frontier models can handle underspecification but struggle with preferences that emerge or evolve mid-interaction and require sophisticated uncertainty modeling. Prompting alone fails to elicit the required uncertainty recognition.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based agents need better uncertainty modeling to handle dynamic real-world user preferences, and AcCoRD provides a resource for developing such capabilities.

title: TACIT-Switch: Cost-Aware Model Escalation for LLM Agents from Censored Supervision
summary: Agents with smaller language-model backbones are less expensive but can drift into persistent failure modes, whereas those with larger backbones are generally more reliable but more costly. This reliability-cost trade-off motivates routing methods that decide when to invoke an agent with a larger backbone: before execution, after a fixed trajectory prefix, or locally at individual steps. Our method, TACIT-SWITCH, learns permanent handoff policies from accumulated trajectory evidence and Teacher-Annotated Censored Intervention Times (TACIT). It represents each annotation as an interval-censored observation on a cumulative-risk scale. The resulting mixture-cure threshold model estimates the probability that the paired Strong rollout succeeds and, conditional on success, the handoff threshold; no teacher is required at deployment. In a mechanism-based multi-step simulation, TACIT-SWITCH improves success by 7.4-11.1 percentage points over task-level, step-level, and fixed-prefix routing baselines at comparable cost. Within that controlled simulation, ablations show that task features and cumulative trajectory risk provide complementary information. With operating points selected on development data, TACIT-SWITCH achieves the highest held-out success among learned policies on both ALFWorld (48.5% with 4B Cheap; 45.5% with 9B Cheap) and DABench (73.1%).

AI.tldr: TACIT-SWITCH: A routing method that learns when to switch from cheap, less reliable LLM agents to expensive, more reliable ones using interval-censored observations from teacher-annotated failure times, achieving better performance than baselines at similar cost.
AI.motivation: There's a trade-off between cost and reliability in language model agents: smaller/cheaper models are less expensive but prone to persistent failures, while larger/expensive models are more reliable but costly. This motivates routing methods that decide when to invoke the more expensive agent.
AI.method: TACIT-SWITCH learns permanent handoff policies using accumulated trajectory evidence and Teacher-Annotated Censored Intervention Times (TACIT). It represents teacher annotations as interval-censored observations on a cumulative-risk scale, using a mixture-cure threshold model that estimates both the probability of strong rollout success and the handoff threshold when needed.
AI.result: In multi-step simulations, TACIT-SWITCH improves success by 7.4-11.1 percentage points over task-level, step-level, and fixed-prefix routing baselines at comparable cost. On ALFWorld, it achieves 48.5% success with 4B model and 45.5% with 9B model; on DABench, 73.1% success. Task features and cumulative trajectory risk provide complementary information.
AI.conclusion: TACIT-SWITCH effectively balances the cost-reliability trade-off in LLM agent routing by learning optimal handoff timing from annotated failure data, achieving superior performance without requiring teacher intervention at deployment.

title: Evidential-Based Higher-Order Set Argumentation Framework
summary: Evidential argumentation extends Dung's abstract argumentation by requiring arguments and interactions to be backed by chains of evidence rooted in prima-facie elements. However, existing formalisms lack a unified treatment of evidential support, higher-order relations (attacks and supports targeting arbitrary elements), and collective interactions (sources as sets). In this paper, we introduce the Evidential-Based Higher-Order Set Argumentation Framework (EHSAF), which conservatively generalises several existing frameworks within a single expressive setting. We develop two complete semantics for EHSAFs: an \emph{adjacent complete labelling semantics} that admits multiple truth values (true, false, undecided) for arguments in support cycles, reflecting an open epistemic attitude toward future evidence; and an \emph{extension-based complete semantics} that follows a strict evidentialist stance, accepting only arguments with well-founded support chains. We show that these two semantics diverge in the presence of support cycles, and prove their equivalence under support-acyclicity. To enable computational reasoning, we provide a normal propositional encoding of EHSAFs and prove that, in three-valued Łukasiewicz logic, its models correspond precisely to the adjacent complete labellings. We further extend this encoding to continuous fuzzy logics (G{ö}del, Product, and Łukasiewicz), defining a continuous fuzzy normal encoded semantics. We establish that this fuzzy semantics satisfies key properties---continuity, monotonicity, boundary conditions, and solution existence---and that its ternarisation recovers the adjacent complete labellings under natural t-norm conditions. Our framework thus unifies expressive argumentation with principled three-valued and fuzzy semantics, bridging the gap between qualitative and quantitative reasoning about evidence.

AI.tldr: EHSAF framework unifies evidential argumentation with higher-order relations and collective interactions, offering both three-valued and fuzzy semantics for reasoning about evidence-based arguments.
AI.motivation: Existing evidential argumentation frameworks lack unified treatment of evidential support, higher-order relations (attacks/supports targeting arbitrary elements), and collective interactions (sources as sets), creating fragmentation in the field.
AI.method: Introduces Evidential-Based Higher-Order Set Argumentation Framework (EHSAF), develops two complete semantics (adjacent complete labeling with multiple truth values and extension-based complete semantics), provides propositional encodings, and extends to continuous fuzzy logics (Gödel, Product, Łukasiewicz).
AI.result: Shows divergence between two semantics in presence of support cycles but equivalence under support-acyclicity; establishes correspondence between three-valued Łukasiewicz logic models and adjacent complete labellings; demonstrates fuzzy semantics satisfies key properties and recovers adjacent complete labellings under ternarisation.
AI.conclusion: EHSAF successfully unifies expressive argumentation with principled three-valued and fuzzy semantics, bridging qualitative and quantitative reasoning about evidence while generalizing existing frameworks.

title: TI$^2$PS: A Topology-Informed Inverse Design Framework for Stochastic Multicellular Pattern Formation
summary: This study proposes a novel framework to estimate parameters for reproducing target multicellular patterns using an agent-based model (ABM). Two major challenges in multicellular ABMs are estimating cell-level parameters (agent-specific variables) and quantitatively evaluating the topological characteristics of multicellular arrangements under stochastic cell proliferation and death. To address these challenges, we integrate two approaches: Betti vectors and inverse surrogate modeling. The Betti vectors obtained through topological data analysis can consistently represent features of a wide range of multicellular spatial configurations. The inverse surrogate modeling enables direct inference of the corresponding ABM parameters from the target patterns. We validated the proposed framework using zebrafish pigment pattern formation, a representative model of pattern formation driven by multicellular interactions. The results demonstrate that our framework successfully estimates ABM parameters and outperforms conventional methods such as PointNet++. Notably, the proposed method, which used only 10% of the training data, outperformed PointNet++, which used 100% of the data, across all evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: A novel framework combining topological data analysis (Betti vectors) and inverse surrogate modeling to estimate agent-based model parameters for reproducing multicellular patterns, validated on zebrafish pigment patterns and outperforming conventional methods like PointNet++.
AI.motivation: Two main challenges in multicellular agent-based models: (1) estimating cell-level parameters (agent-specific variables), and (2) quantitatively evaluating topological characteristics of multicellular arrangements under stochastic cell proliferation and death.
AI.method: Integrated two approaches: Betti vectors from topological data analysis to consistently represent features of multicellular spatial configurations, and inverse surrogate modeling to enable direct inference of ABM parameters from target patterns.
AI.result: The framework successfully estimated ABM parameters for zebrafish pigment pattern formation and outperformed conventional methods (PointNet++). Remarkably, using only 10% of training data, it outperformed PointNet++ using 100% of data across all evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides an effective solution for parameter estimation in multicellular ABMs by leveraging topological data analysis and inverse modeling, demonstrating superior performance with minimal training data requirements.

title: RealSWE: A Compositional Evaluation of Coding Agents under Realistic User Requests
summary: Coding agents are now commonly evaluated on the SWE-bench family of benchmarks, whose tasks are built from curated GitHub issues--long, structured, and information-rich. Real user requests, however, are typically far shorter and less structured. To characterize this gap, we define a six-category information taxonomy and four dimensions of linguistic style, and apply them to real user prompts from SWE-chat and problem statements from SWE-bench Verified and Pro. We find that requests carrying only a problem statement, alone or with limited additional context, account for 88% of real prompts but just 7% of benchmark problems. Furthermore, 87% of real prompts are casually written whereas 94% of benchmark problems are formal. Guided by these observations, we introduce sys, 381 multi-variant task families derived from SWE-bench Verified and Pro. Variants within each family share the same underlying task and gold patch while differing only in information composition and linguistic style. Evaluating seven contemporary LLMs with sys, we find that i) realistic inputs reduce resolution rates by 6.4 pp on average and can change model rankings. Controlled analysis further shows that ii) including Desired Behavior and Motivation significantly affects performance, whereas Environment Information and Reproduction Steps merely add tokens without measurable benefit; iii) linguistic style has only small, model-dependent effects. These findings provide actionable guidance for users and agents: explicitly stating the desired behavior and motivation--which most real prompts omit--substantially improves the LLM's software engineering performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SWE-VAR, a benchmark with 381 multi-variant task families derived from SWE-bench, showing that realistic (short, casual) user prompts significantly reduce LLM performance compared to formal benchmark problems, and providing guidance that stating desired behavior and motivation improves results.
AI.motivation: There's a gap between how coding agents are evaluated on benchmarks (using long, structured, information-rich GitHub issues) versus real-world user requests (typically short, unstructured, casual prompts). The authors aim to characterize this gap and understand how different information types and linguistic styles affect LLM performance on coding tasks.
AI.method: 1) Define a six-category information taxonomy and four dimensions of linguistic style. 2) Apply taxonomy to analyze real user prompts from SWE-chat vs. benchmark problems from SWE-bench Verified and Pro. 3) Introduce SWE-VAR benchmark with 381 multi-variant task families where variants differ only in information composition and linguistic style. 4) Evaluate seven contemporary LLMs using SWE-VAR to measure performance differences across realistic and formal inputs.
AI.result: 1) Real prompts are mostly short (88% contain only problem statements) and casual (87%), while benchmark problems are formal (94%). 2) Realistic inputs reduce resolution rates by 6.4 percentage points on average and can change model rankings. 3) Including "Desired Behavior" and "Motivation" significantly affects performance, while "Environment Information" and "Reproduction Steps" add tokens without measurable benefit. 4) Linguistic style has only small, model-dependent effects.
AI.conclusion: Users and coding agents should explicitly state desired behavior and motivation in prompts, as these significantly improve LLM performance on software engineering tasks, while other information types like environment details and reproduction steps provide little benefit despite being common in benchmark evaluations.

title: Temporal Memory-Aware Online Test-Time Adaptation on Dynamic Graphs
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) on graphs aims to adapt a graph neural network (GNN) that is well-trained on the training graph to the test graph, which involves potential distribution shifts that may harm model generalization and test-time inference. While recent efforts have investigated TTA on static graphs, there is still a research gap on dynamic graphs learned with dynamic GNN (DGNN) models, where both structural connectivity and node semantics evolve continuously over time. This makes adapting a DGNN model for reliable test-time performance substantially challenging. To fill this gap, in this work, we propose a novel framework of temporal memory-aware Online Test-Time Adaptation on Dynamic Graphs, named DGOTTA, to effectively adapt well-trained DGNNs during test time. Specifically, the proposed DGOTTA contains three modules: (1) temporal-aware augmentation, to extend the diversity of test dynamic graphs for addressing complex temporal and spatial shifts; (2) memory-aware model prediction, to alleviate catastrophic forgetting; (3) consistency-guided online adaptation, to enforce temporal alignment and memory smoothness. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets and four DGNN backbones demonstrate that DGOTTA significantly improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and multiple model architectures.

AI.tldr: DGOTTA: A novel framework for temporal memory-aware online test-time adaptation on dynamic graphs that addresses distribution shifts in evolving graph structures and node semantics.
AI.motivation: While test-time adaptation (TTA) has been studied for static graphs, there's a research gap for dynamic graphs where both structural connectivity and node semantics evolve continuously over time, making adaptation of dynamic GNN models challenging for reliable test-time performance.
AI.method: DGOTTA contains three modules: (1) temporal-aware augmentation to extend test dynamic graph diversity, (2) memory-aware model prediction to alleviate catastrophic forgetting, and (3) consistency-guided online adaptation to enforce temporal alignment and memory smoothness.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets and four DGNN backbones demonstrate that DGOTTA significantly improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and multiple model architectures.
AI.conclusion: DGOTTA effectively adapts well-trained dynamic GNN models during test time to handle the complex challenges of evolving dynamic graphs, filling an important research gap in test-time adaptation for dynamic graph neural networks.

title: KLOD: Locality-Preserving Knowledge Editing via Non-Target Distribution Preservation
comment: To be published in EMNLP 2026 Findings
summary: Fine-tuning-based knowledge editing is simple and architecture-agnostic, but standard cross-entropy increases the edited target probability without explicitly constraining changes in the non-target output distribution. In sequential editing, such unconstrained redistribution can accumulate as distributional drift and contribute to locality degradation. We propose KLOD, a bounded and distribution-preserving objective for fine-tuning-based knowledge editing that separates the intended target update from distributions that should remain stable. KLOD stops target amplification once a probability threshold is reached, while preserving the target-excluded non-target distribution at target positions and the full next-token distribution at prefix positions. Experiments on CounterFact and ZsRE with Llama3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that KLOD substantially mitigates locality degradation while maintaining high edit reliability. The target probability threshold further provides a controllable Generalization--Locality trade-off. Ablation, multi-seed, and distributional KL analyses support the interpretation that KLOD's locality gains are associated with preserving output distributions rather than simply weakening the edit. Code is available on GitHub https://github.com/Hostoday/KLOD .

AI.tldr: KLOD: A bounded, distribution-preserving objective for fine-tuning-based knowledge editing that mitigates distributional drift by separating target updates from stable distributions while maintaining edit reliability.
AI.motivation: Standard cross-entropy in fine-tuning-based knowledge editing increases target probability without constraining changes to non-target output distributions, causing distributional drift that accumulates during sequential editing and degrades locality.
AI.method: Propose KLOD (KL-based bounded distribution-preserving objective) that separates intended target updates from distributions that should remain stable. It stops target amplification once a probability threshold is reached while preserving: (1) target-excluded non-target distribution at target positions, and (2) full next-token distribution at prefix positions.
AI.result: Experiments on CounterFact and ZsRE datasets with Llama3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show KLOD substantially mitigates locality degradation while maintaining high edit reliability. The target probability threshold provides controllable Generalization-Locality trade-off.
AI.conclusion: KLOD effectively addresses distributional drift in sequential knowledge editing by preserving output distributions, with ablation studies supporting that locality gains come from distribution preservation rather than simply weakening edits. The method offers a practical solution for fine-tuning-based knowledge editing.

title: PhyMamba: Physics-Modulated Mamba for Robust Battery Health Prognostics
summary: Battery health prognostics is a core function in battery management systems (BMSs), yet long-horizon health forecasting from BMS signals remains challenging due to operating-condition dependency and sensor noise. In this paper, we propose PhyMamba, a two-stage physics-modulated Mamba framework that integrates electrochemical aging into sequence modelling. PhyMamba does not require explicit identification of internal aging parameters, which often relies on intrusive measurements. In stage-1, a lightweight Mamba encoder first processes BMS signals and produces a latent representation that is transformed via an aging parameterization module, into physics-informed aging features. In stage-2, a customized Mamba forecasting backbone performs multi-cycle prediction, where physics is tightly integrated to regulate the model's internal temporal updates toward degradation-consistent evolution. Experiments on three public datasets under multiple forecast horizons show that PhyMamba achieves the best aggregated performance, with an overall mean error reduction of 31.8% compared with a diverse range of baselines. PhyMamba also offers an optimized accuracy-efficiency trade-off, which supports practical deployment for robust battery health prognostics.

AI.tldr: PhyMamba: A two-stage physics-modulated Mamba framework for battery health prognostics that integrates electrochemical aging into sequence modeling without requiring explicit identification of internal aging parameters.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon battery health forecasting from BMS signals is challenging due to operating-condition dependency and sensor noise. Current methods often rely on intrusive measurements for internal aging parameter identification.
AI.method: Two-stage Mamba framework: Stage 1 uses a lightweight Mamba encoder to process BMS signals into latent representations, which are transformed via an aging parameterization module into physics-informed aging features. Stage 2 uses a customized Mamba forecasting backbone for multi-cycle prediction, with physics integrated to regulate temporal updates toward degradation-consistent evolution.
AI.result: PhyMamba achieves the best aggregated performance across three public datasets under multiple forecast horizons, with 31.8% overall mean error reduction compared with diverse baselines. It offers optimized accuracy-efficiency trade-off supporting practical deployment.
AI.conclusion: PhyMamba provides an effective framework for robust battery health prognostics by integrating physics into sequence modeling without requiring explicit identification of internal aging parameters, enabling accurate long-horizon forecasting with practical deployment potential.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Cross-City POI Recommendation on a Large-Scale Benchmark
summary: Cross-city point-of-interest (POI) recommendation is crucial for navigating unfamiliar urban environments, yet its progress has historically been constrained by data limitations. Using the recently proposed large-scale benchmark Trip World, we empirically re-examine whether conclusions drawn on small prior benchmarks still hold under worldwide coverage, low home-destination region overlap, and large, semantically rich POI inventories. Our evaluation surfaces three bottlenecks of representative state-of-the-art methods: (1) hometown-aware models appear to rely more on destination-region priors than on user-specific preference transfer; (2) their accuracy-efficiency trade-off degrades at this scale, where the simplest model is among the strongest; and (3) existing mechanisms for integrating semantic metadata yield little benefit. We further include a diagnostic pilot on agentic methods adapted from next-POI recommendation, finding that naive adaptation trails a simple popularity prior even though the relevant semantic signal is present in the data. These results highlight the need for task-specific designs that support cross-city preference transfer, semantic grounding, and scalable reasoning over unseen destination inventories.

AI.tldr: Current cross-city POI recommendation methods don't scale well to worldwide coverage, with simple models outperforming complex ones and semantic integration providing little benefit, revealing need for task-specific designs.
AI.motivation: Cross-city POI recommendation is important for navigating unfamiliar cities but has been limited by data constraints. The authors want to re-evaluate existing methods using a new large-scale benchmark (Trip World) to see if previous conclusions from small datasets still hold.
AI.method: The researchers empirically evaluate representative state-of-the-art methods using the Trip World benchmark, which provides worldwide coverage, low home-destination region overlap, and large semantically rich POI inventories. They analyze three types of bottlenecks and include a diagnostic pilot on agentic methods adapted from next-POI recommendation.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) hometown-aware models rely more on destination-region priors than user preference transfer; (2) accuracy-efficiency trade-off degrades at scale, with simplest models being among strongest; (3) existing semantic metadata integration mechanisms yield little benefit. Additionally, naive adaptation of agentic methods trails simple popularity prior despite semantic signal being present.
AI.conclusion: Current cross-city POI recommendation methods are inadequate for real-world scale. There's a critical need for task-specific designs that support effective cross-city preference transfer, proper semantic grounding, and scalable reasoning over unseen destination inventories.

title: Is Monte Carlo Tree Search Just Every-Visit Monte Carlo Control?
summary: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and every-visit Monte Carlo (MC) control are usually presented as different methods. MCTS is described in the language of search (selection, expansion, simulation, and backup), whereas MC control is described in the language of reinforcement learning (trajectory sampling, return estimation, action-value updating, and policy improvement). This note argues that, at the level of trajectory generation and action-value updating, the distinction is largely terminological. The tree policy and rollout policy can be viewed as the learned and not-yet-learned parts of a single evolving policy; expansion corresponds to first visit and initialization; and backup is the ordinary every-visit Monte Carlo update. Under this interpretation, the four stages of MCTS reduce to two basic operations: trajectory sampling under the current policy and every-visit Monte Carlo updating. In this sense, MCTS is simply every-visit Monte Carlo control expressed in the language and data structure of search. The purpose of this note is expository: to make this equivalence explicit and easier to recognize.

AI.tldr: MCTS and every-visit Monte Carlo control are essentially the same algorithm expressed in different terminology - MCTS is just every-visit Monte Carlo control framed in search language with tree data structures.
AI.motivation: To clarify the relationship between Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and every-visit Monte Carlo control, which are typically presented as distinct methods with different terminology (search vs reinforcement learning language), but actually represent the same underlying algorithm.
AI.method: Interpret MCTS components through RL lens: tree policy and rollout policy as learned/not-yet-learned parts of evolving policy; expansion as first visit and initialization; backup as ordinary every-visit Monte Carlo update. This reduces MCTS's four stages to two basic operations: trajectory sampling and every-visit Monte Carlo updating.
AI.result: Establishes explicit equivalence between MCTS and every-visit Monte Carlo control - they're the same algorithm expressed differently (search language vs RL language). MCTS is simply every-visit Monte Carlo control using tree data structures and search terminology.
AI.conclusion: The distinction between MCTS and every-visit Monte Carlo control is largely terminological rather than algorithmic. Recognizing this equivalence makes the connection between search methods and reinforcement learning clearer and more explicit.

title: From Uncertainty to Clinical Risk: Severity-Aware Conformal Planning for Interactive Medical Diagnosis
summary: Interactive medical diagnosis dynamically acquires patient information through multiple rounds of questioning, supporting accurate, efficient, and safe clinical decisions under incomplete evidence. Existing methods commonly guide information acquisition with predictive uncertainty or label ambiguity, but overlook the asymmetric clinical risk of missing severe diseases and lack unified long-horizon planning over whether to continue asking questions or commit to a diagnosis. To address these limitations, we propose Severity-Aware Conformal Clinical Planning, which formulates interactive diagnosis as a risk-sensitive sequential decision problem. The framework maintains complementary diagnostic, safety, and masked-evidence beliefs; calibrates turn-specific diagnostic prediction sets and severity-weighted differential-diagnosis risk on held-out diagnostic trajectories; and introduces the calibrated clinical risk into Monte Carlo Tree Search to jointly evaluate long-horizon Ask and Commit trajectories. Experiments on DDXPlus and MediQ show that our method achieves more accurate diagnoses with fewer questions across multiple large language models, while improving differential-diagnosis quality and reducing high-risk errors in severe cases. These findings validate the value of using clinical risk, rather than predictive uncertainty alone, as a planning signal and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for information acquisition and risk-aware diagnostic decision making. They also motivate future work on clinical-risk-oriented interactive diagnosis and information-acquisition methods.

AI.tldr: A severity-aware clinical planning framework for interactive medical diagnosis that uses calibrated clinical risk for sequential decision-making, outperforming uncertainty-based methods with more accurate diagnoses and fewer questions while reducing high-risk errors.
AI.motivation: Existing interactive medical diagnosis methods use predictive uncertainty or label ambiguity but overlook asymmetric clinical risks (missing severe diseases) and lack unified long-horizon planning for when to ask questions versus commit to a diagnosis.
AI.method: Proposes Severity-Aware Conformal Clinical Planning: formulates diagnosis as risk-sensitive sequential decision problem; maintains diagnostic, safety, and masked-evidence beliefs; calibrates turn-specific prediction sets and severity-weighted risk on held-out data; integrates calibrated clinical risk into Monte Carlo Tree Search to evaluate Ask and Commit trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments on DDXPlus and MediQ datasets show method achieves more accurate diagnoses with fewer questions across multiple LLMs, improves differential-diagnosis quality, and reduces high-risk errors in severe cases compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Validates using clinical risk (not just predictive uncertainty) as planning signal; demonstrates effectiveness for risk-aware diagnostic decision-making; motivates future work on clinical-risk-oriented interactive diagnosis and information-acquisition methods.

title: A Method for Layer Bit-Width Allocation in LLM Quantization via Performance Maximization Under a Quality-Degradation Constraint
summary: This paper proposes a layer bit allocation method for Gemma-3-1B, formulating the problem as performance maximization (latency decrease) given a degradation budget constraint (allowable level of generation quality loss). This approach is different from time- and resource-consuming uniform layer quantization methods that are used in the literature (like GPTQ or AWQ) or allocation methods without proven performance-accelerating effect (like MixLLM or TorchAO). The layer sensitivity profile resulting from our prior work SA-PTQ is applied using the activation pass-through mode inside TensorRT-LLM. For each layer precision is determined individually in blocks, according to a grouping introduced in the prior step (5+5, 10+10, all26), differentiating the contribution of FFN, Attention, and lm_head to the overall speedup. The clock speed was measured for 13 W8A8 variants on an RTX 5090. We find that for FFN and lm_head the time cost of quantization/dequantization is compensated for by the use of integer arithmetic, while for short context lengths, the opposite holds true for Attention: an additional step of quantization slows execution down. We propose a manual implementation of SmoothQuant for TensorRT-LLM which was necessary due to export failures, unavailable for lm_head. The best solution found under joint consideration of all three criteria with minimal degradation was FFN 5+5 with lm_head, providing an 11.0% reduction in latency with negligible quality loss (98.90% Top-1 agreement, +0.85% perplexity degradation). With acceptable quality loss for FFN all26 + lm_head, a speedup up to 19.1% was found possible. We suggest further optimizations: fused attention kernels in INT8, KV-cache quantization, using FP8 instead of INT8 and partial Attention quantization analogous to FFN.

AI.tldr: Proposes layer bit allocation for Gemma-3-1B using performance maximization with degradation budget constraints, achieving up to 19.1% speedup with acceptable quality loss through selective INT8 quantization of FFN and lm_head layers.
AI.motivation: Current uniform layer quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ) are time- and resource-consuming, while other allocation methods lack proven performance-accelerating effects. Need for efficient precision allocation that maximizes latency reduction while maintaining acceptable generation quality.
AI.method: Formulates layer bit allocation as performance maximization with degradation budget constraint. Uses layer sensitivity profile from SA-PTQ prior work with activation pass-through mode in TensorRT-LLM. Individual layer precision determined in blocks (5+5, 10+10, all26) differentiating FFN, Attention, and lm_head contributions. Manual SmoothQuant implementation for TensorRT-LLM due to export failures.
AI.result: Best solution: FFN 5+5 with lm_head provides 11.0% latency reduction with negligible quality loss (98.90% Top-1 agreement, +0.85% perplexity degradation). With acceptable quality loss, FFN all26 + lm_head achieves up to 19.1% speedup. Findings show quantization/dequantization cost compensated by integer arithmetic for FFN and lm_head, but additional quantization slows Attention for short contexts.
AI.conclusion: Layer-specific precision allocation based on sensitivity profiles enables significant speedups with controlled quality degradation. The approach demonstrates feasibility of mixed-precision quantization for LLMs. Future optimizations suggested include fused attention kernels in INT8, KV-cache quantization, FP8 usage, and partial Attention quantization.

title: SpikeOPD: Stable On-Policy Distillation for Autoregressive Spiking Language Models
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient language modeling through sparse encoding and event-driven computation, but training capable spiking language models from scratch remains difficult. A practical alternative is ANN-to-SNN migration through knowledge distillation (KD), where a pretrained artificial neural network (ANN) teacher supervises an SNN student. Existing migration approaches distill on fixed corpus prefixes, whereas autoregressive inference conditions on self-generated prefixes, creating prefix-source mismatch. It manifests as output-policy mismatch with the ANN teacher and internal spiking-dynamics drift between self-generated and matched corpus prefixes. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a natural way to mitigate both manifestations by continuing teacher supervision on self-generated prefixes. We evaluate a teacher-only full-KL variant, Vanilla OPD, via a controlled stress test and observe it may suffer from delayed rollout-feedback collapse. This result shows that on-policy coverage alone does not ensure stable adaptation. Motivated by these findings, we propose SpikeOPD, a stable on-policy distillation framework for autoregressive SNNs that learns from self-generated prefixes while maintaining rollout stability. It applies full-KL teacher correction to reduce output-policy mismatch, while matched-prefix policy anchoring constrains policy departure from the frozen reference SNN on the same prefixes. Layerwise spike regularization further limits firing-rate deviations during on-policy adaptation. Across three model scales, SpikeOPD improves average accuracy over the corresponding KD SNNs by 0.8, 1.7, and 2.9 points at 0.125B, 0.35B, and 1.3B, respectively, while preserving their sparse-compute profiles.

AI.tldr: SpikeOPD is a stable on-policy distillation framework that improves spiking language model accuracy by addressing prefix-source mismatch during ANN-to-SNN migration, using full-KL teacher correction, matched-prefix policy anchoring, and layerwise spike regularization.
AI.motivation: Training spiking neural networks (SNNs) for language modeling from scratch is difficult, and existing ANN-to-SNN knowledge distillation methods suffer from prefix-source mismatch - they distill on fixed corpus prefixes while autoregressive inference uses self-generated prefixes, causing output-policy mismatch and internal spiking-dynamics drift.
AI.method: SpikeOPD uses on-policy distillation with three key components: 1) Full-KL teacher correction to reduce output-policy mismatch, 2) Matched-prefix policy anchoring to constrain policy departure from frozen reference SNN on same prefixes, and 3) Layerwise spike regularization to limit firing-rate deviations during on-policy adaptation.
AI.result: SpikeOPD improves average accuracy over corresponding knowledge-distilled SNNs by 0.8, 1.7, and 2.9 points at 0.125B, 0.35B, and 1.3B model scales respectively, while preserving their sparse-computation profiles.
AI.conclusion: On-policy distillation with stabilization techniques like policy anchoring and spike regularization effectively addresses prefix-source mismatch in ANN-to-SNN migration, enabling more accurate spiking language models without sacrificing energy efficiency benefits of sparse computation.

title: Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression
summary: Hanneke, Moran, Shlimovich and Yehudayoff (COLT 2025) posed the following open problem. A selector sees a finite dataset $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$, picks at most $n$ examples together with nonnegative weights, and hands the weighted least squares objective to the minimum-norm ERM. Writing $F_w(d,n)$ for the worst-case ratio between the loss of the returned predictor on all of $D$ and the optimal loss, they proved $F_w(d,n)=\infty$ for $n<d$, $F_w(d,d)=d+1$ and $F_w(d,n)=1$ for $n \ge 2d$, and asked for the value in the open regime $d<n<2d$. We determine this value in several cases. For every $d$ we prove $F_w(d,2d-1)=1+1/d$, which confirms a claim stated without proof in the original note. We further prove $F_w(3,4)=5/3$ and $F_w(4,5)=2$, the two smallest cells not covered by the endpoint formula. For every intermediate budget $n=d+k$ we prove the lower bound $F_w(d,d+k) \ge 1+Γ_{d,k}$, where $Γ_{d,k}$ is an explicit harmonic quantity over balanced partitions, and we show that this bound is the exact minimax value over the class of datasets whose whitened gradient systems carry an orthogonal circuit-block structure. All three exact values match $1+Γ_{d,k}$, and we conjecture that equality holds throughout the open regime. The upper bound proofs run on a common geometric spine: a rigidity theorem for positive spanning configurations of loss gradients, classifications and structural reductions of small positive bases in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\mathbb{R}^4$, and a dimension-free extremal-basis argument that converts sign-cone geometry into five-point selections. We also give explicit counterexamples showing that several shorter routes fail, and constructive polynomial-time selection algorithms for all proved cases.

AI.tldr: The paper solves the open problem of determining the worst-case ratio F_w(d,n) for sample selection in linear regression when d < n < 2d, providing exact values for several cases and conjecturing a general formula.
AI.motivation: Hanneke et al. (COLT 2025) posed an open problem about the worst-case ratio F_w(d,n) between the loss of a predictor selected via weighted sample selection and the optimal loss, leaving the regime d < n < 2d unresolved. The motivation is to understand the fundamental limits of selective data weighting in linear regression.
AI.method: The authors use geometric approaches including: a rigidity theorem for positive spanning configurations of loss gradients, classifications and structural reductions of small positive bases in ℝ³ and ℝ⁴, and a dimension-free extremal-basis argument that converts sign-cone geometry into five-point selections. They also provide constructive polynomial-time selection algorithms.
AI.result: Key results: 1) F_w(d,2d-1)=1+1/d, 2) F_w(3,4)=5/3 and F_w(4,5)=2 for the smallest uncovered cases, 3) Lower bound F_w(d,d+k) ≥ 1+Γ_{d,k} where Γ_{d,k} is an explicit harmonic quantity over balanced partitions, 4) This bound is exact for datasets with orthogonal circuit-block structure, 5) All proved values match the conjectured formula 1+Γ_{d,k}.
AI.conclusion: The paper makes significant progress on the open problem, providing exact solutions for several cases and evidence supporting a general conjecture for the entire d < n < 2d regime. The geometric and combinatorial approach yields both theoretical insights and practical polynomial-time algorithms for sample selection.

title: CoRe-MoE: Compact Reusable MoE for Continual Multimodal Instruction Tuning
summary: Continual multimodal instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to acquire new task abilities sequentially while preserving previously learned knowledge. LoRA-MoE provides a promising solution by introducing expert-based capacity, but repeatedly learning and maintaining full LoRA experts leads to substantial parameter overhead. This raises a natural question: is full expert expansion necessary for every new task? To answer it, we analyze the SVD of task-specific LoRA updates and observe substantial overlap in their input- and output-side LoRA direction subspaces, with task-specific adaptation largely captured by lightweight coordinates over these subspaces. Motivated by this observation, we propose CoRe-MoE, a Compact Reusable MoE framework for parameter-efficient continual multimodal instruction tuning. CoRe-MoE extracts reusable input- and output-side direction bases from an initial expert bank, and for subsequent tasks trains only compact coordinate experts together with task-specific low-rank routers. Experiments on two representative MLLMs show that CoRe-MoE improves final average performance over the strongest competing baseline by up to 5.90 points, while using less than 1% of the trainable parameters required by sequential LoRA for later tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/runzezz/CoRe-MoE.

AI.tldr: CoRe-MoE: A parameter-efficient continual multimodal instruction tuning framework that extracts reusable direction bases from initial experts and trains only compact coordinate experts for new tasks, achieving better performance with minimal parameter overhead.
AI.motivation: Continual multimodal instruction tuning faces challenges with parameter efficiency when using LoRA-MoE approaches. Full expert expansion for every new task leads to substantial parameter overhead. The authors analyze task-specific LoRA updates and observe significant overlap in their subspaces, suggesting that full expert expansion may not be necessary.
AI.method: CoRe-MoE extracts reusable input- and output-side direction bases from an initial expert bank. For subsequent tasks, it trains only compact coordinate experts together with task-specific low-rank routers, rather than full LoRA experts. This approach leverages the observation that task-specific adaptation is largely captured by lightweight coordinates over shared subspaces.
AI.result: Experiments on two representative multimodal large language models show CoRe-MoE improves final average performance over the strongest competing baseline by up to 5.90 points, while using less than 1% of the trainable parameters required by sequential LoRA for later tasks.
AI.conclusion: CoRe-MoE demonstrates that full expert expansion is not necessary for every new task in continual multimodal instruction tuning. By reusing direction bases and training only compact coordinate experts, it achieves superior performance with dramatically reduced parameter overhead, providing an efficient solution for continual learning in multimodal settings.

title: When Can Conditional Flow Matching Replace Pointwise Negative Log-Likelihood?
summary: Flow matching enables likelihood-free training, yet alignment methods increasingly reuse conditional flow matching (CFM) losses as endpoint negative log-likelihoods (NLLs) and their old/new differences as log-likelihood ratios. We characterize when these substitutions are valid. For linear Gaussian paths, we exactly decompose endpoint NLL into entropy, a weighted CFM objective, an interior velocity--score residual, and a boundary residual. Thus CFM-only estimates and differences are exact only when the corresponding residuals cancel. At the off-policy population optimum, ordinary CFM is not generally a pointwise NLL estimator, whereas \(w_{\mathrm{sc}}(t)=(1-t)/t\) removes the interior residual; this positive result does not extend generally to training or on-policy alignment. On-policy log-ratios can remain biased even for identical endpoint laws or after surrogate optimization. Experiments across dimensions, distributions, and geometries support these conclusions and the mechanisms that make inexact ratios useful. **More broadly, the decomposition provides a theoretical basis for adapting likelihood-based LLM methods to flow matching, while distinguishing exact substitutions from controlled surrogates.**

AI.tldr: Flow matching enables likelihood-free training, but substituting CFM losses as endpoint NLLs or log-likelihood ratios is only valid under specific conditions; the paper provides theoretical decomposition and analysis of when these substitutions are exact vs. approximate.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to address the widespread practice in flow matching methods where conditional flow matching (CFM) losses are used as proxies for negative log-likelihoods (NLLs) and log-likelihood ratios without proper theoretical justification. The authors want to characterize when these substitutions are valid versus when they're just controlled approximations.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical decomposition of endpoint negative log-likelihoods into four components: entropy, a weighted CFM objective, an interior velocity-score residual, and a boundary residual. They analyze this decomposition for linear Gaussian paths and characterize when CFM-only estimates and their differences are exact (when residuals cancel). They examine both off-policy and on-policy scenarios, and conduct experiments across various dimensions, distributions, and geometries.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that ordinary CFM is not generally a pointwise NLL estimator at the off-policy population optimum, though weighting with w_sc(t)=(1-t)/t removes the interior residual. On-policy log-ratios can remain biased even for identical endpoint laws or after surrogate optimization. Experiments support these conclusions while showing why inexact ratios can still be useful.
AI.conclusion: The decomposition provides a theoretical foundation for adapting likelihood-based LLM methods to flow matching while distinguishing between exact substitutions and controlled surrogates. It clarifies when CFM losses can properly serve as NLL estimates versus when they should be understood as approximations, offering guidance for future flow matching applications and alignment methods.

title: See, Hypothesize, Validate: Multimodal Agentic Framework for Discovering Governing PDEs
summary: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from observational data remains a core challenge across the sciences. Existing sparse-regression, symbolic-regression, and LLM-based approaches can be constrained by predefined libraries, noise sensitivity, hallucination, or limited iterative refinement. We introduce \textbf{MAGE} (\textbf{M}ultimodal \textbf{A}gentic \textbf{G}overning \textbf{E}quation Discovery), an agentic framework that organizes PDE discovery as a \textit{confidence governed hypothesis validation loop} inspired by the scientific cycle of observation, hypothesis, and falsification. Four role-specialized agents collaborate: a \textit{Differential Observer} computing derivatives and diagnostic visualizations; a VLM-powered \textit{Phenomenology Extractor} distilling qualitative cues from multimodal diagnostics; an LLM-driven \textit{Governing Law Synthesizer} proposing candidates without a predefined library; and an \textit{Equation Arbiter} fitting coefficients and assigning confidence scores. Discovery iterates until the top candidate clears a user-specified threshold, providing a structured process with an explicit accept-reject protocol. On the evaluated canonical PDE suite, MAGE obtains \textbf{8/8} exact structural recovery and the lowest coefficient error among the compared methods on \textbf{7/8} systems, with improvements of up to \textbf{4 orders of magnitude} and a geometric-mean improvement of approximately \textbf{3 orders of magnitude}. The pipeline also recovers the expected operators in two complex geometries and, on one laboratory sensor record, selects a cubic restoring-force model with held-out $R^2=0.98538$. These results support further study of structured agentic reasoning for library-free governing-law discovery, while broader generalization remains to be evaluated.

AI.tldr: MAGE is a multimodal agentic framework for PDE discovery that uses four specialized agents collaborating in a confidence-governed hypothesis validation loop, achieving exact structural recovery for 8/8 canonical PDEs with significant coefficient accuracy improvements.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for discovering governing PDEs from observational data face limitations including dependency on predefined libraries, noise sensitivity, hallucination issues, and limited iterative refinement capabilities.
AI.method: MAGE organizes PDE discovery as a confidence-governed hypothesis validation loop with four specialized agents: Differential Observer (derivatives and visualizations), VLM-powered Phenomenology Extractor (qualitative cues), LLM-driven Governing Law Synthesizer (library-free candidate proposals), and Equation Arbiter (coefficient fitting and confidence scoring).
AI.result: Achieved exact structural recovery for 8/8 canonical PDEs, lowest coefficient error among compared methods for 7/8 systems (improvements up to 4 orders of magnitude, ~3 orders geometric mean). Successfully recovered expected operators in complex geometries and selected appropriate models for laboratory sensor data.
AI.conclusion: Results support further study of structured agentic reasoning for library-free governing-law discovery, though broader generalization capabilities require additional evaluation.

title: Explainable Uncertainty Estimation for Reliable Medical AI
comment: Accepted at the 26th IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM)
summary: Artificial intelligence has strong potential to support clinical decision-making, yet its adoption in healthcare remains limited due to a lack of trust. Uncertainty estimation can signal unreliable predictions, and explainable AI (XAI) can clarify how predictions are made but existing methods treat them separately, providing no feature-level insight into why a prediction is uncertain or which tests to prioritize to reduce it. To address this gap, we propose explainable uncertainty estimation, which unifies uncertainty estimation and XAI to both quantify uncertainty and explain feature-level contributions. We introduce the Expected Gradients Reconstruction Uncertainty Estimate (egRUE), which incorporates prediction explanations into its uncertainty computation and decomposes uncertainty into feature-wise contributions. We prove theoretical properties of egRUE and show through experiments that it improves reliability and interpretability compared to existing methods. A user study with medical experts further demonstrates that egRUE's explanations improve calibrated trust over uncertainty scores alone, increasing confidence in correct predictions and reducing confidence in incorrect ones. By combining prediction uncertainty with feature-level explanations, egRUE strengthens decision-making support in safety-critical healthcare settings, clarifying both when predictions may be unreliable and which features drive that uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Proposes egRUE, a method that unifies uncertainty estimation and explainable AI to provide both uncertainty quantification and feature-level explanations for clinical decision support, improving reliability and trust in healthcare AI.
AI.motivation: AI adoption in healthcare is limited due to lack of trust. Existing methods treat uncertainty estimation and explainable AI separately, providing no feature-level insight into why predictions are uncertain or which tests to prioritize to reduce uncertainty.
AI.method: Introduces Expected Gradients Reconstruction Uncertainty Estimate (egRUE), which incorporates prediction explanations into uncertainty computation and decomposes uncertainty into feature-wise contributions. Proves theoretical properties of egRUE.
AI.result: Experiments show egRUE improves reliability and interpretability compared to existing methods. User study with medical experts demonstrates egRUE's explanations improve calibrated trust over uncertainty scores alone, increasing confidence in correct predictions and reducing confidence in incorrect ones.
AI.conclusion: By combining prediction uncertainty with feature-level explanations, egRUE strengthens decision-making support in safety-critical healthcare settings, clarifying both when predictions may be unreliable and which features drive that uncertainty.

title: HyQuant: Hybrid-Precision Quantization for LLM Attention
summary: Quantization has been widely adopted in LLM training and inference to reduce cost and improve efficiency. However, low-bit quantization of the \emph{attention} module often introduces large errors at very low bit-widths, causing performance degradation. Existing methods mainly rely on smoothing techniques to handle outliers, while we propose a hybrid quantization design to better balance accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, we propose \textbf{HyQuant}, an efficient hybrid quantization framework for LLM attention. HyQuant quantizes most attention states into low-bit formats while retaining a small set of vertical-line tokens and local-window states in high precision. These accuracy-critical regions are selected using lightweight vertical-line-aware attention-pattern signals, reducing quantization error with limited overhead. In the Prefill stage, HyQuant uses a hybrid-precision quantized attention operator that preserves vertical-line tokens and a local sliding window in full precision while quantizing the remaining context. In the Decode stage, HyQuant applies the same principle to KV-cache compression and fuses KV dequantization with attention computation to improve memory and hardware efficiency. Across diverse tasks, models, and datasets, HyQuant maintains nearly lossless accuracy with an extremely simple design, demonstrating the efficiency and practical feasibility of hybrid quantization for LLM attention. Code is available at: https://github.com/jerrysfls/HyQuant .

AI.tldr: HyQuant is a hybrid quantization framework for LLM attention that preserves critical tokens in high precision while quantizing most attention states to low bits, maintaining near-lossless accuracy with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Low-bit quantization of attention modules in LLMs often causes significant performance degradation due to large errors, especially at very low bit-widths. Existing smoothing techniques are insufficient, creating a need for a better balance between accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: HyQuant uses a hybrid quantization approach that quantizes most attention states into low-bit formats while retaining a small set of vertical-line tokens and local-window states in high precision. Lightweight vertical-line-aware attention-pattern signals identify accuracy-critical regions. The framework includes separate strategies for Prefill (hybrid-precision attention operator) and Decode stages (KV-cache compression with fused dequantization-attention computation).
AI.result: Across diverse tasks, models, and datasets, HyQuant maintains nearly lossless accuracy with an extremely simple design. The framework demonstrates efficient memory and hardware utilization while preserving model performance.
AI.conclusion: HyQuant proves the practical feasibility and efficiency of hybrid quantization for LLM attention, offering a balanced solution that reduces quantization errors with limited overhead while maintaining model accuracy.

title: Comparing Classical and Quantum Machine Learning for Regression in High Energy Physics Collision Data
summary: The classification and regression of particle collision events constitute a persistent computational challenge in experimental high energy physics, where large volumes of simulated data must be processed with both speed and precision. This work carries out a systematic comparison of four classical machine learning architectures, support vector machines (SVM), artificial neural networks (ANN), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks against their quantum counterparts: quantum SVM (QSVM), quantum neural networks (QNN), quantum CNN (QCNN), and quantum LSTM (QLSTM). All models are trained on simulated proton-proton collision events with electron-positron and muon-antimuon final states from the CERN Open Data portal, using transverse-momentum components as input features and transverse-momentum magnitude as the regression target. Classical architectures, and in particular the CNN and LSTM, achieve marginally better quantitative performance under current hardware and dataset constraints. Quantum models, however, reach competitive accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters: the QCNN reproduces the performance of the deep classical CNN using only four qubits and a circuit of depth three, pointing to a genuine parameter-efficiency advantage on near-term quantum devices. A baseline analysis confirms that the regression problem is non-trivial for shallow polynomial fits, supporting the relevance of the architectural comparison. These results characterize the trade-offs between classical and quantum approaches under realistic, resource-constrained conditions and provide a benchmark for future studies on actual quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: Systematic comparison of classical ML architectures (SVM, ANN, CNN, LSTM) vs their quantum counterparts (QSVM, QNN, QCNN, QLSTM) for particle collision event regression shows classical models perform slightly better currently, but quantum models achieve competitive accuracy with far fewer parameters, especially QCNN with just 4 qubits.
AI.motivation: Classification and regression of particle collision events in high energy physics require processing large volumes of simulated data with both speed and precision, presenting a persistent computational challenge that needs efficient solutions.
AI.method: Train four classical ML architectures (SVM, ANN, CNN, LSTM) and their quantum counterparts (QSVM, QNN, QCNN, QLSTM) on simulated proton-proton collision events from CERN Open Data portal using transverse-momentum components as input features and transverse-momentum magnitude as regression target, with baseline analysis using shallow polynomial fits.
AI.result: Classical architectures, particularly CNN and LSTM, achieve marginally better quantitative performance under current hardware constraints. Quantum models reach competitive accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters - QCNN reproduces deep classical CNN performance using only 4 qubits and circuit depth 3, showing genuine parameter-efficiency advantage for near-term quantum devices.
AI.conclusion: The study characterizes trade-offs between classical and quantum approaches under realistic resource constraints, showing quantum models can achieve competitive performance with significant parameter efficiency advantages, providing a benchmark for future quantum hardware studies in particle physics applications.

title: Resource Constraints and Performance in Agentic AI Systems
summary: Progress toward more autonomous AI increasingly depends on agentic systems that combine a language model with tools, memory, state management, and multi-step execution. These mechanisms shape both task capability and operational burden. We compare OpenClaw and NanoBot as complete agentic systems using a paired primary benchmark and a more detailed instrumented subset of paired prompts. In the primary benchmark, the rate of full task completion was 31% for OpenClaw and 25% for NanoBot, a six-percentage-point difference with a 95% task-bootstrap interval from -3 to 15 percentage points, providing no statistically established full-completion advantage for either system. In the instrumented layer, both systems achieved 26% full completion, while NanoBot reached at least partial completion on 43% of prompts compared with 26% for OpenClaw. OpenClaw took longer on 83% of prompts and had a higher recorded peak-memory value on every prompt, with geometric mean ratios of 2.98 for wall time and 19.44 for peak memory. Among the ten detailed-layer prompts on which at least one system achieved partial or full completion, NanoBot weakly dominated on eight; across all 23 prompts, however, ten of its eighteen dominance cases were cheaper joint failures. Outcome labels differ across the two evidence layers, showing why agent-system evaluation should connect capability and resource measurements to attempt-level execution and scoring provenance.
