These findings show that progress toward more autonomous AI should be evaluated through verified task completion, observed resource use and records linking each result to the execution that produced it.

AI.tldr: Comparison of two agentic AI systems (OpenClaw vs NanoBot) shows no statistically significant advantage in task completion rates, but reveals important differences in resource usage and the need for comprehensive evaluation metrics linking capabilities to execution provenance.
AI.motivation: As AI systems become more autonomous, understanding how agentic systems (combining language models with tools, memory, state management, and multi-step execution) perform is crucial. Current evaluation needs to consider both task capabilities and operational burdens to properly assess progress toward autonomous AI.
AI.method: Comparative evaluation using a two-tiered approach: (1) a primary benchmark measuring full task completion rates, and (2) a more detailed instrumented subset of paired prompts. The study compares OpenClaw and NanoBot systems using statistical analysis (95% task-bootstrap intervals), resource measurements (wall time, peak memory), and outcome dominance analysis across different prompt sets.
AI.result: Primary benchmark: 31% full completion for OpenClaw vs 25% for NanoBot (no statistically significant difference). Instrumented layer: Both at 26% full completion, but NanoBot achieved partial completion on 43% vs 26% for OpenClaw. OpenClaw was consistently slower (2.98× mean wall time) and used significantly more memory (19.44× mean peak memory). NanoBot weakly dominated on 8 of 10 partially/completed prompts, but had many "cheaper joint failures."
AI.conclusion: Agent-system evaluation must connect capability and resource measurements to attempt-level execution and scoring provenance. Progress toward autonomous AI should be evaluated through verified task completion, observed resource use, and records linking each result to the execution that produced it, rather than simple completion rates alone.

title: Generalized Gibbs Ensemble Weighting for Forecast Combination
summary: Forecast combination is a reliable way to improve predictive performance when several forecasting models are available. Simple aggregation rules such as the mean, median, trimmed mean, inverse-loss weighting, and exponential weighting are often strong baselines, but their relative performance can vary across datasets, forecast horizons, deployment settings, and levels of disagreement among base forecasters. We develop Generalized Gibbs Ensemble Weighting (GGEW), a probabilistic framework that treats forecasting models as experts and assigns ensemble weights using a Gibbs-style exponential transformation of normalized predictive loss. The framework extends this basic weighting rule through numerical stabilization, diversity-aware score corrections, and online hyperparameter adaptation. GGEW produces a family of related methods, including Stable Gibbs weighting, Directional Gibbs-NCL, and Symmetric Gibbs-NCL. These variants share one core algorithm and differ only in the score used inside the exponential weighting rule. For sequential deployment, we adopt a UCB-style bandit mechanism, called online Local-UCB, to adapt the learning rate, diversity strength, and Gibbs variant without evaluating the full hyperparameter grid at every prediction step. We evaluate GGEW on official M4 competition forecast submissions and external rolling-origin deployment experiments using Monash Traffic Hourly, Electricity Hourly, and Solar Weekly datasets. Results suggest that Gibbs-style adaptive weighting is a useful and competitive tool across several benchmark settings, although its relative performance varies across datasets, forecast horizons, deployment protocols, and forecast disagreement groups. The contribution is not a universal dominance claim, but a framework and empirical study motivating further investigation of when adaptive Gibbs-style forecast combination is useful.

AI.tldr: GGEW is a probabilistic forecast combination framework that adapts Gibbs-style exponential weighting with stabilization, diversity corrections, and online hyperparameter tuning to improve prediction performance across varying conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing forecast combination methods (mean, median, weighting schemes) perform inconsistently across different datasets, forecast horizons, deployment settings, and levels of disagreement among base forecasters. There's a need for more adaptive and robust ensemble weighting approaches.
AI.method: Develops Generalized Gibbs Ensemble Weighting (GGEW) framework that treats forecasting models as experts and assigns ensemble weights using Gibbs-style exponential transformation of normalized predictive loss. Extends with numerical stabilization, diversity-aware score corrections (NCL variants), and online hyperparameter adaptation using UCB-style bandit mechanism (Local-UCB) to adapt learning rate, diversity strength, and Gibbs variant.
AI.result: GGEW and its variants (Stable Gibbs weighting, Directional Gibbs-NCL, Symmetric Gibbs-NCL) show competitive performance on M4 competition submissions and external datasets (Monash Traffic Hourly, Electricity Hourly, Solar Weekly). Performance varies across datasets, forecast horizons, deployment protocols, and forecast disagreement groups.
AI.conclusion: Gibbs-style adaptive weighting is a useful and competitive tool for forecast combination across benchmark settings, though not universally dominant. The framework motivates further investigation of when adaptive Gibbs-style combination is beneficial rather than claiming universal superiority.

title: Rubric-to-Code Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Interactive web application generation requires models to produce usable HTML, CSS, and JavaScript applications from natural language requests. Unlike conventional code generation, application quality depends on multiple user-facing functional requirements, each often tied to localized code regions such as event handlers, state updates, DOM fragments, or CSS selectors. Standard GRPO collapses these structured outcomes into a single sequence-level reward and applies the resulting advantage uniformly to all tokens, weakening credit assignment. We propose \textbf{Rubric-to-Code Credit Assignment} (RCCA), a reinforcement learning framework that converts rubric-level functional feedback into localized optimization signals over generated code. RCCA builds training tasks around explicit functional rubrics, uses a hierarchical reward to separate format, source-code, runtime, and functional failures, and aligns evaluator-generated textual attributions with responsible code spans and generated tokens. The resulting model, \textbf{Ling-RCCA-Flash}, scores 41.25 on MiniAppBench, improving Ling-3.0-Flash by 32.20 points and slightly surpassing Claude Opus 4.5. It also reaches 76.19 on ArtifactsBench, improving the SFT model by 4.48 points and establishing a new top score under the official ArtifactsBench leaderboard setting by surpassing the GPT-5 score by 3.64 points, suggesting transferable implementation-level gains.

AI.tldr: RCCA is a reinforcement learning framework that converts rubric-level functional feedback into localized optimization signals for web app generation, significantly improving performance on application benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard RL approaches like GRPO collapse structured outcomes into single sequence-level rewards with uniform token advantages, which weakens credit assignment for interactive web applications where quality depends on multiple localized functional requirements tied to specific code regions.
AI.method: RCCA converts rubric-level functional feedback into localized optimization signals by building tasks around explicit functional rubrics, using hierarchical rewards to separate format, source-code, runtime, and functional failures, and aligning evaluator-generated textual attributions with responsible code spans and generated tokens.
AI.result: The resulting model Ling-RCCA-Flash scores 41.25 on MiniAppBench (improving Ling-3.0-Flash by 32.20 points and slightly surpassing Claude Opus 4.5) and reaches 76.19 on ArtifactsBench (improving SFT model by 4.48 points and establishing new top score, surpassing GPT-5 by 3.64 points).
AI.conclusion: RCCA enables effective credit assignment for web application generation by localizing optimization signals to specific code regions responsible for functional requirements, leading to transferable implementation-level gains across benchmarks.

title: VICT: Verifier-Instrumented Credit Tracing for Long-Horizon LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Fine-grained credit assignment is a central challenge in reinforcement learning for long horizon LLM agents. Standard objectives often train from programmatically verifiable terminal rewards by broadcasting each sparse outcome to every action in a trajectory. Existing methods typically seek finer credit from the rollout side, constructing auxiliary trajectory signals or additional comparisons to estimate action importance. Although useful, these approaches still treat the verifier that judged success as a scalar reward, discarding its internal task structure. Our key insight is that many verifiable tasks already encode the relevant checks inside their terminal verifier. We propose VICT (VerifierInstrumented Credit Tracing), a training-time interface that exposes executable or evidence backed atoms and traces them back to actions through dependency-valid proof edges. VICT redistributes group-relative advantage only along those edges, shifting credit assignment from rollout-side inference to verifierside tracing. It preserves the original terminal reward, abstains when evidence is incomplete or ambiguous, and changes only the training-time advantage tensor, requiring no learned critic, process labels, branch rollouts, or inference-time verifier access. On ALFWorld and WebShop, VICT improves substantially over outcome-only training and achieves strong performance alongside recent fine-grained credit methods; ablations rule out dense atom rewards, final-commit credit, temporal proximity, and sparsity as sufficient explanations.

AI.tldr: VICT is a new method for fine-grained credit assignment in RL for LLM agents that traces credit through verifier-side evidence atoms rather than rollout-side signals, improving performance without needing learned critics or inference-time verifier access.
AI.motivation: Standard RL objectives for long-horizon LLM agents broadcast sparse terminal rewards to all actions in a trajectory, failing to provide fine-grained credit assignment. Existing methods focus on rollout-side signals but ignore the internal task structure already encoded in terminal verifiers that judge success.
AI.method: VICT exposes executable or evidence-backed atoms from the terminal verifier and traces them back to actions through dependency-valid proof edges. It redistributes group-relative advantage only along those edges, shifting credit assignment to verifier-side tracing rather than rollout-side inference.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, VICT substantially improves over outcome-only training and achieves strong performance alongside recent fine-grained credit methods. Ablations show that dense atom rewards, final-commit credit, temporal proximity, and sparsity alone are insufficient explanations for the improvements.
AI.conclusion: Many verifiable tasks already encode relevant checks in their terminal verifiers, and leveraging this internal structure through verifier-side tracing (VICT) provides more precise credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents, requiring no additional learned components or inference-time overhead.

title: AI Alignment through a Game-theoretic Lens: A Survey
comment: This paper has been accepted by EMNLP-2026 as a main conference paper
summary: As large language models and increasingly capable AI agents are deployed in high-risk settings, aligning them with complex human values has become a central challenge. Existing alignment methods, while effective in improving helpfulness, harmlessness, and controllability, often struggle to capture real-world preferences that are context-dependent, non-transitive, and shaped by dynamic multi-party interactions. This survey reviews AI alignment through a game-theoretic lens. Specifically, it organizes recent progress around key game-theoretic elements and synthesizes the literature along three challenges: preference diversity, alignment priority, and temporal dynamics. This perspective clarifies where current alignment methods genuinely benefit from game-theoretic analysis, where the framework is looser, and what challenges remain in building robust, adaptive, and verifiable AI systems.

AI.tldr: Survey paper that examines AI alignment through a game-theoretic lens, analyzing how to handle complex human values in multi-agent, dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: Large language models and AI agents are being deployed in high-risk settings, but existing alignment methods struggle with real-world preferences that are context-dependent, non-transitive, and shaped by dynamic multi-party interactions.
AI.method: The paper conducts a survey review of AI alignment literature through a game-theoretic perspective, organizing progress around key game-theoretic elements and synthesizing work along three main challenges: preference diversity, alignment priority, and temporal dynamics.
AI.result: The survey clarifies where current alignment methods genuinely benefit from game-theoretic analysis, identifies where the game-theoretic framework is applied loosely, and highlights remaining challenges in building robust, adaptive, and verifiable AI systems.
AI.conclusion: Game theory provides a valuable lens for understanding and addressing the complex challenges of AI alignment in multi-agent, dynamic environments with diverse preferences, though gaps remain in applying rigorous game-theoretic analysis throughout the alignment literature.

title: Learning to Difference: Adaptive Reversible Differencing (AdaRDiff) for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Reliable long-horizon time series forecasting is an important yet difficult problem. Trends and seasonality introduce complex temporal structure that challenges learning-based forecasting models. Differencing, which subtracts nearby past values to remove such structure, is the classical remedy, but its reliance on hand-picked orders and periods has kept it largely absent from recent deep architectures. We propose \textbf{\underline{Ada}}ptive \textbf{\underline{R}}eversible \textbf{\underline{Diff}}erencing \textbf{(AdaRDiff)}, a generalized differencing approach that uses learnable weights to simplify the series through weighted differencing with previous time instants. This yields stabilized residuals on which forecasting is performed, after which the removed components are restored autoregressively to reconstruct the forecast, capturing trend and seasonality jointly through a single operator. This reconstruction admits a closed-form convolutional expression, which parallelizes on GPU and yields up to $33.7\times$ speedup over the naive recurrence. We furthermore rely on a two-phase training schedule that separates temporal structure discovery from reconstruction learning, as suggested by a theoretical analysis of the gradient when using a linear forecasting model. AdaRDiff attains state-of-the-art forecast accuracy across eight benchmarks spanning electricity, weather, traffic, and energy, at negligible parameter cost. Furthermore, it is designed as a plug-and-play module: integrating AdaRDiff improves eight diverse backbones, from linear models to Transformers, in the large majority of cases, by up to $25.9\%$ with a linear backbone and $18.3\%$ with iTransformer.

AI.tldr: AdaRDiff is a learnable differencing module that simplifies time series by adaptively removing trends/seasonality, forecasts on residuals, then reconstructs forecasts with GPU-optimized convolutional operations.
AI.motivation: Traditional differencing methods require manual parameter selection (orders and periods) and are absent from modern deep architectures, while existing deep learning models struggle with complex temporal structures like trends and seasonality in long-horizon forecasting.
AI.method: AdaRDiff uses learnable weights for adaptive differencing to remove trends/seasonality, performs forecasting on stabilized residuals, then reconstructs forecasts using an autoregressive process with a closed-form convolutional expression for GPU parallelization. Uses two-phase training to separate structure discovery from reconstruction learning.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across 8 benchmarks (electricity, weather, traffic, energy) with negligible parameter cost. Provides up to 33.7× speedup via GPU parallelization. As a plug-and-play module, improves 8 diverse backbones (linear models to Transformers) by up to 25.9% with linear backbone and 18.3% with iTransformer.
AI.conclusion: AdaRDiff effectively bridges classical differencing concepts with modern deep learning, offering an efficient, adaptive solution for long-horizon forecasting that can be easily integrated into various architectures while maintaining interpretability and computational efficiency.

title: From Documents to Reasoning: A Validated Synthetic Data Pipeline and Semantic-Aware Fine-Tuning for Financial Numerical Reasoning
summary:
Financial question answering (QA) has emerged as a key benchmark for evaluating the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on domain-specific tasks involving complex data formats such as tables, charts, and rich textual narratives. While recent advancements have enabled models to reason across modalities and perform multi-step arithmetic operations, limitations remain in performance consistency, and evaluation reliability. In particular, standard evaluation metrics like Exact Match (EM) often fail to account for minor variations such as differences in units or formats, misleading performance assessments.
  In this work, we propose a comprehensive pipeline for improving financial QA systems through high-quality synthetic data generation and fine-tuning of smaller language models (SLMs) using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA). Our pipeline includes aggressive data validation for synthetic question answer generation to ensure the relevance and correctness of synthetic question-answer pairs. We introduce a novel evaluation metric that matches answers computed from arithmetic expressions rather than ground-truth answers; providing a more accurate reflection of model reasoning capability. Furthermore, we propose a modified loss function that aligns predicted and reference expressions using semantic similarity, our novel evaluation metric and standard cross-entropy, resulting in improved performance. Experimental results on benchmark datasets, ConvFinQA demonstrate significant gains in QA accuracy after fine-tuning using synthetic dataset and proposed loss function.

AI.tldr: Financial QA systems are enhanced through synthetic data generation and fine-tuning of smaller language models using QLoRA, with improved evaluation metrics that focus on reasoning capabilities rather than exact answer matching.
AI.motivation: Financial QA serves as a key benchmark for LLMs on domain-specific tasks with complex data formats, but current systems have limitations in performance consistency and evaluation reliability. Standard metrics like Exact Match often fail to account for minor variations (units/formats), leading to misleading performance assessments.
AI.method: 1. Comprehensive pipeline for improving financial QA through high-quality synthetic data generation and fine-tuning of smaller language models using QLoRA. 2. Aggressive data validation for synthetic question-answer generation to ensure relevance and correctness. 3. Novel evaluation metric that matches answers computed from arithmetic expressions rather than ground-truth answers. 4. Modified loss function that aligns predicted and reference expressions using semantic similarity, the novel evaluation metric, and standard cross-entropy.
AI.result: Experimental results on benchmark dataset ConvFinQA demonstrate significant gains in QA accuracy after fine-tuning using synthetic dataset and the proposed loss function.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline, combining synthetic data generation with QLoRA fine-tuning and improved evaluation metrics, significantly enhances financial QA systems by focusing on reasoning capabilities rather than exact answer matching, addressing limitations of current evaluation methods.

title: Conditional Diffusion Models for Energy-Efficient Driving
summary: Electrification of commercial delivery fleets is shifting fleet routing from distance- and time-based optimization toward energy-aware decision-making. Existing sequence models primarily provide deterministic point estimates or limited uncertainty summaries, which do not capture the range of plausible energy-consumption trajectories required for operational decision-making. In this work, we introduce a conditional diffusion framework that generates EV battery-current profiles conditioned on route features such as vehicle velocity and ambient temperature. The model combines a latent conditioning encoder with a temporal 1D U-Net denoising backbone that enables trip-related conditions to be mapped into a shared representation and guides the reverse diffusion process. We evaluate the framework on an open-access commercial EV telemetry dataset containing 12k trips from 9 vehicles. The proposed latent-conditioned diffusion model generates realistic cur- rent trajectories that capture both the dominant temporal envelope and sharp transient events. The model achieves a Wasserstein distance of 0.0029 between generated and measured current distributions below the real vs real reference distance of 0.0085 indicating that generated samples lie within the empirical variability of the test set. We further demonstrate that learned latent conditioning substantially improves performance over direct condition injection, reducing the Wasserstein distance by 89.1% and MAE by 52.8%. This work demonstrates a generative modeling framework for characterizing EV energy consumption under real-world operating conditions, providing an essential foundation for uncertainty-aware fleet planning in large-scale operational settings.

AI.tldr: A conditional diffusion model generates realistic EV battery-current trajectories for energy-aware fleet routing, capturing both temporal envelopes and transient events with performance exceeding direct conditioning methods.
AI.motivation: Electrification of commercial delivery fleets requires energy-aware decision-making, but existing models only provide deterministic estimates or limited uncertainty summaries that don't capture the full range of plausible energy-consumption trajectories needed for operational planning.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion framework that combines a latent conditioning encoder with a temporal 1D U-Net denoising backbone. The model generates EV battery-current profiles conditioned on route features like vehicle velocity and ambient temperature, mapping trip-related conditions into shared representations to guide the reverse diffusion process.
AI.result: The model generates realistic current trajectories capturing both temporal envelopes and sharp transient events. It achieves a Wasserstein distance of 0.0029 between generated and measured distributions (below the real vs real reference of 0.0085). Latent conditioning improves performance significantly over direct injection, reducing Wasserstein distance by 89.1% and MAE by 52.8%.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a generative modeling framework for characterizing EV energy consumption under real-world conditions, providing a foundation for uncertainty-aware fleet planning in large-scale operational settings by capturing the empirical variability needed for robust decision-making.

title: A Deep Learning-Based Stacking Ensemble Framework for Turbofan Engine Remaining Useful Life Prediction
summary: This study proposes a two-level stacking ensemble framework for Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction of turbofan engines, evaluated on the NASA C-MAPSS benchmark using the FD001 and FD003 subsets. The framework integrates four heterogeneous deep learning base learners: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), CNN-LSTM, and CNN-GRU, whose out-of-fold predictions are combined by an XGBoost meta-learner to capture complex degradation patterns while mitigating individual model biases. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the stacking ensemble achieves superior predictive performance, with Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 9.989 and 8.613, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 7.081 and 5.195, and R-squared values of 0.899 and 0.906 for FD001 and FD003, respectively. Compared to the best-reported baseline (TCAT: RMSE 11.12 and 11.02), the proposed method achieves RMSE reductions of 10.2 percent and 21.8 percent for FD001 and FD003, respectively. Feature correlation analysis, residual diagnostics, and training convergence curves validate the model's robustness. These findings underscore the efficacy of stacking ensemble methods for prognostics and health management in safety-critical aerospace applications.

AI.tldr: Two-level stacking ensemble framework with LSTM, CNN, CNN-LSTM, CNN-GRU base learners and XGBoost meta-learner achieves state-of-the-art RUL prediction performance on NASA C-MAPSS turbofan engine datasets.
AI.motivation: The need for accurate remaining useful life (RUL) prediction in turbofan engines for prognostics and health management in safety-critical aerospace applications. Traditional single models may have biases and limitations in capturing complex degradation patterns.
AI.method: Proposes a two-level stacking ensemble framework that integrates four heterogeneous deep learning models (LSTM, CNN, CNN-LSTM, CNN-GRU) as base learners, with an XGBoost meta-learner that combines their out-of-fold predictions to mitigate individual model biases and capture diverse degradation patterns.
AI.result: Superior predictive performance on NASA C-MAPSS FD001 and FD003 subsets: RMSE of 9.989 and 8.613, MAE of 7.081 and 5.195, R² of 0.899 and 0.906 respectively. Achieves 10.2% and 21.8% RMSE reduction compared to best-reported baseline (TCAT). Model robustness validated through feature correlation analysis, residual diagnostics, and convergence curves.
AI.conclusion: The stacking ensemble method effectively improves RUL prediction accuracy for turbofan engines, demonstrating its efficacy for prognostics and health management in aerospace applications and providing a robust framework for safety-critical systems.

title: The Approximation Rank of Softmax Attention: Sharp Geometric Laws and Robust Interaction Dimension
summary: Which geometry controls the rank complexity of normalized softmax attention? We study maximum-row-$\ell_1$ approximation rank, exactly the least unrestricted rank preserving every bounded vector-valued output. Two sharp worst-case laws isolate support geometry: for fixed $d$ and error $\varepsilon$, spherical self-attention has rank $Θ_{d,\varepsilon}(\min\{n,(1+β)^{(d-1)/2}\})$, while full-ball geometry adds one radial degree and, for $β\geβ_0(d,\varepsilon)$ and $n\ge C_d e^{β/8}$, gives $Θ_{d,\varepsilon}(β^{d/2})$. For a fixed head, row-softmax quotients out row-scalar logit directions: the remaining visible query--key interaction dimension $r$ yields an $r/2$ per-instance upper law, and bounded constructions show this exponent is minimax sharp. Approximate interaction subspaces incur an explicit residual output error and yield a tolerance-indexed SVD dimension. On an 84-head BERT-base calibration set, we observe modest effective-dimension reductions across many head--temperature settings, together with positive associations with finite constructive rank upper certificates. Together, these results separate support geometry, which sets worst-case temperature scaling, from softmax-visible interaction geometry, which controls per-head approximation complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how geometry affects the rank complexity of softmax attention, showing that spherical self-attention has different scaling laws than full-ball geometry, and separates support geometry (which sets worst-case temperature scaling) from softmax-visible interaction geometry (which controls per-head approximation complexity.
AI.motivation: Understanding which geometric factors control the rank complexity of normalized softmax attention, particularly distinguishing between worst-case scaling laws determined by support geometry and per-head approximation complexity governed by visible interaction geometry.
AI.method: Studying maximum-row-ℓ₁ approximation rank and analyzing two sharp worst-case laws that isolate support geometry effects. Using spherical self-attention vs full-ball geometry comparisons, developing r/2 per-instance upper laws, and validating with BERT-base calibration experiments across head-temperature settings.
AI.result: Two distinct geometric scaling laws: spherical self-attention has rank Θ(min{n,(1+β)^{(d-1)/2}}), while full-ball geometry gives Θ(β^{d/2}). For a fixed head, row-softmax yields r/2 per-instance upper bound where r is visible query-key interaction dimension. Experimental results show modest effective-dimension reductions in BERT-base with positive associations with constructive rank upper certificates.
AI.conclusion: The research successfully separates support geometry (setting worst-case temperature scaling) from softmax-visible interaction geometry (controlling per-head approximation complexity), providing fundamental understanding of attention mechanism behavior and approximation complexity.

title: CASTANET: Causality-Aware Spatio-Temporal Adversarial Network Using Traffic Incident Effects
summary: Predicting non-periodic traffic congestion caused by sudden incidents (e.g., accidents and road damage) is crucial for advanced intelligent transportation systems. However, incident-driven congestion is difficult to forecast because incidents are extremely sparse, occur at specific times and locations, and have heterogeneous impacts depending on the traffic context. While recent deep learning approaches have significantly improved periodic traffic forecasting, their performance on non-periodic congestion remains limited, partly because incident records are not explicitly incorporated and their occurrence is strongly biased in space and time. To address these challenges, we propose CASTANET, which integrates spatio-temporal graph neural networks and causal treatment effect estimation to utilize incident records while mitigating selection bias. Experiments on real-world traffic data and accident records from Tokyo, which we treat as incidents, show that CASTANET reduces RMSE by 4.0% overall compared to the best baseline and by 10.1% on incident-conditioned evaluation, with gains reaching 14.55% under severe congestion.

AI.tldr: CASTANET integrates spatio-temporal graph neural networks with causal treatment effect estimation to better predict non-periodic traffic congestion caused by incidents like accidents, addressing sparsity and bias issues in incident data.
AI.motivation: Incident-driven traffic congestion is difficult to forecast due to extreme sparsity of incidents, specific spatio-temporal occurrence patterns, and heterogeneous impacts based on traffic context. Existing deep learning approaches fail to adequately handle non-periodic congestion as they don't explicitly incorporate incident records and struggle with the strong spatial and temporal biases in incident occurrence.
AI.method: CASTANET integrates spatio-temporal graph neural networks with causal treatment effect estimation to utilize incident records while mitigating selection bias. The approach explicitly incorporates accident/incident records and addresses the biased distribution of incidents in space and time through causal inference techniques.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world Tokyo traffic and accident data show CASTANET reduces RMSE by 4.0% overall compared to best baseline, by 10.1% on incident-conditioned evaluation, with gains reaching 14.55% under severe congestion conditions.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating incident records through causal inference techniques combined with spatio-temporal graph neural networks effectively improves non-periodic traffic congestion prediction, particularly for incident-driven scenarios and severe congestion conditions.

title: HARTS: Efficient Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Hybrid-Attention Models over Arbitrary Rollout Trees
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) often produces irregular rollout trees with shared histories. Training root-to-leaf trajectories independently recomputes these shared prefixes. Existing systems primarily target full-attention models and lack dense, differentiable hybrid-attention execution compatible with activation recomputation. We present HARTS (Hybrid-Attention RL over Tree Structures). HARTS jointly plans microbatches, data-parallel (DP) replica assignments, and microbatch-slot schedules using non-replay compact-token work after prefix compression. For chunkwise linear attention, a linear-time algorithm coordinates chunk-boundary state recovery and replay and produces the minimum number of sequential linear-attention calls under our packed execution model. HARTS preserves the chunkwise state partitioning of trajectory-wise training: it does not repeat projections, MLP/MoE computation, or final outputs, and performs only bounded state replay for numerical alignment. Per round, HARTS batches all branches into one packed call, propagates gradients through differentiable state handoffs, supports activation recomputation, and restores per-token log-probabilities. For deterministic, no-token-drop top-$k$ MoE routing, semantic multiplicities restore MoE-objective token weights and load statistics. Existing RL objectives retain their interface. To our knowledge, HARTS is the first system to demonstrate arbitrary-rollout-tree prefix-sharing speedups on a real hybrid-attention model. On an Agentic RL workload generated from SWE-bench tasks, HARTS achieves $4.81$--$4.87\times$ forward/backward/gradient speedup with activation recomputation across multiple parallel configurations. Its numerical differences are comparable to baseline self-rerun variation, and its reward trend is similar to the baseline over the first 120 steps of $τ^3$-Bench training.

AI.tldr: HARTS is a novel system for efficient hybrid-attention reinforcement learning that eliminates redundant prefix computations in irregular rollout trees, achieving 4.8x speedup while maintaining numerical alignment.
AI.motivation: Agentic RL produces irregular rollout trees with shared histories, leading to inefficient recomputation of shared prefixes. Existing systems lack dense, differentiable hybrid-attention execution compatible with activation recomputation, resulting in wasted computation.
AI.method: HARTS uses joint planning of microbatches, DP replica assignments, and microbatch-slot schedules with prefix compression. It employs non-replay compact-token work, chunkwise linear attention with coordinated state recovery, and packed execution to batch all branches. The system preserves chunkwise state partitioning and supports differentiable state handoffs with activation recomputation.
AI.result: HARTS achieves 4.81-4.87x forward/backward/gradient speedup with activation recomputation on SWE-bench tasks. Numerical differences are comparable to baseline self-rerun variation, and reward trends match baseline over 120 steps of training. It's the first system demonstrating arbitrary-rollout-tree prefix-sharing speedups on real hybrid-attention models.
AI.conclusion: HARTS successfully addresses the inefficiency of prefix recomputation in agentic RL through its hybrid-attention approach, providing substantial speedups while maintaining training stability and compatibility with existing RL objectives.

title: Cross-Session Decomposition Attacks: Scaling Risk and Intent-Aligned Retrieval Defense
summary: Scaling laws are usually read as a capability story: lower language-modeling loss yields more useful models. We study a safety consequence of this mechanism in \emph{cross-session decomposition attacks}, where benign-looking subqueries are asked across independent interactions and later recomposed toward a forbidden objective. We formalize this setting as \emph{compositional safety risk} and prove a conditional risk-transfer bound: when the reference environment already contains dispersed evidence for a risky reconstruction, the gap between deployed composed risk and reference composed risk is controlled by the model's excess loss on allowed subqueries. Synthetic withholding experiments show that wider transformers assign lower loss to held-out instructions that never appear verbatim in training but are recoverable from injected supporting facts. A 600-intent pretrained-LLM evaluation shows that larger Qwen3 and Gemma3 family members can yield greater harmful-capability uplift under a fixed decomposition-composition pipeline. As a defense, IntentAlign-MiniLM, our 22M-parameter intent-aligned retriever, outperforms much larger embedding models on held-out intent retrieval and yields the best learned-retriever harmful recall across tested guardrails. Code is available in \href{https://github.com/liaodisen/Cross-Session-Decomposition-Attacks}{our GitHub repository}.

AI.tldr: Cross-session decomposition attacks pose a safety risk where benign subqueries spread across multiple sessions can be recomposed into harmful objectives, with larger LLMs showing greater vulnerability due to better loss reduction on allowed subqueries.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a safety risk in large language models: while scaling laws typically improve capabilities by reducing language modeling loss, this same mechanism can inadvertently enable safety vulnerabilities through compositional attacks.
AI.method: The authors formalize compositional safety risk, prove a conditional risk-transfer bound, conduct synthetic withholding experiments with transformers, evaluate 600-intent pretrained LLMs (Qwen3 and Gemma3 families), and propose IntentAlign-MiniLM, a 22M-parameter intent-aligned retriever defense.
AI.result: Larger models (Qwen3 and Gemma3 family members) show greater harmful-capability uplift under decomposition attacks; wider transformers assign lower loss to held-out instructions recoverable from injected facts; IntentAlign-MiniLM outperforms larger embedding models on intent retrieval and harmful recall across guardrails.
AI.conclusion: Scaling laws that improve model capabilities also increase vulnerability to cross-session decomposition attacks, necessitating new defense mechanisms like intent-aligned retrieval to mitigate compositional safety risks.

title: Biologically Inspired Mechanisms for Facilitating Grokking in Multilayer Perceptrons
summary: Grokking is a delayed transition from memorization to generalization that is often accompanied by substantial reorganization of internal representations. This paper studies whether biologically inspired mechanisms, many of which are not commonly incorporated into artificial neural networks, can actively promote this transition by regulating hidden-layer computation at the levels of neuronal activity, response, and effective connectivity. We augment a multilayer perceptron with input gating, structural plasticity, gain modulation, threshold modulation, homeostasis, lateral inhibition, and activation decorrelation, and evaluate these mechanisms through systematic ablations on two established grokking benchmarks: sparse parity and noisy XOR classification. The results show that the mechanisms contribute unequally to generalization. Homeostasis provides the strongest and most consistent benefit, while structural sparsification emerges as the second major mechanism. The remaining biologically inspired mechanisms have smaller or less consistent effects in the present experiments. For both problems, the results support the common principle that explicit regulation of neuron utilization and effective connectivity can improve the emergence of generalizable internal computation. These findings motivate broader investigation of biologically inspired activity regulation and adaptive sparsification, including in large language models, where they may accelerate the development of generalizable representations and reduce the optimization time required for robust generalization.

AI.tldr: Biologically-inspired mechanisms like homeostasis and structural sparsification can actively promote grokking (delayed generalization) by regulating neural activity and connectivity.
AI.motivation: Grokking represents a delayed transition from memorization to generalization that involves substantial internal reorganization. The paper investigates whether biologically-inspired mechanisms, which are typically absent in artificial neural networks, can actively promote this transition by regulating neural computation at various levels.
AI.method: Researchers augmented a multilayer perceptron with multiple biologically-inspired mechanisms: input gating, structural plasticity, gain modulation, threshold modulation, homeostasis, lateral inhibition, and activation decorrelation. They systematically evaluated these mechanisms through ablation studies on two established grokking benchmarks: sparse parity and noisy XOR classification.
AI.result: The mechanisms contributed unequally to generalization. Homeostasis provided the strongest and most consistent benefit, while structural sparsification emerged as the second major mechanism. Other mechanisms had smaller or less consistent effects. The results support that regulating neuron utilization and effective connectivity improves emergence of generalizable computation.
AI.conclusion: Explicit regulation of neural activity and connectivity through biologically-inspired mechanisms, particularly homeostasis and structural sparsification, can accelerate the development of generalizable representations. This motivates broader investigation in larger models like LLMs to potentially reduce optimization time needed for robust generalization.

title: The Illusion of $\textit{What If}$: Evaluating the Breakdown of Counterfactual Reasoning in LLMs
summary: Counterfactual reasoning requires models to reason beyond the observed world and explain how altered conditions propagate through downstream consequences. Existing benchmarks largely target bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios requiring causal-process evaluation. To this end, we present $\textbf{WhatIfBench}$, a diagnostic benchmark for open-domain, open-form, long-horizon counterfactual causal reasoning, containing 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios. To evaluate free-form responses, we further propose $\textbf{PRISM}$, which first converts each natural-language explanation into a Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graph of events, states, and mechanisms. On top of this graph, PRISM then jointly applies a Process Metric assessing graph-level causal validity and a Rubric Metric assessing answer-level explanatory adequacy. Evaluating six frontier LLMs with this framework, we find that WhatIfBench remains far from saturated: even the strongest model reaches only a 64.62% final score. Further analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation, suggesting that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes. The benchmark, code, and evaluation scripts are available at $\href{https://github.com/zju-gt/WhatIfBench}{WhatIfBench}$.

AI.tldr: WhatIfBench is a new benchmark for open-domain, long-horizon counterfactual reasoning with 220 questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios, evaluated using the PRISM framework that converts natural language explanations into causal graphs for joint assessment.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual reasoning benchmarks focus on bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios that require comprehensive causal-process evaluation. There's a need for diagnostic tools to assess models' ability to reason beyond observed conditions through altered downstream consequences.
AI.method: 1) Created WhatIfBench with 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid domains; 2) Developed PRISM evaluation framework that converts natural language explanations into Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graphs; 3) Applies Process Metric for graph-level causal validity and Rubric Metric for answer-level explanatory adequacy; 4) Evaluated six frontier LLMs using this framework.
AI.result: Even the strongest LLM achieves only 64.62% final score on WhatIfBench, showing the benchmark is far from saturated. Analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation in model responses, indicating that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual reasoning remains a challenging open problem for current LLMs, with significant gaps in causal understanding despite surface fluency. The WhatIfBench benchmark and PRISM evaluation framework provide diagnostic tools to identify these weaknesses and advance research in open-domain causal reasoning.

title: Beyond Flat Netlist: Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning for Scalable Analysis of Sequential Circuits
summary: Circuit Representation Learning (CRL) offers a powerful paradigm to guide and optimize core Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tasks, but its practical adoption is hindered by the immense scale of industrial netlists and a failure to explicitly model register-level temporal dynamics. To overcome these barriers, we introduce DeepSeq3, a novel hierarchical framework that abstracts circuits into a two-level representation: fine-grained combinational subgraphs partitioned by flip-flops (FFs), and a high-level Super-Node Graph (SNG) that models the register-transfer structure. A dual Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture learns representations at both levels, capturing local Boolean logic and global state transitions. Crucially, we introduce a state-centric pre-training scheme that predicts the reachability between FF states, endowing the model with a deep understanding of temporal behavior. Demonstrated on large-scale benchmarks, DeepSeq3's approach yields superior scalability and richer representations, reducing bounded model checking (BMC) solving time by 18% while guaranteeing correctness.

AI.tldr: DeepSeq3: Hierarchical framework for circuit representation learning that captures both combinational logic and register-level temporal dynamics, improving scalability for industrial netlists and reducing model checking time by 18%.
AI.motivation: Current Circuit Representation Learning (CRL) approaches face two major barriers: difficulty scaling to industrial-scale netlists and failure to explicitly model register-level temporal dynamics, which limits practical adoption in Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tasks.
AI.method: Hierarchical framework that abstracts circuits into two levels: 1) fine-grained combinational subgraphs partitioned by flip-flops, and 2) high-level Super-Node Graph (SNG) modeling register-transfer structure. Uses dual Graph Neural Networks to learn representations at both levels, with a state-centric pre-training scheme that predicts reachability between FF states.
AI.result: Demonstrated superior scalability and richer representations on large-scale benchmarks, reducing bounded model checking (BMC) solving time by 18% while guaranteeing correctness.
AI.conclusion: DeepSeq3 overcomes key barriers to CRL adoption by providing a scalable hierarchical approach that explicitly models temporal dynamics, enabling more efficient EDA optimization with correctness guarantees.

title: When Teacher Guidance Misleads: Reward-Aligned On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently emerged as a popular post-training paradigm for large language models (LLMs), providing an efficient way to transfer the knowledge and capabilities of teacher models into student models. However, teacher guidance on student-generated prefixes is not always reliable. Training should optimize the model to generate responses that are more likely to be correct, or equivalently, to get higher outcome rewards. But during OPD, the teacher model may provide guidance that discourages the student from moving toward correct trajectories or moves the student toward incorrect ones, which is misaligned with outcome reward. Such misaligned guidance is unreliable, as it would mislead the optimization process and ultimately degrade model performance. To mitigate misaligned teacher guidance, we propose Reward-Aligned On-Policy Distillation (RA-OPD). The key insight is to keep only trajectories whose induced updates move the student toward correct trajectories or discourage the student from moving toward incorrect ones. Specifically, for each sampled trajectory, RA-OPD checks whether its trajectory-level distillation return is consistent with its outcome reward and then filters out the misaligned trajectories. RA-OPD selects more reliable trajectories to improve student model performance without requiring additional computational cost. We evaluate RA-OPD on math and code benchmarks using models from the Qwen3 family and the DeepSeek-R1 family. Across seven math benchmarks and three code benchmarks, RA-OPD significantly outperforms standard OPD and other tested OPD variants.

AI.tldr: RA-OPD improves on-policy distillation by filtering out teacher guidance that is misaligned with outcome rewards, ensuring students only learn from reliable trajectories that move toward correct responses.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation suffers from unreliable teacher guidance where teachers may provide feedback that discourages students from correct trajectories or encourages incorrect ones, misaligning with the desired outcome rewards and degrading model performance.
AI.method: RA-OPD filters distillation trajectories by checking consistency between trajectory-level distillation returns and outcome rewards, keeping only aligned trajectories that move students toward correct responses or away from incorrect ones, without adding computational cost.
AI.result: RA-OPD significantly outperforms standard OPD and other OPD variants across seven math benchmarks and three code benchmarks using Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1 family models.
AI.conclusion: By selectively filtering misaligned teacher guidance, RA-OPD provides a more effective on-policy distillation approach that improves student model performance while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Performative Privacy: When Differential Privacy Maximizes Utility
summary: Privacy-preserving learning is often motivated by the idea that protecting users' data can preserve trust and thus participation, improving utility in the long term. However, this claim has not been formalized so far. In parallel, performative learning provides a framework for studying learning systems whose deployment affects the data they later observe. In this work, we bring these two perspectives together and introduce \emph{performative privacy}, where data leakage reduces future participation. We study a simple model where agents repeatedly contribute data for mean estimation but may leave the system when their data is leaked. Privacy is implemented through differentially private mechanisms, creating a trade-off between estimation noise and future participation. We show, through a theoretical study of the dynamics and numerical experiments, that a finite privacy budget can outperform non-private estimation in the long term when the feedback loop between leakage and participation is sufficiently strong. This provides first evidence that differential privacy can be optimal not only as a protection mechanism, but also from the perspective of long-term utility.

AI.tldr: Differential privacy can improve long-term utility by balancing data protection with user participation, creating a performative feedback loop where less leakage leads to more future data contributions.
AI.motivation: Privacy-preserving learning claims to improve long-term utility by maintaining user trust and participation, but this hasn't been formally studied. The paper aims to formalize this connection using performative learning frameworks.
AI.method: Introduced 'performative privacy' combining differential privacy with performative learning. Studied a model where agents contribute data for mean estimation but may leave when data is leaked. Analyzed trade-off between estimation noise (from DP) and future participation using theoretical dynamics and numerical experiments.
AI.result: Showed that a finite privacy budget (non-zero privacy protection) can outperform non-private estimation in the long term when the feedback loop between data leakage and participation is sufficiently strong. Provides evidence that differential privacy can be optimal for long-term utility.
AI.conclusion: This work formalizes the intuitive connection between privacy and utility, demonstrating that differential privacy can be optimal not just for protection, but also for maximizing long-term utility through sustained participation.

title: SABER: Stability-Aware Early Exit for LLM Reasoning via Adversarial Branch Probing
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong reasoning capabilities, yet long-chain reasoning becomes inefficient once the intermediate answer stabilizes across reasoning steps: additional reasoning yields little marginal benefit while incurring substantial inference cost. Existing early-exit methods based on confidence or entropy poorly capture reasoning stability, while consistency-based approaches rely on multi-step trajectory agreement, requiring sequential evaluations that delay exit. To better balance efficiency and reliability, we propose SABER, a training-free framework for stability-aware early exit via adversarial branch probing. SABER constructs simple yet effective semantic perturbations around intermediate reasoning states to form adversarial branches, and applies lightweight probing to estimate their likely final outcomes without full trajectory rollouts. When the probed outcomes remain consistent across branches, SABER exits early; otherwise, it continues reasoning. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks and model architectures show that SABER reduces reasoning token consumption by 30.2\%--39.8\% on average while maintaining competitive accuracy with full-length reasoning.

AI.tldr: SABER is a training-free early-exit framework for Large Reasoning Models that reduces token consumption by 30-40% through stability-aware adversarial branch probing, maintaining accuracy with full-length reasoning.
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models become inefficient in long-chain reasoning once intermediate answers stabilize - additional reasoning provides little benefit while incurring substantial inference costs. Existing early-exit methods based on confidence or entropy poorly capture reasoning stability, while consistency-based approaches require sequential evaluations that delay exit.
AI.method: SABER (Stability-Aware Early Exit via Adversarial Branch Probing) constructs semantic perturbations around intermediate reasoning states to form adversarial branches, then applies lightweight probing to estimate their likely final outcomes without full trajectory rollouts. When probed outcomes remain consistent across branches, it exits early; otherwise continues reasoning.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks and model architectures show SABER reduces reasoning token consumption by 30.2-39.8% on average while maintaining competitive accuracy with full-length reasoning.
AI.conclusion: SABER effectively balances efficiency and reliability in Large Reasoning Models by enabling early exit based on reasoning stability, significantly reducing inference costs without compromising accuracy, outperforming existing confidence/entropy-based early-exit methods.

title: Generalized Context in Cross Attention for Transfer Learning of Disjoint Tabular Data
comment: Accepted for publication at Neural Networks (Elsevier)
summary: Unlike images and text, applying transfer learning to tabular data is challenging due to heterogeneity in feature types, structures, and semantics across disparate domains. Existing methods assume shared features across data tables to enable knowledge transfer between domains, which is unrealistic in practice. \mds{This paper introduces generalized context learning to remove the requirement of shared features across domains. The generalized context captured by transformer projection weights for $key$, $value$, and $query$ provides rule-based generalization rather than the domain-specific context conventionally learned from transformer activations. Projection weights for $key$ from the source domain interact with the weight for $query$ in the target domain to achieve Cross-domain Attention Transfer Learning (CATTLE) in a data-agnostic manner. Our experiments on ten pairs of disjoint source-target data sets show that CATTLE can learn generalized context from a single source data set and is rank-wise and statistically superior to nine state-of-the-art baselines, including machine learning, deep learning, and transfer learning methods using large-scale pre-trained models. CATTLE achieves the best average rank (2.9) and delivers a 3.7% average AUROC gain over the baseline methods.} The CATTLE source code is available at https://tinyurl.com/pr5s8ywn.

AI.tldr: CATTLE introduces cross-domain attention transfer learning for tabular data that works without shared features between domains by using transformer projection weights for generalized context learning.
AI.motivation: Transfer learning for tabular data is challenging due to feature heterogeneity across domains. Existing methods assume shared features, which is unrealistic in practice.
AI.method: Proposes generalized context learning using transformer projection weights (key, value, query). Source domain key weights interact with target domain query weights to enable cross-domain attention transfer learning (CATTLE) in a data-agnostic manner.
AI.result: Tested on ten pairs of disjoint source-target datasets. CATTLE achieves best average rank (2.9) and 3.7% average AUROC gain over nine state-of-the-art baselines, including ML, DL, and transfer learning methods with pre-trained models.
AI.conclusion: CATTLE successfully enables transfer learning for tabular data without requiring shared features across domains, outperforming existing methods through generalized context learning from transformer projection weights.

title: AERA: Adaptive Evidence Residual Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
summary: Test-time scaling improves language-model reasoning by generating additional candidate solutions, but allocating the same inference budget to every problem is computationally wasteful. Existing adaptive stopping methods commonly rely on confidence, agreement, or answer stability, implicitly assuming that stronger current evidence indicates that further computation is unnecessary. We show that this assumption can fail: checkpoint-level correctness evolves non-monotonically, and observable evidence may strengthen before an answer collapses or weaken before it recovers. Motivated by this mismatch, we introduce Adaptive Evidence Residual Allocation (AERA), a sequential controller that learns whether additional computation is likely to recover a better answer from checkpoint-observable evidence. AERA characterizes cumulative response prefixes using answer-distribution, temporal, re-solving, semantic, and compute features, and repeatedly decides whether to stop or allocate the next response block. Future checkpoint correctness is used only to construct offline supervision and is never available to the controller at inference time. Across GSM8K and GPQA Diamond, AERA identifies question-specific residual opportunities while substantially reducing inference computation. In a frozen-threshold incremental-generation evaluation on 300 untouched GSM8K questions, AERA achieves 92.61% accuracy versus 93.01% with 128 responses while reducing completion tokens by 95.99%. These results suggest that adaptive reasoning should estimate the future value of computation rather than equating present confidence with correctness.

AI.tldr: AERA is a sequential controller that learns whether additional computation is likely to recover better answers by analyzing checkpoint evidence, achieving near-optimal accuracy with significantly reduced computation compared to fixed-budget methods.
AI.motivation: Current adaptive stopping methods rely on assumptions that stronger current evidence indicates further computation is unnecessary, but these assumptions can fail as checkpoint-level correctness evolves non-monotonically - observable evidence may strengthen before answers collapse or weaken before recovery.
AI.method: AERA (Adaptive Evidence Residual Allocation) uses a sequential controller that learns whether additional computation is likely to recover better answers. It characterizes cumulative response prefixes using answer-distribution, temporal, re-solving, semantic, and compute features, and repeatedly decides whether to stop or allocate the next response block. Future checkpoint correctness is only used for offline supervision and not available during inference.
AI.result: On GSM8K and GPQA Diamond, AERA identifies question-specific residual opportunities while substantially reducing inference computation. On 300 GSM8K questions, it achieves 92.61% accuracy vs 93.01% with 128 responses while reducing completion tokens by 95.99%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive reasoning should estimate the future value of computation rather than equating present confidence with correctness, as AERA demonstrates that intelligently allocating computation based on likelihood of answer recovery can maintain near-optimal performance with dramatic computational savings.

title: D-TAIA: Domain-Aware LLM Adaptation for Multi-Task Predictive Process Monitoring
summary: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) enables organizations to forecast future process behavior, such as the next activity and remaining time of ongoing cases. In practice, three conditions cause existing methods to degrade, namely data scarcity, high process entropy and distributional shift. While Foundation Models (FMs), especially Large Language Models (LLMs), offer a new paradigm through broad sequential reasoning, adapting them to multi-task PPM under these conditions remains an open challenge. Existing FM-based approaches either lack mechanisms for handling distributional shift or rely on direct regression heads that can be structurally misaligned with continuous time prediction tasks. This paper introduces D-TAIA (Domain-aware Training and Attention-based Inference Architecture), a framework for a joint next activity and remaining time prediction task via parameter-efficient fine-tuning of an FM backbone. Our approach combines domain-aware triplet loss (DATL) pre-training with FAISS-based nearest neighbor retrieval for remaining time prediction, and adopts the TAIA inference strategy to preserve pre-trained sequential reasoning during fine-tuning. Evaluated across four real-world event logs, D-TAIA consistently shows SOTA or competitive performance compared to a fine-tuned LLM and a recurrent neural network baseline. Ablation studies confirm that techniques from NLP and computer vision can be transferred effectively to PPM with only a 10M-parameter backbone, though component contributions vary by dataset entropy.

AI.tldr: D-TAIA is a framework that uses parameter-efficient fine-tuning of foundation models for predictive process monitoring, combining domain-aware triplet loss pre-training with FAISS-based nearest neighbor retrieval for joint next activity and remaining time prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing Predictive Process Monitoring methods degrade under three conditions: data scarcity, high process entropy, and distributional shift. While Foundation Models offer broad sequential reasoning capabilities, adapting them to multi-task PPM under these challenging conditions remains an open challenge, especially as current FM-based approaches either lack mechanisms for handling distributional shift or use structurally misaligned regression heads for continuous time prediction.
AI.method: Introduces D-TAIA framework with: 1) Domain-aware triplet loss (DATL) pre-training, 2) FAISS-based nearest neighbor retrieval for remaining time prediction, 3) TAIA inference strategy to preserve pre-trained sequential reasoning during fine-tuning, 4) Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of an FM backbone (only 10M parameters), 5) Joint approach for next activity and remaining time prediction tasks.
AI.result: D-TAIA consistently shows state-of-the-art or competitive performance across four real-world event logs compared to fine-tuned LLM and recurrent neural network baselines. Ablation studies confirm that techniques from NLP and computer vision can be effectively transferred to PPM, though component contributions vary by dataset entropy.
AI.conclusion: The D-TAIA framework successfully addresses key challenges in Predictive Process Monitoring (data scarcity, high process entropy, distributional shift) through domain-aware pre-training and specialized inference architecture. The approach demonstrates that foundation models can be effectively adapted to multi-task PPM with minimal parameter overhead, opening new possibilities for robust process prediction under real-world conditions.

title: openJiuwen: Beyond Static Harnesses for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
summary: Long-horizon coding agents operate over evolving repository states while increasingly relying on heterogeneous capabilities, delegated agents, and multi-agent coordination. These trends pose two complementary challenges for the agent harness. First, developers need to compose capabilities, reconfigure execution logic, and scale increasingly complex agent systems without repeatedly rebuilding orchestration. Second, complex coding tasks continuously produce new evidence---such as semantic diagnostics, execution outcomes, task progress, and changing context relevance---that should dynamically influence subsequent runtime decisions. We characterize these challenges as Structural Composability and Runtime Adaptivity. We present openJiuwen, an open-source harness designed for both developer composability and adaptive task execution. openJiuwen provides a shared execution substrate and Rail-based capability composition across single agents, delegated sub-agents, and Swarm Flow, enabling developers to construct sophisticated agent harnesses under common execution semantics. It further adapts framework-controlled runtime decisions around a fixed model policy, allowing evolving evidence to dynamically affect context, feedback, and task control toward successful completion. We systematically evaluate openJiuwen on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, where it achieves 82.6% and 87.19%, respectively, exceeding the strongest selected official-leaderboard point estimates by 3.4 and 3.39 percentage points. These results show that openJiuwen achieves strong performance on complex coding tasks while providing a composable and adaptive harness design.

AI.tldr: openJiuwen is an open-source harness that addresses structural composability and runtime adaptivity challenges in long-horizon coding agents through a unified execution substrate and evidence-based adaptive task execution.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon coding agents face challenges in structural composability (difficulty in composing capabilities and scaling complex agent systems) and runtime adaptivity (need to dynamically incorporate new evidence from coding tasks into execution decisions).
AI.method: Developed openJiuwen harness with a shared execution substrate, Rail-based capability composition across single agents, delegated sub-agents, and Swarm Flow, plus framework-controlled runtime decisions that adapt to evolving evidence around a fixed model policy.
AI.result: Achieved 82.6% on SWE-bench Verified and 87.19% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, exceeding strongest official-leaderboard point estimates by 3.4 and 3.39 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: openJiuwen demonstrates strong performance on complex coding tasks while providing a composable and adaptive harness design that addresses key challenges in modern agent systems.

title: Efficient Online Continual Foundation Model Fine-Tuning for Predictive Process Monitoring
summary: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) models are increasingly deployed in dynamic environments where concept drift causes the underlying process distribution to shift over time. While recent work has moved toward online continual learning, existing methods train compact, task-specific networks entirely from scratch, leaving a persistent cold-start problem. Foundation Models (FMs) offer a compelling solution to this problem, but their continual fine-tuning in the process mining domain remains unexplored. We propose COMPASS (Continual Online foundation Model-based PPM with Adaptive SubSpaces), the first framework for online continual fine-tuning of FMs for PPM. COMPASS adapts loss-plateau drift detection to autonomously identify task boundaries in event streams and maintains a unified knowledge subspace including both pre-trained and task-specific directions. We evaluate our approach on nine event streams covering synthetic and real-world concept drift scenarios, across task-free and task-aware settings with multiple backbones and with consistent hyperparameter tuning across all methods. Our approach outperforms three SOTA non-FM competitors and two update strategy baselines, with particularly strong gains on streams exhibiting recurrent drift and complex, long-running cases, while incurring acceptable computational overhead compared to the non-FM competitors.

AI.tldr: COMPASS introduces the first framework for online continual fine-tuning of Foundation Models for Predictive Process Monitoring, using adaptive subspaces to handle concept drift without cold-start problems.
AI.motivation: Predictive Process Monitoring models struggle in dynamic environments with concept drift, facing persistent cold-start problems when training task-specific networks from scratch. Foundation Models offer potential solutions but their continual fine-tuning in process mining remains unexplored.
AI.method: COMPASS adapts loss-plateau drift detection to autonomously identify task boundaries in event streams and maintains a unified knowledge subspace that includes both pre-trained and task-specific directions for continual learning.
AI.result: COMPASS outperforms three state-of-the-art non-FM competitors and two update strategy baselines across nine event streams covering synthetic and real-world concept drift scenarios, with strong gains on recurrent drift and complex long-running cases.
AI.conclusion: Foundation Model-based continual fine-tuning with adaptive subspaces effectively addresses concept drift in Predictive Process Monitoring, offering superior performance over existing methods while incurring acceptable computational overhead.

title: Learning from Hard Prompts: Difficulty-aware Advantage Amplification in Dynamic Sampling
summary: Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) is a prominent variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). DAPO introduces several improvements over GRPO. Among these, Dynamic Sampling contributes the most to DAPO's accuracy gains relative to GRPO. To improve accuracy, Dynamic Sampling enhances training stability by eliminating zero policy gradients from zero advantages. Specifically, it avoids such zero gradients by filtering out prompts where sampled responses are either entirely correct or incorrect. However, our theoretical analysis shows that Dynamic Sampling decrease training efficiency as it cannot effectively utilize hard-to-sample correct responses on hard prompts. Formally, it asymmetrically amplifies the advantages of distinct responses to the same prompts. On hard prompts, incorrect responses undergo greater amplification than correct ones. This leads the model to avoid generating the observed incorrect responses rather than capitalizing on the hard-to-sample correct ones on hard prompts, resulting in low training efficiency. To improve training efficiency, we propose Direct Advantage Amplification (DAA), which amplifies the advantages of hard-to-sample correct responses on hard prompts, as obtained by Dynamic Sampling. This ensures that, when Dynamic Sampling is used, these hard-to-sample responses can be effectively capitalized on, implying higher training efficiency. By integrating DAA into DAPO, we obtain Difficulty-aware Advantage Amplification Policy Optimization (DA3PO), which is implemented with fewer than 30 lines of code from DAPO. Experiments show that DA3PO significantly outperforms GRPO and other classical GRPO variants.

AI.tldr: DA3PO improves on DAPO/GRPO by adding Direct Advantage Amplification to better utilize hard-to-sample correct responses on hard prompts, boosting training efficiency.
AI.motivation: Dynamic Sampling in DAPO improves accuracy but reduces training efficiency by failing to effectively utilize hard-to-sample correct responses on hard prompts, instead causing the model to avoid incorrect responses rather than capitalize on correct ones.
AI.method: Proposed Direct Advantage Amplification (DAA) that amplifies advantages of hard-to-sample correct responses on hard prompts obtained by Dynamic Sampling. Integrated DAA into DAPO to create DA3PO (Difficulty-aware Advantage Amplification Policy Optimization), implemented with <30 lines of code changes.
AI.result: DA3PO significantly outperforms GRPO and other classical GRPO variants in experiments.
AI.conclusion: By addressing the efficiency limitation of Dynamic Sampling through DAA, DA3PO achieves both improved accuracy and training efficiency compared to previous GRPO variants, with minimal code changes.

title: Spectral Features Dominate BCG Respiratory-Event Detection: A Large-Scale Patient-Independent Comparison of Feature Groups in Sleep Apnea Patients
summary: Unobtrusive ballistocardiographic (BCG) sensing is a promising modality for long-term sleep-apnea monitoring, yet it remains unclear which signal features are most discriminative for respiratory-event detection. We present a literature-guided, patient-independent comparison of ten BCG feature groups using a 512-sensor capacitive pressure mat recorded simultaneously with respiratory polygraphy in 155 patients (52 female, 103 male) undergoing in-hospital evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea. Features were extracted from six spatially distinct signal channels, yielding a 191-dimensional feature vector spanning general statistical, time-domain, frequency-domain, wavelet, frame-energy, and nonlinear complexity descriptors. Under strict leave-one-patient-out cross-validation for binary classification of respiratory-event windows versus event-free reference windows, Random Forest and Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved AUC-ROC of 0.967 and 0.969 and AUC-PR of 0.977 and 0.979, respectively. Feature-importance analysis revealed that frequency-domain features dominate discrimination: breathing-band power in the 0.1-0.4 Hz range accounted for 30.3% of total discriminative information across all spatial channels, and Fast Fourier Transform spectral-shape descriptors of the adaptively preprocessed channel contributed a further 15.1%. AUC and curve-length features provided the main complementary time-domain evidence (21.5%), whereas wavelet-derived and nonlinear features contributed smaller secondary effects (10.4% combined across 59 features). Frequency-domain and time-domain features together accounted for 67% of total discriminative information, demonstrating that a compact, interpretable subset of the full feature library achieves clinically relevant performance under patient-independent validation and providing an empirical basis for feature selection in future BCG systems.

AI.tldr: This study systematically compares BCG features for sleep apnea detection, finding frequency-domain features (breathing-band power) most discriminative, with high-performing models achieving ~0.97 AUC under patient-independent validation.
AI.motivation: While unobtrusive ballistocardiographic (BCG) sensing shows promise for long-term sleep-apnea monitoring, it's unclear which signal features are most discriminative for respiratory-event detection. There's a need for systematic comparison to identify optimal features for reliable patient-independent monitoring systems.
AI.method: Used a literature-guided approach to compare ten BCG feature groups from 512-sensor capacitive pressure mat data synchronized with respiratory polygraphy from 155 sleep apnea patients. Extracted 191-dimensional feature vectors from six spatial channels covering statistical, time-domain, frequency-domain, wavelet, frame-energy, and nonlinear complexity descriptors. Applied strict leave-one-patient-out cross-validation with Random Forest and Histogram Gradient Boosting classifiers.
AI.result: Both classifiers achieved excellent performance: AUC-ROC of 0.967/0.969 and AUC-PR of 0.977/0.979. Feature importance analysis revealed frequency-domain features dominated: breathing-band power (0.1-0.4 Hz) accounted for 30.3% of discriminative information, with FFT spectral-shape adding 15.1%. AUC and curve-length time-domain features provided 21.5%, while wavelet and nonlinear features contributed only 10.4% combined.
AI.conclusion: A compact subset of interpretable frequency-domain and time-domain features (67% of total discriminative information) can achieve clinically relevant sleep apnea detection performance under patient-independent validation, providing an empirical basis for feature selection in future BCG monitoring systems.

title: When Evidence Shapes Collaboration: Knowledge-Conditioned Topology Generation for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have recently moved from static workflows toward dynamically generated collaboration topologies. However, existing topology generation methods rely primarily on the parametric knowledge of large language models, with external search or retrieval used only as a reactive tool rather than an explicit determinant of collaboration structure. This leads to structure-knowledge misalignment, where systems exhibit redundant interactions or insufficient verification in knowledge-intensive tasks. We propose K-GAT (Knowledge-Guided Agent Topology Generator), a neuro-symbolic framework that formulates collaboration topology design as a knowledge-conditioned structure learning problem, integrating external evidence directly into autoregressive graph generation.
