We perform extensive evaluation on three domains: code generation (HumanEval), mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), and instruction following (AlpacaEval) on Llama-2-7B models, and show DARTS achieves significant improvement over the standard surgery approach while adding negligible parameters ($0.1\%$ of total parameters).

AI.tldr: DARTS (Decoder-Aware Representation Tuning via Surgery) is a method to mitigate representation bias in merged decoder LLMs using entropy-weighted L1 loss and position-dependent correction, achieving significant improvement over standard approaches with minimal parameter overhead.
AI.motivation: Model merging creates multi-task LLMs but suffers from representation bias - systematic drift in hidden states between merged and individual source models. While prior work addressed this for encoder models, decoder models present unique challenges due to their autoregressive nature that haven't been studied.
AI.method: DARTS addresses two decoder-specific challenges: (1) causal attention causing bias accumulation across tokens requiring position-dependent correction, and (2) high-entropy positions being more critical for generation quality. The method uses entropy-weighted L1 loss to prioritize correction at high-entropy positions and per-position additive bias for position-dependent error correction without overparameterization.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on code generation (HumanEval), mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), and instruction following (AlpacaEval) using Llama-2-7B models shows DARTS achieves significant improvement over standard surgery approach while adding only 0.1% of total parameters.
AI.conclusion: DARTS effectively mitigates representation bias in merged decoder models by addressing their unique challenges through entropy-aware weighting and position-dependent correction, offering a lightweight solution that significantly improves performance across diverse domains.

title: Expert Knowledge & Machine Understanding: Bridging Reactome's Ontology with LLM Semantic Embeddings
summary: Biological knowledgebases like Reactome provide high-quality pathways that include biological elements' relationships and textual descriptions (metadata). The quality of such pathways is granted by manual curation, that presents, however, significant scalability challenges. Lately, numerous NLP tools have been proposed to cope with this issue, leveraging textual information to automatically expand biological knowledgebases. However, little exploration has been done so far to assess whether relationships among textual descriptions mirror higher order biological relationships. This study explores whether human-written descriptions in Reactome can be used to infer the experts' defined global hierarchical structure. To test this, we extracted from Reactome the Homo Sapiens hierarchy of pathways and their reactions (Reactome Hierarchy), and used textual metadata to reconstruct a Semantic Hierarchy, combining a sentence transformer model (SPECTER2) with a modified agglomerative nesting algorithm and a graph reconstruction algorithm. Quantitative (Laplacian Spectral Distance and Bootstrapping) and qualitative (global topological metrics) analyses confirm our hypothesis and indicate that the global hierarchical structure of pathways can be inferred by experts textual metadata.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that textual descriptions in Reactome can be used to reconstruct biological pathway hierarchies, validating that expert-written metadata reflects underlying biological relationships.
AI.motivation: Biological knowledgebases like Reactome are manually curated for quality but face scalability challenges. While NLP tools exist for automatic expansion, little research has explored whether textual descriptions mirror higher-order biological relationships. The study aims to test if human-written descriptions can infer experts' defined hierarchical structures.
AI.method: Extracted Homo Sapiens pathway and reaction hierarchy from Reactome, then used textual metadata to reconstruct a Semantic Hierarchy using SPECTER2 sentence transformer model, a modified agglomerative nesting algorithm, and a graph reconstruction algorithm.
AI.result: Quantitative analyses (Laplacian Spectral Distance and Bootstrapping) and qualitative analyses (global topological metrics) confirm the hypothesis that global hierarchical structure of pathways can be inferred from experts' textual metadata.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that textual descriptions in biological knowledgebases effectively capture underlying hierarchical relationships, supporting the use of NLP approaches for scaling manual curation while maintaining biological coherence.

title: Advancing Interaction-Sensitive Feature Selection: Novel Relief-Based Algorithms, Expanded Comparisons, and Recommendations for Biomedical Data Mining
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables, submitted for journal review
summary: As a precursor to high-dimensional biomedical data modeling, reliable feature selection can reduce computational expense, improve modeling performance, and yield simpler, more interpretable models. However, most filter-based feature selection methods struggle to detect feature interactions, while wrapper or embedded feature selection methods are computationally expensive. Relief-based algorithms (RBAs) are filter methods that are sensitive to feature interactions while mitigating these other limitations. This study (1) refactors, optimizes, and expands the scikit-rebate Python package with existing and newly proposed RBA variants and (2) conducts rigorous RBA benchmark comparisons across diverse genomic simulations. We expand scikit-rebate to include SWRF*, mu-Relief, and 5 novel RBA variants implementing alternative strategies for neighbor selection and feature scoring. All RBAs were evaluated to compare predictive feature ranking and runtime across simulated genomic datasets varying in sample size, number of features, heritability, and underlying association type (e.g. main effects and interactions). All RBAs, except mu-Relief, were proficient in detecting 2-way interactions in noisy data. RBAs utilizing 'far' scoring were best at detecting 2-way interactions - with MultiSWRFDB* top-performing - but were far less sensitive to main effects. SWRF, MultiSWRF, MultiSURF, and MultiSWRFDB yielded top performance across main effect and 2-way interaction datasets with MultiSWRFDB performing best when also considering 3-way interactions. Refactoring of scikit-rebate resulted in 10 to 35-fold reductions in RBA runtimes. The newly introduced RBAs were among the strongest performing, and by robustly retaining both main effects and 2-way epistatic interactions, these algorithms preserve predictive signals for downstream modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper refactors and expands the scikit-rebate Python package with new Relief-based algorithm variants, conducts rigorous benchmarking on genomic simulations, and shows the new algorithms perform well in detecting both main effects and feature interactions with significantly reduced runtime.
AI.motivation: Feature selection is crucial for high-dimensional biomedical data modeling, but existing methods have limitations: filter methods struggle with feature interactions, while wrapper/embedded methods are computationally expensive. Relief-based algorithms offer a promising middle ground by being sensitive to interactions while avoiding high computational costs.
AI.method: The study refactors, optimizes, and expands the scikit-rebate Python package with existing and newly proposed RBA variants. It adds SWRF*, mu-Relief, and 5 novel RBA variants implementing alternative neighbor selection and feature scoring strategies. All RBAs were evaluated across simulated genomic datasets varying in sample size, features, heritability, and association types.
AI.result: Refactoring reduced runtimes by 10-35x. Most RBAs (except mu-Relief) detected 2-way interactions in noisy data. Algorithms using 'far' scoring were best at detecting 2-way interactions (MultiSWRFDB* top-performing) but less sensitive to main effects. SWRF, MultiSWRF, MultiSURF, and MultiSWRFDB performed best across main effect and 2-way interaction datasets, with MultiSWRFDB excelling with 3-way interactions.
AI.conclusion: The expanded scikit-rebate package provides efficient, high-performing RBA variants that preserve both main effects and feature interactions, making them valuable for downstream biomedical modeling. The new algorithms demonstrate strong performance while offering significant computational improvements.

title: Generative AI Alignment with Hinduism's Theological Plurality and Sacred Representation
summary: Generative AI systems are increasingly used to answer personal questions and mediate everyday practices, including religion. However, existing discussions around AI alignment and ethics have largely centered secular, Western, and Abrahamic assumptions about religion, offering limited attention to other faith-based traditions. In this paper, we examine how Hindu users engage with generative AI systems in relation to their religious knowledge, belief, and practice. Drawing on 15 semi-structured interviews with Bangladeshi Hindu participants, we analyze how users interpret AI-generated religious representations, scriptural explanations, devotional interactions, and synthetic religious media. We found that AI can be both accessible and ethically troubling. While AI supported scriptural inquiry, devotional visualization, and religious storytelling, our study also identified concerns about theological flattening, cultural misrepresentation, devotional manipulation, and the simulation of sacred presence and authority. We conclude by arguing that religious alignment in generative AI requires interpretive alignment: systems that disclose their limits, preserve plurality, and avoid simulating sacred authority and sycophantic personalization.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how Hindu users in Bangladesh interact with generative AI for religious purposes, finding AI can provide scriptural access but raises concerns about theological flattening, cultural misrepresentation, and inappropriate simulation of sacred authority.
AI.motivation: Current AI alignment and ethics discussions focus primarily on secular, Western, and Abrahamic religious perspectives, neglecting other faith traditions like Hinduism. There's a need to understand how generative AI systems interact with diverse religious practices and knowledge systems.
AI.method: The study conducted 15 semi-structured interviews with Bangladeshi Hindu participants to analyze their engagement with generative AI systems for religious purposes, examining AI-generated religious representations, scriptural explanations, devotional interactions, and synthetic religious media.
AI.result: AI supported scriptural inquiry, devotional visualization, and religious storytelling, making religious knowledge more accessible. However, it raised concerns about theological flattening (simplifying complex traditions), cultural misrepresentation, devotional manipulation, and inappropriate simulation of sacred presence and authority.
AI.conclusion: Religious alignment in generative AI requires "interpretive alignment": systems that clearly disclose their limitations, preserve religious plurality, avoid simulating sacred authority, and resist sycophantic personalization that might manipulate religious devotion.

title: Blog: Survey of Optimizers
summary: Neural-network optimization in 2025-2026 is no longer well described as a succession of new Adam variants. The design space has expanded from coordinates to matrices and layers, from fixed training horizons to policies over time, and from mathematical update rules to state representations that must survive sharding and low-precision computation. This survey organizes recent optimizers and training optimization methods along four largely independent axes: temporal estimation, update geometry, horizon management, and representation and systems. It connects the spectral normalization of Muon, the historical matrix statistics of Shampoo and SOAP, adaptive and hybrid matrix methods, memory-efficient optimizers, schedule-free training, small-batch corrections, and quantized optimizer states. The central empirical conclusion is deliberately non-triumphal: matrix-aware methods represent a genuine advance, but there is no context-independent replacement for AdamW. Rankings change with model scale, data-to-parameter ratio, batch size, schedule, parameter partition, tuning budget, and whether the target metric is tokens, FLOPs, wall-clock time, or memory. The practical consequence is a compositional view of optimizer design and a stricter protocol for evaluating optimizer claims.

AI.tldr: A survey of neural network optimization advances (2025-2026) organized along four axes: temporal estimation, update geometry, horizon management, and representation/systems, finding no universal replacement for AdamW despite genuine advances in matrix-aware methods.
AI.motivation: Neural network optimization has evolved beyond just Adam variants, with expanded design spaces including matrices/layers, temporal policies, and system considerations like sharding and low-precision computation. The field lacks a comprehensive organizational framework for these diverse advances.
AI.method: Organizes recent optimizers along four independent axes: 1) Temporal estimation (handling time-dependent statistics), 2) Update geometry (matrix vs coordinate methods), 3) Horizon management (training schedule policies), and 4) Representation and systems (surviving sharding/low-precision). Examines methods like spectral normalization (Muon), historical matrix statistics (Shampoo/SOAP), adaptive matrix methods, memory-efficient optimizers, schedule-free training, small-batch corrections, and quantized states.
AI.result: Matrix-aware methods represent genuine advances, but there is no context-independent replacement for AdamW. Optimizer rankings change depending on multiple factors: model scale, data-to-parameter ratio, batch size, schedule, parameter partition, tuning budget, and target metric (tokens, FLOPs, wall-clock time, memory).
AI.conclusion: The field requires a compositional view of optimizer design where methods combine components from different axes, and stricter evaluation protocols that account for practical constraints rather than seeking universal solutions.

title: Stay Within Your Bounds: Distance-Guided Decoding for Guaranteed Context-Free Grammar Compliance
summary: Grammar-constrained decoding helps large language models produce syntactically valid structured outputs, such as code, JSON, and SQL. For context-free grammars, many practical decoders enforce local prefix feasibility: each token must keep the current prefix extendable to some valid completion. Yet, under tokenizer-grammar mismatch and finite token budgets, feasible prefixes may still fail to reach acceptance. We propose a lookahead-guided decoding framework for context-free grammars based on pushdown automata. Offline, we compute bounded pushdown summaries with reachability labels and upper-bound distances to acceptance. Online, these estimates guide horizon-aware pruning and beam search. The resulting decoder is syntactically sound: every output is accepted by the target grammar. Experiments on JSON, SQL, and Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) show both consistent syntactic validity and improved completion quality over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: A lookahead-guided decoding framework for context-free grammars using pushdown automata that ensures syntactic validity and improves output quality in structured text generation.
AI.motivation: Current grammar-constrained decoding methods enforce local prefix feasibility, but under tokenizer-grammar mismatch and finite token budgets, feasible prefixes may still fail to reach full acceptance, leading to invalid structured outputs.
AI.method: Proposes a lookahead-guided decoding framework based on pushdown automata: 1) Offline computation of bounded pushdown summaries with reachability labels and upper-bound distances to acceptance; 2) Online use of these estimates to guide horizon-aware pruning and beam search.
AI.result: Experiments on JSON, SQL, and Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) show both consistent syntactic validity (every output is accepted by the target grammar) and improved completion quality over existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lookahead-guided decoding framework successfully addresses limitations of existing grammar-constrained decoding methods by ensuring syntactic soundness while improving output quality for structured text generation tasks.

title: QGPINNs: A Physics-Informed Neural Network Framework for Nonlocal Differential Equations on Quantum Graphs
summary: We propose QGPINNs, a physics-informed neural network framework developed in PyTorch for the numerical solution of nonlocal differential equations on quantum graphs. The framework is designed as a general computational implementation in which the solution on each edge of the graph is approximated by a neural network, while a unified graph-based loss function enforces the governing equations together with initial, boundary, and vertex transmission conditions. In particular, the formulation incorporates standard continuity and Kirchhoff-Neumann vertex conditions and Dirichlet boundary conditions into the learning process to couple the local edge-wise neural approximations into a global solution on the graph. The framework is developed for two representative classes of nonlinear models: multi-order fractional elliptic problems and time-fractional evolution equations on quantum graphs. To improve accuracy and training stability, QGPINNs integrates several graph-adapted learning strategies, including soft and hard constraint enforcement, dynamic loss balancing, Fourier feature embeddings, and a learnable singularity-capturing feature for weakly singular solutions arising in the considered problems. The framework also extends naturally to inverse problems, including the identification of the orders of fractional operators and physical parameters from noisy observational data. We validate the accuracy, computational efficiency, and physical consistency of the proposed framework through numerical experiments on benchmark graph structures and real-world networks, including the IEEE 14-bus system and an open-channel agricultural drainage network.

AI.tldr: QGPINNs is a PyTorch-based physics-informed neural network framework for solving nonlocal differential equations on quantum graphs, using edge-wise neural approximations with graph-based loss functions and specialized learning strategies for improved accuracy.
AI.motivation: There is a need for efficient computational frameworks to solve complex nonlocal differential equations on quantum graphs, which arise in various scientific and engineering applications like power systems and drainage networks.
AI.method: Developed QGPINNs in PyTorch with neural network approximations on each graph edge, unified graph-based loss functions enforcing governing equations with vertex transmission conditions (continuity, Kirchhoff-Neumann) and boundary conditions, and integrated graph-adapted learning strategies including soft/hard constraint enforcement, dynamic loss balancing, Fourier feature embeddings, and learnable singularity-capturing.
AI.result: Validated framework accuracy, computational efficiency, and physical consistency through numerical experiments on benchmark graph structures and real-world networks including IEEE 14-bus system and agricultural drainage networks, with successful application to both forward problems and inverse problems like parameter identification from noisy data.
AI.conclusion: QGPINNs provides an effective, general-purpose framework for solving challenging nonlocal differential equations on quantum graphs with good accuracy and efficiency, and extends naturally to inverse problems with practical applications in real-world networks.

title: REINS: Refusal-Enhanced Inhibitory Steering with Sparse Autoencoder Features
summary: Steering with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offers a lightweight inference-time path for adapting the behavior of large language models without retraining. By exposing sparse and interpretable features, SAE steering provides a promising interface for safety control that guides harmful continuations toward refusal. However, we observe that complex wrappers can still undermine existing SAE steering methods on harmful prompts. To evaluate this failure mode systematically, we construct Generalized Undercover Instruction Safety Evaluation (GUISE), a dataset of harmful prompts with complex wrappers. Existing single direction SAE steering methods do not reliably produce refusals on harmful prompts, suggesting that refusal enhancement alone can be too weak when the harmful continuation path remains active. This motivates us to propose Refusal-Enhanced INhibitory Steering (REINS), which suppresses harmful continuation features and enhances safe refusal features in the same SAE feature space. Experiments on GUISE and other datasets show that prior methods either intervene too weakly or achieve only apparent safety through collapse, while REINS substantially reduces harmful responses, markedly improves safe refusals and largely preserves general capabilities.

AI.tldr: SAE steering can be undermined by complex prompt wrappers; REINS combines suppression of harmful features with enhancement of refusal features to achieve better safety while preserving capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing SAE steering methods fail on harmful prompts with complex wrappers, showing that refusal enhancement alone is insufficient when harmful continuation paths remain active.
AI.method: Proposes REINS (Refusal-Enhanced INhibitory Steering) that simultaneously suppresses harmful continuation features and enhances safe refusal features within the same SAE feature space.
AI.result: REINS substantially reduces harmful responses, markedly improves safe refusals, and largely preserves general capabilities, outperforming prior methods on the GUISE dataset.
AI.conclusion: REINS provides a more robust approach to SAE steering for safety control by addressing both harmful feature suppression and refusal enhancement, overcoming limitations of previous single-direction methods.

title: Beyond Task-Only Matching: Personalized Skill Routing with Counterfactual Evaluation
summary: The rapid expansion of reusable skill repositories makes skill routing a critical capability for large language model (LLM) agents. Existing methods treat routing as task-only semantic matching. However, when users with incompatible constraints issue an identical request, this assumption conflates task relevance with skill suitability: a task-only router can select a semantically plausible skill that is unsuitable for the requesting user. To expose this failure mode, we formulate \textit{personalized skill routing} as profile-conditioned retrieval, in which relevance depends jointly on the task and the user profile. We first introduce a profile-counterfactual benchmark, in which the task is held fixed while changes in the user profile induce changes in the reference skill. We further construct paired counterfactual supervision and propose SkillFeed, a progressive retrieve-and-rerank framework that first establishes task--skill alignment and then learns profile-conditioned discrimination. By retrieving body-level evidence and reranking semantically similar but profile-conflicting candidates, SkillFeed identifies skills that satisfy both task requirements and user constraints. On SkillFeed-Bench, SkillFeed attains 75.1\% top-1 retrieval accuracy, a 23.1-point improvement over the corresponding pretrained routing baseline. Adding profile conditioning yields a 35.1-point gain on queries where user profile changes the reference skill. This contrast shows that user profiles are most consequential precisely when they change skill suitability. Our website is publicly available at http://www.aiskillfeed.com .

AI.tldr: SkillFeed introduces personalized skill routing for LLM agents by considering user profiles, not just task semantics, to select skills that satisfy both task requirements and user constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing skill routing methods only consider task semantic matching, which fails when users with incompatible constraints issue identical requests - a task-only router may select semantically plausible but unsuitable skills for the requesting user.
AI.method: Propose SkillFeed, a progressive retrieve-and-rerank framework that first establishes task-skill alignment, then learns profile-conditioned discrimination through retrieving body-level evidence and reranking semantically similar but profile-conflicting candidates.
AI.result: SkillFeed attains 75.1% top-1 retrieval accuracy on SkillFeed-Bench, a 23.1-point improvement over pretrained routing baseline, with a 35.1-point gain on queries where user profile changes the reference skill.
AI.conclusion: User profiles are critical for skill routing when they affect skill suitability, and personalized skill routing with profile conditioning significantly improves selection of appropriate skills for LLM agents.

title: Regime-Aware Portfolio Management via Retrieval-Augmented LLM-Guided Expert Switching
summary: Financial markets are inherently non-stationary, making the effectiveness of individual portfolio-management strategies highly dependent on changing market conditions. This work proposes a retrieval-augmented expert-switching framework that dynamically selects portfolio management experts based on their historical performance under similar market situations. A dual-stream variational autoencoder represents asset-level and market-wide information, while a retrieval-based knowledge base stores historical situations and expert performance. During inference, an instruction-tuned LLM reasons over the retrieved evidence to identify the most appropriate expert rather than directly generating portfolio actions. We further establish a monotonicity property showing that adding a locally superior expert cannot degrade the switching mechanism's performance. Experiments across cryptocurrency, stock, and foreign-exchange markets show that the proposed selector achieves the highest cumulative return and Sharpe ratio among the evaluated selection strategies in all three markets. In the stock market, for example, cumulative return increases from 26% for the best fixed expert to 34%, while the Sharpe ratio improves from 0.74 to 0.96. Ablation results confirm the importance of both retrieval and LLM reasoning, while experiments with different expert-pool sizes demonstrate the value of complementary expertise. Overall, the findings support retrieval-grounded expert switching as an effective approach to adaptive portfolio management in non-stationary financial environments.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented expert-switching framework dynamically selects portfolio management experts based on historical performance in similar market conditions, using a dual-stream variational autoencoder, retrieval knowledge base, and instruction-tuned LLM for reasoning.
AI.motivation: Financial markets are inherently non-stationary, making individual portfolio-management strategies ineffective when market conditions change. Current approaches lack adaptability to changing market environments.
AI.method: The framework uses a dual-stream variational autoencoder to represent asset-level and market-wide information. It maintains a retrieval-based knowledge base of historical situations and expert performance. During inference, an instruction-tuned LLM reasons over retrieved evidence to select the most appropriate expert rather than directly generating portfolio actions.
AI.result: The proposed selector achieves the highest cumulative return and Sharpe ratio among evaluated selection strategies across cryptocurrency, stock, and foreign-exchange markets. In the stock market, cumulative return increased from 26% (best fixed expert) to 34%, while Sharpe ratio improved from 0.74 to 0.96. The framework shows monotonicity property - adding a locally superior expert cannot degrade performance.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-grounded expert switching is an effective approach to adaptive portfolio management in non-stationary financial environments. Both retrieval and LLM reasoning are crucial, and complementary expertise in the expert pool adds value to the framework.

title: Physics-Guided Flow Matching for CT Image Reconstruction
summary: Deep generative models have recently emerged as powerful priors for solving ill-posed inverse problems in CT, with diffusion-based approaches achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction performance. However, diffusion models typically rely on stochastic sampling procedures, long inference trajectories, and carefully tuned noise schedules, which can limit computational efficiency and numerical stability, especially at high spatial resolutions. In this work, we investigate Flow Matching as an alternative generative prior for CT reconstruction. We train a high-resolution Rectified Flow Matching model on 256x256 chest images from the Mayo Clinic Low-Dose CT dataset. To mitigate overfitting and limited anatomical variability, we employ a two-stage training strategy consisting of an initial phase with strong, anatomically informed data augmentation, followed by a fine-tuning phase with reduced or no augmentation to refine structural fidelity. The resulting model is capable of generating high-quality and anatomically coherent CT-like images, serving as a strong learned prior. We then evaluate multiple reconstruction methods specifically designed for Flow Matching models, including Plug-and-Play Flow, FlowDPS, Flower, and Flow-Priors (ICTM), and compare them against state-of-the-art diffusion-based reconstruction algorithms such as DDRM, DPS, and DiffPIR. Experimental results across several CT inverse problem settings show that Flow Matching-based approaches consistently outperform diffusion-based methods in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and perceptual quality, while requiring fewer sampling steps. Finally, we publicly release the trained Flow Matching model and accompanying code to facilitate reproducibility and future research. Overall, this work demonstrates that Flow Matching provides a stable, efficient, and effective alternative to diffusion models for high-resolution CT image reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Flow Matching models outperform diffusion models for high-resolution CT reconstruction, achieving better metrics with fewer sampling steps and greater stability.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models have limitations for CT reconstruction: stochastic sampling procedures, long inference trajectories, and sensitivity to noise schedule tuning, which impact computational efficiency and numerical stability at high resolutions. Flow Matching offers a potentially better alternative.
AI.method: 1. Train a high-resolution Rectified Flow Matching model on 256x256 chest CT images from Mayo Clinic dataset. 2. Use two-stage training: initial phase with strong anatomically-informed data augmentation, then fine-tuning with reduced/no augmentation for structural fidelity. 3. Evaluate multiple Flow Matching reconstruction methods (Plug-and-Play Flow, FlowDPS, Flower, Flow-Priors/ICTM) and compare against diffusion-based methods (DDRM, DPS, DiffPIR).
AI.result: Flow Matching approaches consistently outperform diffusion-based methods across multiple CT inverse problem settings in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and perceptual quality, while requiring fewer sampling steps. The trained model generates high-quality, anatomically coherent CT-like images.
AI.conclusion: Flow Matching provides a stable, efficient, and effective alternative to diffusion models for high-resolution CT image reconstruction, with released code and model to facilitate reproducibility and future research.

title: Finding Where the Buck Stops: An Automated Failure Attribution-Based Reflection Framework for Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models have shown promise for complex tasks but suffer from high failure rates. Current self-reflection methods for MAS require all agents to reflect upon failure, overlooking a critical reality: failures typically stem from a specific agent leading the task astray, namely the decisive error agent, while others merely fulfill their regular duties. Forcing regular-behaving agents to reflect contaminates their memory with wrong insights. Hence, we propose DoCtOR (Diagnose-then-Correct PPO-enhanced Reflection), a novel reflection framework that enhances multi-agent collaboration. DoCtOR first identifies the decisive error step and decisive error agent through automated failure attribution, then employs counterfactual reasoning to generate a corrected decisive error step, and finally engages only the decisive error agent to produce targeted reflections. Experimental results show DoCtOR achieves 22%, 26%, and 27% improvements over initial success rates on HotPotQA, ChartQAPro, and Mind2Web datasets, outperforming Reflexion, Retroformer, and COPPER. We further establish the generalizability of our diagnose-then-correct paradigm and demonstrate that in low-resource settings, focusing reflection on reasoning steps after the decisive error step achieves comparable quality to reflecting on the complete failure trajectory.

AI.tldr: DoCtOR is a new framework that improves multi-agent system performance by first identifying which specific agent caused a failure (decisive error agent), then having only that agent reflect and correct its mistake, rather than forcing all agents to reflect unnecessarily.
AI.motivation: Current self-reflection methods for multi-agent systems force all agents to reflect on failures, but failures typically originate from just one decisive error agent. Forcing regular-behaving agents to reflect contaminates their memory with incorrect insights and is inefficient.
AI.method: DoCtOR uses a three-step process: 1) Automated failure attribution to identify the decisive error step and agent, 2) Counterfactual reasoning to generate a corrected decisive error step, and 3) Targeted reflection only by the decisive error agent.
AI.result: DoCtOR achieves 22%, 26%, and 27% improvements over initial success rates on HotPotQA, ChartQAPro, and Mind2Web datasets, outperforming existing methods like Reflexion, Retroformer, and COPPER.
AI.conclusion: The diagnose-then-correct paradigm is effective for multi-agent systems, and in low-resource settings, focusing reflection only on steps after the decisive error achieves similar quality to reflecting on the entire failure trajectory.

title: RECAST: Recent & Context-Aware Sampling for Test-Time Adaptation in Streaming Biosignals
summary: Streaming biosignals vary across subjects and drift over time, so population-trained models lose accuracy during long-term monitoring. Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables online personalization by updating the model on incoming samples. But in a stream, a basic question is left open: \emph{which samples should drive each update?} Using all buffered samples blurs the update with irrelevant segments. Using only the latest segment makes the update noisy and unstable. The most useful samples are recent, aligned with the current physiological state, and reliable enough to learn from. We propose \textbf{RECAST} (REcent \& Context-Aware Sampling for TTA), a lightweight sampling module for buffered TTA frameworks. RECAST builds each adaptation batch from three signals: temporal recency, contextual similarity, and predictive reliability. It changes only which samples are used, leaving the model and the training objective unchanged. On two blood-pressure datasets, RECAST improves estimation accuracy and trend tracking over baselines and ablations. The per-patient gains are statistically significant on both datasets, with broad improvement on the regular benchmark and gains concentrated on the hardest patients in the emergency-department setting. RECAST stays practical, adding only sub-second latency per segment on a single GPU and CPU core.

AI.tldr: RECAST proposes a lightweight sampling module for test-time adaptation that selects the most useful samples from streaming biosignals based on temporal recency, contextual similarity, and predictive reliability to improve personalization accuracy.
AI.motivation: Streaming biosignals vary across subjects and drift over time, causing population-trained models to lose accuracy during long-term monitoring. While test-time adaptation enables online personalization, existing approaches struggle with determining which samples from the stream should drive model updates - using all buffered samples introduces irrelevant segments, while using only the latest segment creates noisy and unstable updates.
AI.method: RECAST (REcent & Context-Aware Sampling for TTA) is a lightweight sampling module for buffered TTA frameworks. It builds adaptation batches from three signals: 1) temporal recency, 2) contextual similarity, and 3) predictive reliability. The approach changes only which samples are used for updates while leaving the model architecture and training objective unchanged.
AI.result: On two blood-pressure datasets, RECAST improves estimation accuracy and trend tracking over baseline methods and ablations. The per-patient gains are statistically significant on both datasets, showing broad improvement on regular benchmarks and concentrated gains on the hardest patients in emergency-department settings. The method adds only sub-second latency per segment on a single GPU and CPU core.
AI.conclusion: RECAST provides an effective, practical solution for sample selection in test-time adaptation of biosignal models, addressing the core challenge of which streaming samples should drive personalized updates. The three-signal approach (recency, context, reliability) enables stable, accurate adaptation with minimal computational overhead.

title: LoopArena: Benchmarking Models as Runtime Controllers for Loop Engineering
summary: Loop Engineering is emerging as a practice for organizing development work around coding agents. Instead of writing each prompt by hand, practitioners design loops that monitor progress, assign work, run checks, and decide what the agent should do next. Even with a capable coding agent, a loop may trust a stale progress note, skip needed verification, spend its budget in the wrong direction, or stop before the task is safe to submit. Yet the final outcome of one end-to-end run cannot tell whether success or failure reflects the loop's guidance or the coding agent's ability to carry out the task. We introduce LoopArena, a benchmark for evaluating how well one model can guide a separate coding agent through a long-running task. The model under evaluation is the \textbf{Controller}: after each coding round, it receives a structured summary of the run and instructs a separate, fixed coding agent, the \textbf{Worker}, on what to do or verify next, or decides whether to stop. LoopArena evaluates this ability in three complementary settings that differ in execution scope and cost. Type I scores next-step Loop Contract selection through execution-validated questions without running the Worker at evaluation time. Type II executes repeated control over a selected slice of a full task, while Type III evaluates the paired full task from its original state. On full tasks, the best observed Strict Success Rate is \textbf{24.69\%}, leaving substantial room for improvement in long-horizon loop control. Across Controllers, the paired reduction in estimated inference cost averages \textbf{64.4\%}, and Type II produces a similar ordering under the main Core criterion (Spearman's \(ρ=\textbf{0.9747}\)). We release the benchmark data and evaluation code at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/LoopArena .

AI.tldr: LoopArena is a benchmark for evaluating how well a model (Controller) can guide a separate coding agent (Worker) through long-running tasks, with three evaluation settings of increasing cost and complexity.
AI.motivation: As Loop Engineering emerges for organizing development work around coding agents, there's a need to evaluate loop control separately from agent capability. Current end-to-end runs can't distinguish whether success/failure comes from loop guidance or agent ability.
AI.method: Introduces LoopArena benchmark with three evaluation types: Type I (low-cost, execution-validated questions without running Worker), Type II (intermediate cost, repeated control over task slices), and Type III (full task execution from original state). Evaluates Controllers guiding fixed coding Workers.
AI.result: Best Strict Success Rate on full tasks is 24.69%, showing substantial room for improvement. Controllers reduce estimated inference cost by 64.4% on average, and Type II evaluation correlates strongly with main criterion (Spearman's ρ=0.9747).
AI.conclusion: LoopArena provides a needed benchmark for evaluating loop control in coding agent systems, demonstrates current limitations in long-horizon guidance, and shows promise for cost reduction while maintaining task progress ordering.

title: GRACE:Gradient-guided Coreset Selection for LLM Unlearning
comment: 20 pages, 16 tables, 5 figures, accepted to EMNLP Findings
summary: Machine Unlearning methods for Large Language Models typically assume pre-specified forget and retain sets. In realistic settings, however, requests may provide only a few examples of undesired behavior, requiring forget and retain sets to be inferred from heterogeneous corpora. We study this data-selection problem and propose GRACE , a gradient-guided coreset selection method that constructs both forget and retain sets for LLM unlearning. GRACE first computes a forget direction from seed examples that elicit the undesired behavior, then selects a compact forget coreset whose gradients approximate this direction using non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit. To preserve model utility, it selects retain examples after projecting out the forget direction and applying clustered orthogonal matching pursuit in the remaining gradient space. Across two target domains, two model families, and four unlearning algorithms, GRACE improves model utility while maintaining comparable forget quality, with particularly consistent gains over prior gradient-based selection methods.

AI.tldr: GRACE is a gradient-guided coreset selection method for LLM unlearning that constructs both forget and retain sets from heterogeneous corpora using only a few seed examples of undesired behavior, improving model utility while maintaining forget quality.
AI.motivation: Current machine unlearning methods for LLMs assume pre-specified forget and retain sets, but in realistic settings, requests often provide only a few examples of undesired behavior, requiring these sets to be inferred from heterogeneous corpora.
AI.method: GRACE computes a forget direction from seed examples, selects a compact forget coreset using non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit, then selects retain examples after projecting out the forget direction and applying clustered orthogonal matching pursuit in the remaining gradient space.
AI.result: Across two target domains, two model families, and four unlearning algorithms, GRACE improves model utility while maintaining comparable forget quality, showing consistent gains over prior gradient-based selection methods.
AI.conclusion: GRACE provides an effective solution for the data-selection problem in LLM unlearning, enabling practical unlearning with minimal supervision while preserving model performance.

title: Memristive-Friendly Hadamard Reservoir Computing: Structured, Multiplier-Free Recurrences at Scale
summary:
Reservoir Computing (RC) designs Recurrent Neural Networks around a fixed, i.e., untrained, recurrent layer, and is a natural candidate for neuromorphic hardware. Memristive-friendly reservoirs derive the neuron dynamics from memristive-device kinetics, but still rely on dense recurrent matrices, which are expensive to realize physically. In this paper, we replace the dense matrix with a structured orthogonal operator, built from sign diagonals, a permutation, and a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform. The operator is multiplier-free, requires $O(N)$ parameters and $O(N\log N)$ operations per step, and is never materialized as a matrix. We instantiate it in a standard and in a memristive-friendly Echo State Network, with one binary input connection per unit.
  Our mathematical analysis shows that exact orthogonality yields an echo state condition that is tight in the recurrent scaling, and a noise response that is predictable at design time. Moreover, the operator mixes the whole state in a single application. Experiments on twenty classification and seven regression benchmarks, at reservoir sizes up to $N = 8192$, show that the structured models match dense orthogonal reservoirs, and achieve better mean performance than the cycle reservoir by a margin that widens with size. Furthermore, we time the recurrent step on three hardware platforms, where it is up to $50\times$ faster than a dense product and $10^4\times$ smaller in memory. Finally, we ablate the operator and measure the response to noise, quantization, device mismatch and discrete faults.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a structured orthogonal operator to replace dense recurrent matrices in Reservoir Computing (RC), offering significant computational and memory efficiency while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional memristive-friendly reservoirs in RC still rely on dense recurrent matrices that are expensive to realize physically and computationally intensive, motivating the search for more efficient alternatives.
AI.method: The authors replace dense matrices with a structured orthogonal operator built from sign diagonals, a permutation, and a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform. This operator is multiplier-free, requires O(N) parameters and O(N log N) operations, and is never materialized as a matrix. It's instantiated in both standard and memristive-friendly Echo State Networks with one binary input connection per unit.
AI.result: Experiments on 20 classification and 7 regression benchmarks (up to N=8192 reservoir size) show the structured models match dense orthogonal reservoirs and outperform cycle reservoirs with widening margins at larger sizes. The recurrent step is up to 50x faster than dense products and 10^4x smaller in memory on three hardware platforms. Mathematical analysis shows tight echo state condition and predictable noise response.
AI.conclusion: The structured orthogonal operator provides an efficient alternative to dense matrices in Reservoir Computing, offering significant hardware advantages while maintaining or improving performance, making it particularly suitable for neuromorphic implementations.

title: Timing-Aware Repurchase Prediction for Web-Scale E-Commerce: Survival Models for Multi-Surface Grocery Recommendation
summary: Repurchase recommenders in e-commerce are commonly framed as a binary question asking "will this customer buy this item within W days", a formulation that requires a separately trained model for every horizon of interest. We replace this stack with survival models that predict time-to-repurchase directly, and evaluate them on millions of customers from a major grocery e-commerce platform across more than thirty ablation configurations. Our study makes three contributions. First, an empirical hazard analysis reveals a slightly decreasing marginal hazard (k ~ 0.9), differing from the common intuition that grocery items become more likely to be repurchased the longer since the last purchase (increasing hazard, k > 1). Log-Normal achieves the best marginal fit (R^2 = 0.998) and the best ranking, despite Weibull providing the best conditional residual fit, revealing an apparent discrepancy we analyze in detail. Second, a single Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) model replaces three per-horizon binary classifiers, matching or exceeding each at its own horizon while using roughly 3x fewer total trees. Feature importance reshuffles under the survival objective: channel-cadence and recency signals rise while aggregate frequency counts fall. Third, a 4-parameter parametric calibration maps raw survival CDFs to per-horizon probabilities with zero cross-horizon monotonicity violations. Calibration quality varies by an order of magnitude across the AFT family: Exponential AFT (Weibull k=1) achieves expected calibration error (ECE) ~1e-4, roughly 10x lower than Log-Normal, while ranking metrics agree within 0.3% relative. We adopt Exponential AFT for probability-consuming surfaces and Log-Normal for pure ranking, exposing a principled calibration-ranking trade-off within a single AFT family.

AI.tldr: Survival models (AFT framework) outperform binary classifiers for repurchase recommendation, with Log-Normal best for ranking and Exponential best for calibrated probabilities, reducing model count from 3 to 1.
AI.motivation: Current repurchase recommenders use separate binary classifiers for each time horizon, requiring multiple models. Survival models that predict time-to-repurchase directly could simplify the system and improve performance.
AI.method: Evaluated survival models (Accelerated Failure Time framework) on millions of customers from a major grocery e-commerce platform across 30+ ablation configurations. Compared Weibull, Log-Normal, and Exponential distributions, analyzing hazard rates, ranking metrics, and calibration quality.
AI.result: 1) Empirical hazard analysis shows slightly decreasing marginal hazard (k~0.9), contrary to intuition. 2) Single AFT model replaces 3 per-horizon binary classifiers, matching/exceeding each at its own horizon with 3x fewer trees. 3) Log-Normal best for ranking (R²=0.998), Exponential best for calibrated probabilities (ECE~1e-4, 10x better than Log-Normal).
AI.conclusion: Survival models effectively replace binary classifiers for repurchase recommendation, revealing principled calibration-ranking trade-offs within the AFT family. Different distributions suit different use cases: Log-Normal for ranking, Exponential for calibrated probability surfaces.

title: MAIL: Memory-driven, Adaptive, Incremental, and Literature-grounded Framework for Hypothesis Generation in Chemistry
summary:
The ever-expanding volume of the chemical literature offers unprecedented opportunities to generate novel and impactful hypotheses. However, the bottleneck lies in efficiently navigating this vast knowledge base to formulate high-quality, experimentally meaningful insights.
  While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for this task, existing methods often rely on static inspiration corpora, predefined heuristics, or laborious human-in-the-loop pipelines and decision-support frameworks that limit scalability and novelty. In this work, we propose an automated approach, a Memory-augmented, Adaptive, Incremental, and Literature-grounded (MAIL) framework for hypothesis generation in chemistry. Our MAIL method formulates hypothesis generation as a temporally grounded, memory-driven reasoning process, where hypotheses emerge from an evolving conceptual path that continuously accumulates and reinterprets prior knowledge. We evaluated the MAIL framework on a public TOMATO-Chem dataset and a newly curated and disseminated high-novelty nature/science challenge (HN-NS) dataset. Across both datasets, MAIL generates structurally coherent and mechanistically plausible hypotheses, achieves the highest MIOS and MPOS by more effectively recovering the central ideas and methodological elements of the historical target hypotheses, and obtains the highest overall expert-evaluation scores for scientific quality. These results demonstrate the potential of LLMs to autonomously explore chemical domains and generate hypotheses that are both innovative and chemically plausible.

AI.tldr: MAIL: A memory-augmented, adaptive, incremental framework for automated chemical hypothesis generation using LLMs that outperforms existing methods by creating more novel and chemically plausible hypotheses.
AI.motivation: The chemical literature is growing exponentially, offering opportunities for novel hypotheses, but navigating this vast knowledge base efficiently is a bottleneck. Existing LLM approaches use static corpora, predefined heuristics, or labor-intensive human-in-the-loop pipelines that limit scalability and novelty in hypothesis generation.
AI.method: Proposes MAIL (Memory-augmented, Adaptive, Incremental, and Literature-grounded) framework that treats hypothesis generation as a temporally grounded, memory-driven reasoning process. Hypotheses emerge from an evolving conceptual path that continuously accumulates and reinterprets prior knowledge through adaptive learning.
AI.result: Tested on TOMATO-Chem dataset and newly curated HN-NS dataset. MAIL generates structurally coherent and mechanistically plausible hypotheses, achieves highest MIOS and MPOS scores by better recovering central ideas and methodological elements of historical target hypotheses, and obtains highest expert-evaluation scores for scientific quality.
AI.conclusion: The MAIL framework demonstrates LLMs' potential to autonomously explore chemical domains and generate hypotheses that are both innovative and chemically plausible, offering an automated solution to the knowledge navigation bottleneck in chemistry research.

title: Real-Valued Hyperdimensional Sequence Representations with Hadamard Product Binding and Shift Equivariance
summary: Encoding temporal order is a fundamental requirement for sequence representations in Hyperdimensional Computing. Fractional Power Encoding provides similarity-preserving position vectors whose inner products approximate shift-invariant kernels, and it supports shift-equivariant transformations of encoded sequence representations. However, standard formulations of Fractional Power Encoding are primarily designed for binding operations such as circular convolution or complex-valued multiplication, which limits their compatibility with Hadamard product binding of real-valued vectors. This paper develops real-valued position encodings motivated by Random Fourier Features, aiming to retain the desirable properties of Fractional Power Encoding while supporting Hadamard-based operations. We propose three real-valued position-encoding variants: a real-valued baseline based on the inverse Fourier transform, and Sinusoid and Cosine-only representations derived from Random Fourier Features. Among them, the Sinusoid variant provides an explicit algebraic shift operator, allowing temporal shifts to be applied directly to the vector-encoded sequence representation without re-encoding the shifted sequence. Experiments on time-series classification datasets show that the proposed real-valued representations achieve performance comparable to standard Fractional Power Encoding while enabling computationally efficient Hadamard product binding. The Sinusoid variant offers the most favorable trade-off, combining efficient real-valued implementation with exact shift-equivariant transformations.

AI.tldr: Real-valued position encodings for Hyperdimensional Computing that retain Fractional Power Encoding's desirable properties while enabling efficient Hadamard product binding operations.
AI.motivation: Standard Fractional Power Encoding is designed for binding operations like circular convolution or complex multiplication, limiting its compatibility with real-valued Hadamard product binding, which is more computationally efficient.
AI.method: Developed three real-valued position encoding variants inspired by Random Fourier Features: 1) real-valued baseline using inverse Fourier transform, 2) Sinusoid representation, and 3) Cosine-only representation.
AI.result: The proposed real-valued representations achieve performance comparable to standard Fractional Power Encoding on time-series classification datasets while enabling computationally efficient Hadamard product binding. The Sinusoid variant offers the best trade-off with explicit algebraic shift operator.
AI.conclusion: Real-valued position encodings successfully bridge the gap between Fractional Power Encoding's desirable properties and Hadamard-based operations, with the Sinusoid variant providing efficient real-valued implementation with exact shift-equivariant transformations.

title: AGENT-O: A Semantic Agent Card Framework for Interoperable and Governed Healthcare AI Agents
summary: AGENT-O is a modular ontology framework that defines a semantic Agent Card for representing health-oriented AI agent systems and supports assessment of reporting completeness in scientific publications. AGENT-O was developed as an OWL 2/RDF ontology covering runtime, models, workflow, tools, clinical use, evaluation, provenance, governance, and reporting assessment. Evaluation included ontology inventory, OWL-RL reasoning, three SHACL suites, 12 SPARQL competency queries, three cases, and model-assisted reporting-completeness assessment of 279 papers across five dimensions. The ontology contained 1,962 RDF triples and 1,922 Protege axioms, with 252 active classes, 198 active object properties, and 51 datatype properties. All SHACL suites conformed on example graphs, all competency queries returned prespecified evidence, and all 279 papers were scored. Incomplete reporting was highest for runtime/architecture (84.6%), governance/safety (82.8%), and provenance/reproducibility (78.1%), compared with evaluation (25.8%) and benchmark-process alignment (29.8%). AGENT-O supported semantic Agent Card representation and reporting assessment while revealing an evaluation-specification gap: evaluation and benchmark procedures were reported more consistently than runtime architecture, governance, and reproducibility. AGENT-O provides a reusable ontology, semantic Agent Card profile, and reporting-completeness workflow for structured reporting and gap identification, but does not assess agent quality or deployment readiness.

AI.tldr: AGENT-O is a modular ontology framework for representing health AI agent systems and assessing reporting completeness in publications, revealing significant gaps in reporting of runtime architecture, governance, and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: There is a need for structured representation of health-oriented AI agent systems and assessment of reporting completeness in scientific publications, as current reporting practices may be inconsistent or incomplete, particularly for critical aspects like runtime architecture, governance, and reproducibility.
AI.method: Developed AGENT-O as an OWL 2/RDF ontology covering 9 key dimensions: runtime, models, workflow, tools, clinical use, evaluation, provenance, governance, and reporting assessment. Evaluation included ontology inventory, OWL-RL reasoning, three SHACL validation suites, 12 SPARQL competency queries, three case studies, and model-assisted reporting-completeness assessment of 279 papers across five dimensions.
AI.result: The ontology contained 1,962 RDF triples, 1,922 Protege axioms, with 252 active classes and 249 active properties. All SHACL suites conformed on example graphs, all competency queries returned prespecified evidence, and all 279 papers were successfully scored. Incomplete reporting was highest for runtime/architecture (84.6%), governance/safety (82.8%), and provenance/reproducibility (78.1%), while evaluation (25.8%) and benchmark-process alignment (29.8%) were reported more consistently.
AI.conclusion: AGENT-O provides a reusable ontology, semantic Agent Card profile, and reporting-completeness workflow for structured reporting and gap identification in health AI agent research. It reveals an "evaluation-specification gap" where evaluation procedures are reported more consistently than critical implementation details like runtime architecture, governance, and reproducibility. The framework does not assess agent quality or deployment readiness.

title: Propagating construction-time knowledge quality into medical question answering: A framework grounded in clinical guidelines
summary: Large language models have facilitated knowledge graph (KG) construction from clinical guidelines, but extracted triples vary in structural validity and evidential support. Meanwhile, graph-augmented question answering (QA) systems typically optimize query relevance during retrieval, with limited reuse of quality information produced during KG construction. This creates a disconnect between construction-time quality control and inference-time evidence use. We investigate whether construction-time triple quality can serve as a persistent signal for downstream evidence selection and presentation. We propose a quality-aware framework that models structural conformance (SchemaConf) and evidential support (EvidScore) as complementary dimensions and fuses them into a per-triple quality signal, Q(t). Rather than using quality solely for filtering, the framework retains Q(t) and derived quality tiers as graph attributes and propagates them into quality-weighted subgraph retrieval and tier-conditioned evidence prompting, while preserving passage-level provenance. Experiments on Chinese diabetes clinical guidelines show that the utility of the quality signal is distribution dependent. Under cross-version and cross-model shift, the fused Q(t) provides stronger triple-quality discrimination than either component alone (AUC 0.748 vs. 0.703 for EvidScore and 0.645 for SchemaConf). In guideline-grounded QA, propagating construction-time quality reduces required-knowledge omission from 16.3% to 5.3% and conflicting outputs from 16.3% to 2.7%, with an evidence-grounded precision of 81.6% and near-zero invalid citations. Blinded clinician ratings favor the full framework over no retrieval (4.68 vs. 4.21 on a five-point scale) and approach the oracle condition (4.80), while cross-generator experiments show consistent trends.

AI.tldr: Proposes a quality-aware framework that uses construction-time triple quality from knowledge graph building to improve downstream clinical QA by propagating quality signals into retrieval and evidence presentation.
AI.motivation: Current KG construction from clinical guidelines produces triples of varying quality, but downstream QA systems don't reuse this quality information, creating disconnect between construction-time quality control and inference-time evidence use.
AI.method: Proposes quality-aware framework that models structural conformance (SchemaConf) and evidential support (EvidScore) as complementary dimensions, fuses them into per-triple quality signal Q(t). Retains quality signals as graph attributes, propagates them into quality-weighted subgraph retrieval and tier-conditioned evidence prompting while preserving passage-level provenance.
AI.result: Experiments on Chinese diabetes clinical guidelines show: fused Q(t) provides stronger triple-quality discrimination (AUC 0.748 vs. 0.703 for EvidScore and 0.645 for SchemaConf); reduces required-knowledge omission from 16.3% to 5.3% and conflicting outputs from 16.3% to 2.7%; achieves 81.6% evidence-grounded precision with near-zero invalid citations; blinded clinician ratings favor full framework over no retrieval (4.68 vs. 4.21) and approach oracle condition (4.80).
AI.conclusion: Construction-time triple quality can effectively serve as persistent signal for downstream evidence selection and presentation in clinical QA systems, bridging the gap between KG construction quality control and inference-time evidence use.

title: EvoUndo: Recoverability-Constrained Self-Evolution for LLM Agent Harnesses
summary: LLM agents increasingly modify their own prompts, tools, middleware, resources, and execution harnesses at runtime. Such self-evolution can improve capability, but a successful mutation may leave persistent effects that cannot be safely reversed in states different from the one in which it was created. We introduce EvoUndo, a framework for representing, synthesizing, diagnosing, and independently verifying recoverability of model-generated self-modifications across counterfactual states. Across 600 unseen one-shot self-evolution tasks, we identify 197 capability-improving mutations that fail recoverability verification. Under the original recovery representation, conventional repair strategies recover 0/197 of these natural failures. Deterministic oracle analysis recovers 48/197 under the original recovery language L0, while the extended recovery calculus increases empirical oracle recovery to 191/197. A protocol-locked 2x2 grounding-by-expressivity intervention then separates two bottlenecks: exact state-address grounding increases successful recovery from 0/48 to 38/48 (79.2%) when the original language is sufficient, while extending the recovery language enables recovery on 142/143 (99.3%) failures in the oracle-defined S1 stratum. On the primary gpt-oss-120b backbone, adding exact-address diagnostics to the richer language reduces recovery to 133/143 (93.0%); a Qwen3.8-27B replication preserves the grounding and expressivity effects but not this negative interaction, indicating that the latter is model-dependent. These results indicate that reliable agent self-evolution requires co-designing verification, state grounding, witness semantics, and recovery-language expressivity rather than relying on iterative prompting alone.

AI.tldr: EvoUndo framework enables verification and recovery of LLM agent self-modifications across different system states, addressing critical recoverability failures that conventional methods cannot fix.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly modify their own runtime components, which can improve capability but creates persistent effects that cannot be safely reversed in states different from where the mutation was created, risking system instability.
AI.method: Introduces EvoUndo framework with: 1) representation and synthesis of model-generated self-modifications, 2) diagnostics for recoverability, 3) independent verification across counterfactual states, 4) extended recovery calculus language, and 5) protocol-locked grounding-by-expressivity interventions.
AI.result: On 600 self-evolution tasks, identified 197 capability-improving mutations that failed recoverability verification. Original methods recovered 0/197 failures; deterministic oracle recovered 48/197 with original language and 191/197 with extended calculus. Grounding interventions improved recovery from 0/48 to 38/48 when original language sufficed, while extended language enabled 142/143 (99.3%) recovery in oracle-defined stratum. Model-dependent effects observed with gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3.8-27B backbones.
AI.conclusion: Reliable agent self-evolution requires co-designing verification, state grounding, witness semantics, and recovery-language expressivity, rather than relying solely on iterative prompting.

title: MAP: A Benchmark on Multimodal Accessibility Planning for Real World Places
summary: We introduce MAP, the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal AI systems as assistants for users with accessibility requirements when planning visits to places in the real world. In our evaluation, systems are presented with requests to verify or recommend a point of interest meeting an accessibility requirement. MAP contains two novel assessments: Claim verification for accessibility planning assesses if information on places and stated accessibility features is supported and identifies places that satisfy requested accessibility features. Visual evidence retrieval for accessibility planning checks if a multimodal AI system can select visual evidence for the requested place and accessibility feature. Our methodology supports comparison of AI systems in a setting where place information and accessibility information can change over time by evaluating systems and refreshing ground truth data at scheduled times. The benchmark is based on automatic rating and human rating for a proportion of responses.

AI.tldr: MAP is the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal AI systems as accessibility assistants for real-world place visits, focusing on verifying accessibility claims and retrieving visual evidence.
AI.motivation: There's a need to evaluate how well multimodal AI systems can assist users with accessibility requirements when planning visits to real-world places, as current benchmarks don't adequately address accessibility planning needs.
AI.method: The benchmark presents systems with requests to verify or recommend points of interest meeting accessibility requirements. It includes two novel assessments: claim verification for accessibility planning (checking if place accessibility information is supported) and visual evidence retrieval for accessibility planning (selecting visual evidence for requested features). The methodology supports temporal comparisons by evaluating systems and refreshing ground truth data at scheduled times.
AI.result: The paper introduces the MAP benchmark framework that enables systematic evaluation of multimodal AI systems for accessibility planning tasks, incorporating both automatic and human rating of system responses.
AI.conclusion: MAP provides a comprehensive benchmark for assessing multimodal AI systems as accessibility assistants, addressing the unique challenges of accessibility planning with evaluations that account for changing information over time.

title: RetailAgent: Structured Adverse Timing in Self-Conditioned Multimodal LLM Trading Agents
summary: In financial markets, a sequential policy that reacts systematically to price movements may become predictable to other market participants. This paper studies whether large language model (LLM) agents exhibit such directional structure through RetailAgent, an experimental framework in which an LLM observes anonymized intraday equity price histories and permitted state, then repeatedly chooses long (hold the stock) or flat (stay out) before the subsequent interval return is revealed. We compare returns during long and flat intervals along the same stock's intraday path after removing the overall fraction of long decisions. This exposure-matched measure reveals persistent negative timing across modality, horizon, state, and model family. Shuffling saved action sequences substantially attenuates the effect, showing that alignment between actions and subsequent returns drives the negative score. Feeding self-authored memories into decisions further increases policy persistence, while timing becomes more negative among stock-days on which the agent uses both actions. These results reveal stable, recoverable directional structure in sequential LLM financial decisions and a behavioral signal for studying how another participant could respond to a predictable policy.

AI.tldr: LLM agents in financial decision-making show systematic negative timing patterns - their decisions to hold stocks tend to precede negative returns, creating predictable directional structure that could be exploited by other market participants.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether LLM agents exhibit predictable sequential patterns in financial decision-making, as such predictability could make them vulnerable to exploitation by other market participants who could detect and respond to their systematic timing tendencies.
AI.method: The researchers developed RetailAgent, an experimental framework where LLMs observe anonymized intraday equity price histories and choose between "long" (hold) and "flat" (stay out) positions. They compare returns during long vs. flat intervals after controlling for overall long frequency, and use shuffling experiments to test whether the alignment between actions and subsequent returns drives the observed patterns.
AI.result: LLM agents consistently show persistent negative timing across different conditions - their long decisions tend to precede negative returns. This effect is attenuated when action sequences are shuffled, confirming that the alignment between actions and subsequent returns drives the negative timing. The effect strengthens when agents use self-authored memories and is more pronounced on stock-days where both actions are used.
AI.conclusion: LLM financial decision-making exhibits stable, recoverable directional structure with systematic negative timing patterns. This reveals a behavioral signal that other market participants could potentially detect and exploit, providing a framework for studying how predictable policies in financial markets could be targeted.

title: VERA-8B: Evidence-Grounded Audit Risk Reasoning from SEC Filings
summary: Across audit applications, judgments must be supported by reasonable evidence. However, standard financial language models prioritize fluency over evidence. They are built for general financial reasoning and may produce plausible but ambiguous answers, creating a grounding gap that makes them unsuitable for audit work. We address this gap with VERA-8B, a new end-to-end audit reasoning system that identifies audit risks before enforcement actions occur. Constructing such a model raises several challenges, as no prior machine learning work targets pre-enforcement audit prediction. To our knowledge, we are the first to unify SFT and GRPO for evidence-grounded audit reasoning under one evidence standard, achieving performance that surpasses all evaluated baselines. Because auditing cannot tolerate unsupported claims, we introduce abstention and uncertainty qualification to defer uncertain or evidence-incomplete cases. Finally, we design an AuditBridge to ground model reasoning for practical audit work. It transforms raw filings into verified records and then into reviewer-ready reports, bridging finance and computation with broad generality. Together, these components produce auditable, review-ready outputs suitable for practical audit work.

AI.tldr: VERA-8B is a new audit reasoning system that bridges the grounding gap in financial language models by providing evidence-supported judgments for pre-enforcement audit risk prediction.
AI.motivation: Standard financial language models prioritize fluency over evidence, creating a grounding gap that makes them unsuitable for audit work. They produce plausible but ambiguous answers without proper evidence support, which is unacceptable in auditing where judgments must be supported by reasonable evidence.
AI.method: The paper introduces VERA-8B as an end-to-end audit reasoning system that: 1) unifies SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) and GRPO for evidence-grounded audit reasoning under one evidence standard, 2) introduces abstention and uncertainty qualification to defer uncertain or evidence-incomplete cases, and 3) designs an AuditBridge that transforms raw filings into verified records and then into reviewer-ready reports.
AI.result: VERA-8B achieves performance that surpasses all evaluated baselines and produces auditable, review-ready outputs suitable for practical audit work. The system bridges finance and computation with broad generality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system addresses the grounding gap in audit applications by providing evidence-supported reasoning, making language models suitable for practical audit work through a combination of unified training approaches, uncertainty handling, and practical workflow integration via AuditBridge.

title: Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards: Symbolic Backpropagation for Post-Training LLMs
summary: Post training a language model to reason means updating its weights. Supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning both place the acquired capability inside the model where it cannot be inspected cannot be checked step by step and cannot be moved to another model. We argue that for tasks whose intermediate steps admit verification, reasoning is better placed outside the base models weights as an explicit program composed from deterministic and neural primitives. We introduce PLVR (Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards): a post training method that learns such programs directly from input-output examples. Its mechanism is symbolic backpropagation: each program layer carries a typed ontology a loss is computed at the output against ground truth and required input ontologies are propagated backward by type inference over primitive signatures: an analogue of the chain rule in which credit assignment is a derivation rather than an estimate. Where RLVR verifies a terminal outcome, PLVRs reward is a per step contract verdict dense over program structure. On LiveCodeBench v6 and Tau2Bench, 30B base models with PLVR outperform RL at matched budget by 27.8 points on average and frontier models an order of magnitude larger by 13.6 points. A single primitive library serves two benchmarks, so the marginal cost of a new task is 100 examples of program search and no new finetuning data. Replacing the loss guided search with uniform sampling over the same type admissible space at equal budget collapses the median program from 65.6 to 17.5, identifying the backward pass rather than the type system as the source of the advantage. We release the symbolic backpropagation library and a conformance checker so the method can be applied to primitive libraries other than our own.

AI.tldr: PLVR introduces symbolic backpropagation for learning verifiable reasoning programs from input-output examples, outperforming RL approaches on code generation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional post-training methods (supervised finetuning and RL) embed reasoning capabilities within model weights, making them un-inspectable, uncheckable step-by-step, and not transferable between models. For tasks with verifiable intermediate steps, reasoning should be placed outside model weights as explicit programs.
AI.method: PLVR (Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards) uses symbolic backpropagation: programs are composed from deterministic and neural primitives, each layer has a typed ontology, loss is computed at output, and required input ontologies are propagated backward by type inference over primitive signatures - analogous to chain rule but with credit assignment as derivation rather than estimate.
AI.result: On LiveCodeBench v6 and Tau2Bench, 30B base models with PLVR outperform RL at matched budget by 27.8 points on average, and outperform frontier models an order of magnitude larger by 13.6 points. A single primitive library serves two benchmarks with only 100 examples needed per new task. The backward pass (not type system) is key: replacing loss-guided search with uniform sampling collapses median program length from 65.6 to 17.5.
AI.conclusion: PLVR demonstrates that separating reasoning capabilities from model weights into verifiable programs enables better performance, inspectability, and transferability for tasks with verifiable intermediate steps, with symbolic backpropagation providing efficient credit assignment through type inference.

title: Learning to Use Tools: Reinforcement Learning for Tool-Integrated Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Current large language models (LLMs) increasingly benefit from external tool integration, especially for tasks requiring reliable computation and verification. Motivated by this, we study calculator tool calling for improving mathematical reasoning on the Countdown task. We first analyze reasoning failures and find that calculation errors account for a substantial portion of incorrect responses.
