We then construct supervised fine-tuning datasets to teach the model useful tool-use patterns and how to interpret returned outputs. Building on this tool-formatted policy, we apply several on-policy reinforcement learning methods, including RLOO, RLOO++, GRPO, and DAPO, using automatically verifiable final-answer rewards. To enable a more reliable evaluation, we construct a fresh 1,024-problem held-out Countdown benchmark with no exact overlap with the training data. Our results show that calculator tool integration consistently improves both SFT and RL baselines, yielding roughly 10 percentage-point gains across pass@k. Among the RL methods, Tool-DAPO achieves the strongest performance, improving pass@1 from 35.8% for Tool-SFT to 66.0%. Further analysis shows that RL encourages more effective tool use even when only final-answer rewards are provided. These findings suggest that tool integration reduces arithmetic and verification errors, while RL increases the probability of correct reasoning traces.

AI.tldr: TLDR: Integrating calculator tools with reinforcement learning significantly improves mathematical reasoning on the Countdown task, with Tool-DAPO achieving 66.0% pass@1 from 35.8% baseline.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs benefit from external tool integration for tasks requiring reliable computation and verification. The study addresses calculation errors as a substantial portion of incorrect responses in mathematical reasoning tasks.
AI.method: 1) Analyzed reasoning failures to identify calculation errors; 2) Constructed supervised fine-tuning datasets to teach tool-use patterns; 3) Applied multiple on-policy reinforcement learning methods (RLOO, RLOO++, GRPO, DAPO) with automatically verifiable final-answer rewards; 4) Built a fresh 1,024-problem Countdown benchmark for reliable evaluation.
AI.result: Calculator tool integration consistently improves both SFT and RL baselines (~10 percentage-point gains across pass@k). Tool-DAPO achieves strongest performance: 66.0% pass@1 vs 35.8% for Tool-SFT. RL encourages more effective tool use even with only final-answer rewards.
AI.conclusion: Tool integration reduces arithmetic and verification errors, while RL increases probability of correct reasoning traces. The approach demonstrates significant improvements in mathematical reasoning through strategic tool use and reinforcement learning optimization.

title: COVER: Identifiable Evaluation of Coalition Routing
summary: When a multi-agent system changes its team, it also changes the messages and final answer it produces, so an end-to-end accuracy gap does not by itself identify a routing effect. We introduce method, an evaluation contract that fixes a public information boundary, downstream stack G, and finite legal team family before outcomes are generated. Complete coverage identifies exact finite-benchmark oracle regret conditional on that stack. For any finite collection of frozen policies, executing the union of their distinct selected teams is the minimal assumption-free support for every pairwise policy contrast, though not for absolute oracle regret. Two controlled tables with source-ID-disjoint splits test the instrument. On MuSiQue-12, a pre-specified privileged positive control improves regret from 0.532 to 0.402; a later public-interface control reaches 0.424 versus 0.554 but is retrospective. On HotpotQA-4, a pre-specified public direct scorer improves regret from 0.313 to 0.110. In fixed-stack Llama execution, verified route regret improves by 0.190, while the raw-answer gain is 0.010 with an interval crossing zero. A five-family ToolSandbox variant-shift validation exhaustively evaluates 16 declared teams on 14 untouched task variants (224/224 valid rows): the declared-family oracle reaches 0.768 safe-evidence completion, while the prospectively frozen router gets 0.637 (regret 0.131), failing the predeclared 0.10 criterion. A later retrospective comparator reaches 0.655, matching all-workers with 4.57 versus 5.00 workers on average. Thus COVER exposes selection headroom without manufacturing a routing win. A crossed-stack diagnostic shows absolute scores depend on G but finds no detectable router-by-finalizer interaction. COVER is an auditable measurement methodology, not a claim of stack-invariant or universal agent-routing superiority.

AI.tldr: COVER is an evaluation framework that measures routing effects in multi-agent systems by fixing information boundaries and execution stacks, enabling precise regret measurement without manufacturing artificial routing wins.
AI.motivation: When multi-agent systems change teams, it's difficult to isolate routing effects from overall accuracy changes because different teams produce different messages and answers, making end-to-end accuracy insufficient for identifying pure routing impact.
AI.method: COVER introduces an evaluation contract that fixes public information boundaries, downstream stack G, and legal team family before outcomes. It uses complete coverage to identify exact finite-benchmark oracle regret. For any frozen policies, executing the union of their distinct selected teams provides assumption-free support for pairwise contrasts.
AI.result: On MuSiQue-12, a pre-specified control improved regret from 0.532 to 0.402. On HotpotQA-4, regret improved from 0.313 to 0.110. In fixed-stack Llama execution, verified route regret improved by 0.190 while raw-answer gain was minimal (0.010). ToolSandbox validation showed declared-family oracle reached 0.768 completion vs router's 0.637 (regret 0.131).
AI.conclusion: COVER exposes selection headroom without artificially claiming routing superiority. It's an auditable measurement methodology rather than a claim of stack-invariant or universal agent-routing superiority, providing controlled evaluation of routing effects while acknowledging that absolute scores depend on the execution stack G.

title: AcrossVAM1.0: Particle World Modeling for Text-Assisted Robot Video Prediction
summary: Predicting robot videos requires both precise motion reasoning and preservation of high-frequency appearance, yet monolithic pixel models entangle these objectives and often conceal their progress behind a strong last-frame baseline. We present AcrossVAM1.0, a lightweight, text-assisted video action model that factorizes future prediction into object-centric motion and dense appearance. A frozen SAM3-DLP codec decomposes four context frames into semantic particles for the robot, arm, and gripper, together with a background latent. A 0.28M-parameter spatio-temporal Transformer aligns particle identities, rolls their states forward, and is modulated by a frozen OpenCLIP instruction embedding through FiLM. A causal dual-stream decoder combines particle-rendered motion with appearance encoded exclusively from the last observed frame; a residual refiner and learned delivery mask produce five future frames without access to future appearance. On our VRS benchmark constructed from diverse real-robot trajectories, particle dynamics reduce trajectory error by 21.0\% over persistence. Across three delivery-mask seeds, AcrossVAM1.0 improves future-frame PSNR/SSIM from 19.97/0.796 to 20.573/0.8004, while raw particle generation improves motion-region PSNR from 11.89 to 13.23. The delivered model does not yet beat persistence in LPIPS, and correct-versus- shuffled language changes trajectory error by only 2.8--3.1%. We report these limitations alongside oracle, negative-control, multi-seed, and per-robot analyses. The results show that explicit particle dynamics are a promising low-dimensional interface for robot video prediction, while robust language grounding and appearance delivery remain the principal open challenges.

AI.tldr: AcrossVAM1.0: A lightweight video prediction model that factorizes robot video forecasting into object-centric particle motion and appearance preservation using frozen vision models and a small spatio-temporal transformer.
AI.motivation: Current monolithic pixel models for robot video prediction entangle motion reasoning and appearance preservation, making it hard to assess progress and often relying heavily on last-frame baselines. There's a need for factorization approaches that separate these objectives.
AI.method: The model decomposes video prediction into: 1) Using frozen SAM3-DLP codec to extract semantic particles (robot, arm, gripper) and background latents from context frames, 2) A 0.28M-parameter spatio-temporal Transformer that aligns particle identities and rolls states forward, modulated by frozen OpenCLIP embeddings via FiLM, 3) A causal dual-stream decoder combining particle-rendered motion with appearance from the last observed frame, using residual refinement and learned delivery masks.
AI.result: On VRS benchmark: Particle dynamics reduce trajectory error by 21.0% over persistence baseline. Across three seeds, improves future-frame PSNR/SSIM from 19.97/0.796 to 20.573/0.8004. Raw particle generation improves motion-region PSNR from 11.89 to 13.23. However, the model doesn't beat persistence in LPIPS, and language guidance has limited impact (2.8-3.1% trajectory error change).
AI.conclusion: Explicit particle dynamics show promise as a low-dimensional interface for robot video prediction, but robust language grounding and appearance delivery remain significant challenges. The factorization approach enables clearer analysis of motion vs. appearance components.

title: Training Communication-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Models with Layer Re-Configuration
summary: When training Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models with expert parallelism, all-to-all token dispatch and combine collectives can consume a substantial fraction of end-to-end training time. In this work, we study communication-efficient MoE models (CE-MoE), in which we adopt a heterogeneous layer pattern that decouples token-mixing and channel-mixing depth. Compared to conventional models which interleave MoE layers after each token-mixing layer (e.g., attention, Mamba-2), CE-MoE models concentrate expert capacity in a select few routed MoE layers, while maintaining depth by adding additional token-mixing and dense-FFN layers. Across a scaling ladder from 2B to 31.5B total parameters, under matched total and activated parameters, CE-MoE models consistently reduce training cost while matching validation loss and downstream benchmarks with full-MoE baselines. At the 31.5B scale, CE-MoE uses 33.3\% fewer GPU-hours while improving average downstream score and inference throughput.

AI.tldr: CE-MoE models reduce training communication overhead by decoupling token-mixing and channel-mixing depth, concentrating experts in fewer layers while maintaining model capacity through additional token-mixing layers.
AI.motivation: The communication overhead from all-to-all token dispatch and combine collectives in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models with expert parallelism consumes substantial training time, creating a bottleneck for efficient MoE training.
AI.method: CE-MoE adopts a heterogeneous layer pattern that decouples token-mixing and channel-mixing depth. Instead of interleaving MoE layers after each token-mixing layer, it concentrates expert capacity in select few routed MoE layers while maintaining depth by adding additional token-mixing and dense-FFN layers.
AI.result: Across scaling from 2B to 31.5B parameters, CE-MoE models reduce training cost while matching validation loss and downstream benchmarks with full-MoE baselines. At 31.5B scale, CE-MoE uses 33.3% fewer GPU-hours while improving average downstream score and inference throughput.
AI.conclusion: CE-MoE provides an effective architecture for reducing communication overhead in MoE models without sacrificing performance, offering a more efficient alternative to conventional interleaved MoE designs while maintaining competitive results.

title: When Robots Mishear Us: Mapping the Safety Risks of Voice-Controlled Embodied AI
summary: We investigate whether automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors in user input can lead to unsafe outputs from Embodied AI (EAI) models. We find that ASR errors can lead to harmful instructions being accepted and executed by EAI models, thereby reducing safety. We simulate ASR errors and combine them with existing safety benchmarks (SafeAgentBench and POEX) to evaluate how different errors affect embodied AI safety. We find that some of them preserve semantic structure but increase harmful ambiguity, while others weaken the model refusal behaviour and allow unsafe plans to be generated and executed. We show that in some cases automatic correction of ASR errors can reduce the risk, but this is not always effective. Overall, we show that ASR errors lead to significant safety risks for embodied AI.

AI.tldr: ASR errors in user input to Embodied AI models can cause harmful instructions to be accepted and executed, creating significant safety risks.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors in user inputs can lead to unsafe outputs from Embodied AI (EAI) models, addressing a critical safety concern in voice-controlled AI systems.
AI.method: Researchers simulate ASR errors and combine them with existing safety benchmarks (SafeAgentBench and POEX) to evaluate how different types of ASR errors affect embodied AI safety. They also test automatic correction of ASR errors as a mitigation strategy.
AI.result: The study finds that ASR errors can indeed lead to harmful instructions being accepted and executed by EAI models. Some errors preserve semantic structure but increase harmful ambiguity, while others weaken model refusal behavior and allow unsafe plans to be generated and executed. Automatic error correction can reduce risk in some cases but is not consistently effective.
AI.conclusion: ASR errors present significant safety risks for embodied AI systems, creating vulnerabilities where harmful instructions may bypass safety mechanisms. While automatic error correction shows some promise, it's not a complete solution, highlighting the need for more robust safety measures in voice-controlled AI systems.

title: InstructMesh: Selective Refinement of Generative 3D Models for Fabrication
summary: Recent advances in generative AI allow users to create 3D models from text or images. However, these models prioritize visual plausibility over geometric accuracy, often generating results with flaws that compromise their intended use post-fabrication. We present InstructMesh, an interactive post-generation refinement tool that enables selective repair of generative 3D models through region selection and targeted operations, such as opening or sealing voids, or adjusting local thickness. Users can invoke edit operations via natural language prompts or slider controls. By operating directly on the intermediate latent representation, InstructMesh allows users to apply robust geometric corrections without requiring expert modeling skills. To inform our design, we first analyze common fabrication-related failure modes in outputs from state-of-the-art generative tools. We then conduct two user studies, demonstrating that novices can identify and perform fabrication-relevant repairs on generative outputs using InstructMesh, and revealing user preference for hybrid interfaces that combine slider controls with natural language input.

AI.tldr: InstructMesh is an interactive refinement tool that enables selective repair of generative 3D models for fabrication purposes, allowing users to fix geometric flaws through region selection and targeted operations via natural language or slider controls.
AI.motivation: Current generative AI models for 3D creation prioritize visual plausibility over geometric accuracy, resulting in models with flaws that compromise their suitability for physical fabrication. There's a need for tools that can repair these fabrication-related issues without requiring expert modeling skills.
AI.method: 1) First analyze common fabrication failure modes in state-of-the-art generative tools. 2) Develop InstructMesh as a post-generation refinement tool that operates directly on the intermediate latent representation. 3) Users select regions and apply targeted operations (opening/sealing voids, adjusting thickness) via natural language prompts or slider controls. 4) Conduct two user studies to evaluate effectiveness and user preferences.
AI.result: The user studies demonstrated that: 1) Novices can successfully identify and perform fabrication-relevant repairs on generative 3D models using InstructMesh. 2) Users prefer hybrid interfaces that combine slider controls with natural language input rather than relying on either method alone.
AI.conclusion: InstructMesh provides an effective solution for bridging the gap between visually plausible generative 3D models and fabrication-ready models, enabling non-experts to make robust geometric corrections through an intuitive interface that combines natural language and direct manipulation controls.
